lesson.why: Register updates by auto-increment and auto-decrement drive stack and array questions, and GATE asks for the register value or the address accessed after a sequence of them.
lesson.intro: Auto-increment and auto-decrement are register indirect addressing with a built-in update of the register. With auto-increment, written (R)+, the machine uses the register as the address and afterwards adds the size of the item to it. With auto-decrement, written -(R), the machine first subtracts the size and then uses the new value as the address. The step always matches the data size: 4 for a 4-byte word on a byte-addressable machine.

definitions.meaning: Use the register as the address first, then add the item size to it.
Subtract the item size from the register first, then use it as the address.

principle.text: Post-increment uses the old register value as the address; pre-decrement uses the new one. In both the register changes by the size $s$ of the item.
principle.tex: (R)+:\ \text{EA} = R,\ R \leftarrow R + s \qquad -(R):\ R \leftarrow R - s,\ \text{EA} = R

lesson.limits: The step equals the item size only when memory is byte-addressable and the access is one item wide; on a word-addressable machine the step is 1. The register change is a side effect, so a later instruction sees the updated register. The pair -(R) for push and (R)+ for pop assumes a stack growing toward lower addresses.

example.problem: R1 holds 2000 and words are 4 bytes. Three instructions run in order: LOAD R2, (R1)+ then LOAD R3, (R1)+ then LOAD R4, -(R1). At which address does each load read, and what does R1 hold at the end?
steps: The first load reads address 2000, then R1 becomes 2004.
The second load reads address 2004, then R1 becomes 2008.
The third subtracts first: R1 becomes 2004, and the load reads address 2004.
example.result: The loads read addresses 2000, 2004 and 2004, and R1 ends at 2004.

misconceptions: Using the new value as the address for (R)+. It is the old value; the increment comes afterwards.
Using the old value for -(R). The decrement comes first, so the address is the lowered value.
Adding 1 to the register on a byte-addressable machine with 4-byte words; the step is the item size, 4.

recall.q: In (R)+, is the address taken before or after the register update?
recall.a: Before: the old register value is the address and the update follows.

recall.q: What is the step for a 4-byte word on a byte-addressable machine?
recall.a: 4, the item size in bytes.

recall.q: Which pair of modes builds a downward-growing stack?
recall.a: Pre-decrement to push and post-increment to pop.

practice.stem: A stack grows toward lower addresses and SP starts at 1000. A push is STORE R, -(SP) and a pop is LOAD R, (SP)+. Words are 4 bytes. After three pushes and one pop, what does SP hold?
practice.explanation: Three pushes lower SP by $3 \times 4 = 12$ to 988. The pop reads address 988 and then raises SP by 4 to 992. Ignoring the pop gives 988, and adding 1 per step instead of 4 gives a value near 1000, which tempts if the word size is forgotten.

lesson.summary: Post-increment uses then adds, pre-decrement subtracts then uses, and the step is the item size; together they give one-instruction push and pop.

topics.title: PC-relative addressing and branch range
points: PC-relative: EA = PC + offset, where PC already points past the current instruction once it has been fetched. A 4-byte branch at address 1000 with an offset of −12 words targets 1004 + 4 × (−12) = 956.
A signed n-bit offset reaches −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1 units from the updated PC: an 8-bit offset gives −128 to +127.
When the offset counts words, multiply by the word size: a 16-bit word offset on 4-byte instructions spans about ±128 KB.
Targets are distances, not absolute addresses, so code using them is position independent and runs unchanged wherever the loader places it.
Branches outside the offset range need a register-indirect or absolute jump, which costs an extra instruction to build the full address.

lesson.why: Branch-target questions are short calculations, and almost every wrong answer comes from measuring from the wrong place.
lesson.intro: A branch instruction needs to say where to go. Instead of a full address it can store a distance from the program counter. By the time the branch runs, the program counter already points at the next instruction, so the distance is measured from there. A negative distance jumps backwards, which is how loops are written.

definitions.meaning: The register that holds the address of the next instruction to run.
Code that runs correctly wherever it is loaded, because it uses distances and not absolute addresses.

principle.text: The target is the address of the next instruction plus the signed offset. If the offset counts words, multiply it by the word size first.

lesson.limits: Some machines measure from the branch itself, and the question states the rule, so read it before you compute. An $n$-bit signed offset reaches only $-2^{n-1}$ to $2^{n-1} - 1$ units; a farther target needs a register or absolute jump.

example.problem: Instructions are 4 bytes long and the offset is measured in bytes from the next instruction. A branch at address 2000 must jump to address 1960. What offset is stored?
steps: The next instruction is at $2000 + 4 = 2004$.
The offset is the target minus that address: $1960 - 2004 = -44$ bytes.
If the machine counts words instead, the stored value is $-44 / 4 = -11$.
example.result: The byte offset is -44, which is -11 in words.

misconceptions: Measuring from the branch instruction itself gives a result that is 4 bytes off, so a backward loop appears to need -40 instead of -44.
Forgetting that a word offset must be multiplied by the instruction size before it is added to the address.

recall.q: From which address is a PC-relative offset measured?
recall.a: From the address of the next instruction, because the program counter has already moved past the branch.

recall.q: Why is PC-relative code position independent?
recall.a: The target is a distance from the branch, and a distance stays the same wherever the program is loaded.

recall.q: What range does an n-bit signed offset reach?
recall.a: $-2^{n-1}$ to $2^{n-1} - 1$ units from the updated program counter.

practice.stem: Each instruction is 4 bytes. A branch at address 3000 jumps to address 3100, and its offset is counted in instructions from the next instruction. What offset is stored?
practice.explanation: The next instruction is at 3004, so the distance is 3100 - 3004 = 96 bytes, which is 96 / 4 = 24 instructions. Measuring from the branch at 3000 gives 100 bytes or 25 instructions, which tempts because it forgets the program counter has advanced.

lesson.summary: The branch target is the next instruction's address plus the signed offset in its unit; measuring from the branch itself is the usual error.

topics.title: Choosing a mode: constants, pointers, arrays, relocation
points: Constants use immediate mode; global variables at fixed addresses use direct mode.
Pointers use memory indirect or register indirect: the operand's address is itself data held in memory or in a register.
Arrays use indexed or base + index mode; sequential traversal uses auto-increment; stack push and pop use auto-decrement and auto-increment.

Run-time relocation needs modes whose EA does not embed an absolute address: based (change the base register when the program moves) and PC-relative (distances do not change). Absolute and memory-indirect fields hold fixed addresses and break when the program moves.
Local variables and parameters use base + offset from the frame pointer; procedure-relative branches use PC-relative.

lesson.why: Questions of this type give a data shape or a requirement and ask for the right mode, so you need a ready mapping from need to mode.
lesson.intro: Each addressing mode fits one shape of data. A constant that never changes can sit inside the instruction. A variable at a fixed place has its address in the instruction. A pointer holds the address of another value, so one extra step is needed. An array or a struct is reached from a start plus a distance. A program that may be moved to another place in memory must avoid addresses that are written into the instruction.

principle.text: Match the mode to what the operand is: a constant needs immediate, a global needs direct, a pointer needs indirect, an array element needs index or base plus index, a record field needs base plus offset, and a movable program needs base or PC-relative.

lesson.limits: Several modes can reach the same data, so the question usually asks for the one that is most natural or efficient. Which modes a machine supports also varies; on a machine without one, the compiler builds it from simpler steps.

example.problem: Choose a mode for each: (a) the constant 10 in n = n + 10; (b) the value that pointer q points to; (c) a local variable at offset 8 in the stack frame; (d) a branch inside code that the loader may place anywhere.
steps: The constant 10 never changes, so it is stored in the instruction: immediate.
The pointer holds an address, so the operand is reached through it: register indirect or memory indirect.
The frame pointer holds the start of the frame and 8 is the fixed distance: base plus offset.
A branch should not hold an absolute address if the code may move, so it stores a distance: PC-relative.
example.result: (a) immediate, (b) indirect, (c) base plus offset, (d) PC-relative.

misconceptions: Choosing immediate for a variable: immediate holds a value written at assembly time, so it cannot follow a variable that changes.
Assuming based addressing breaks on relocation; it survives, because only the base register changes when the program moves.

recall.q: Which mode suits a pointer?
recall.a: Indirect, because the operand is reached through an address that is itself stored in a register or in memory.

recall.q: Which modes survive run-time relocation?
recall.a: Based and PC-relative, because the address is built from a register or a distance rather than fixed in the instruction.

recall.q: Why does direct addressing break when a program moves?
recall.a: The instruction holds an absolute address, which stays the same while the data has moved.

practice.stem: A loader moves a program to a new place in memory after it was assembled. Which instruction stops working correctly unless it is patched?
options: A load of a local variable using the frame pointer plus an offset
A load of a global variable with its absolute address in the instruction
An add that uses an immediate constant
practice.explanation: The absolute address is fixed in the instruction while the global has moved, so it must be patched. The PC-relative branch keeps its distance, the frame-pointer access follows the register, and an immediate constant does not depend on any address. The frame-pointer option tempts because it uses a register, but the register is updated at run time.

lesson.summary: Immediate for constants, direct for fixed variables, indirect for pointers, index or base plus offset for arrays and records, and base or PC-relative when code must be relocatable.

topics.title: Counting memory references and tracing instruction addresses
points: Operand accesses per mode: immediate and register 0, direct and register indirect 1, displacement 1, memory indirect 2. Instruction fetch adds one access per instruction word.
A two-word LOAD @A (opcode word plus address word) costs 4 accesses: 2 fetches, 1 to read the pointer M[A], 1 to read the operand.

To count data references in a loop, count the accesses in one iteration, multiply by the trip count, and add the accesses outside the loop. A loop body with one load and one store run 10 times after one initial load makes 1 + 10 × 2 = 21 data references.
Instruction k starts at start + Σ sizes of instructions 1 to k − 1; on a byte-addressable machine with sizes given in words, multiply each size by the bytes per word.
An interrupt is recognised only after the current instruction completes, so the return address pushed is the address of the next instruction, not of the interrupted one.

lesson.why: Trace and counting questions ask for exact memory accesses or addresses, and one forgotten instruction fetch or one wrong instruction size changes the answer.
lesson.intro: Every instruction costs memory accesses before it does anything else: each word of the instruction itself has to be fetched. After that, the operand may need zero, one or two more accesses, depending on where the addressing mode says the data lives. Add the two parts for one pass, multiply by how many times the code runs, and add whatever runs only once. Addresses are traced the same way: the next instruction starts where the current one ends.

definitions.meaning: The number of times a loop body runs.
The address of the instruction after the one that was interrupted or called; execution resumes there.
The instruction holds the address of the operand, so one memory read fetches it.
The instruction holds the address of a word that holds the operand's address, so two reads are needed.
A signal that makes the processor finish the current instruction, save the return address and run a handler.

principle.text: Total accesses are instruction-word fetches plus operand accesses. Immediate and register operands add none, direct and register indirect add one, and memory indirect adds two. Instruction k starts at the start address plus the sizes of all earlier instructions.

lesson.limits: The counts assume no cache and no prefetch, and that every instruction word is fetched separately; a question that gives a different cost model overrides these rules. Sizes must be converted to bytes first when memory is byte addressable.

example.problem: A one-word instruction CLR R1 runs once. Then a loop runs 5 times: LOAD @A (two words, memory indirect), ADD R1,R2 (one word, registers only) and STORE B (two words, direct). Count all memory accesses.
steps: LOAD @A: 2 fetches, 1 read of the pointer at A and 1 read of the operand, so 4 accesses.
ADD R1,R2: 1 fetch and no operand access, so 1. STORE B: 2 fetches and 1 write, so 3. One pass costs $4 + 1 + 3 = 8$.
Five passes cost $5 \times 8 = 40$, and CLR R1 adds 1 fetch.
example.result: The program makes 41 memory accesses.

misconceptions: Counting only data references and leaving out the instruction fetches, which are accesses too unless the question asks for data references only.
Treating the interrupted instruction as the return address; the interrupt is recognised after it completes, so the next instruction's address is saved.
Assuming a conditional branch back to the loop returns to the first instruction; it lands on the address it names, and instructions before that target (such as an initial load) run only once.

recall.q: How many operand accesses does a memory indirect mode need?
recall.a: Two: one to read the pointer and one to read the operand it points to.

recall.q: How do you find the start address of the k-th instruction?
recall.a: Add the sizes of instructions 1 to k-1 to the start address, converting words to bytes on a byte-addressable machine.

recall.q: Which address is pushed when an interrupt arrives?
recall.a: The address of the next instruction, because the current one finishes first.

recall.q: A loop ends with DEC R1 then BNZ to its second instruction. Which instructions repeat?
recall.a: Those from the branch target through BNZ repeat until R1 reaches zero; the first instruction runs once, so values it loads are not reloaded each pass.

practice.stem: Memory is byte addressable and a word is 4 bytes. A program starts at address 600 with instructions of 2, 1, 3 and 2 words in that order. At what address does the fourth instruction start?
practice.explanation: The first three instructions occupy 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 words, which is 24 bytes, so the fourth starts at 600 + 24 = 624. Answering 606 tempts because it adds the word counts without multiplying by 4 bytes.

lesson.summary: Count fetched instruction words plus operand accesses per pass, scale by the trip count, and find addresses by summing earlier instruction sizes in bytes.

topics.title: Instruction classes and control transfer
points: Data transfer (MOV, LOAD, STORE, PUSH, POP), arithmetic and logic (ADD, SUB, AND, OR, SHL, SHR), control flow (JMP, BEQ, BNE, CALL, RET), I/O (IN, OUT or memory-mapped loads and stores) and system (INT, TRAP, SYSCALL).
Unconditional branches always change PC; conditional branches test condition codes or a register comparison and fall through to PC + size when the test fails.
A direct branch carries its target (absolute or PC-relative) in the instruction; an indirect branch takes it from a register or memory word, which is how RET, switch tables and virtual calls work.
CALL saves the address of the next instruction (on the stack or in a link register) and jumps; RET restores it into PC. Nested calls need the stack, because one link register would be overwritten.

With a stack that grows toward lower addresses and 4-byte return addresses, a 4-byte CALL at 2000 with SP = 1000 sets SP ← 996, M[996] ← 2004 and PC ← target; the matching RET sets PC ← M[996] = 2004 and SP ← 1000.

lesson.why: Control-transfer questions test whether you know what CALL and RET do to the stack pointer and program counter, and a one-step slip in either gives a wrong address.
lesson.intro: Instructions fall into a few groups: moving data, doing arithmetic or logic, changing the flow of execution, input and output, and requests to the system. Flow-changing instructions are the interesting ones. A jump simply replaces the program counter. A call also has to remember where to come back to, so it saves the address of the next instruction before jumping, and a return puts that saved address back. Moving data has its own rule on a load-store machine: only LOAD and STORE touch memory, so arithmetic such as ADD works on registers alone and an operand in memory must be loaded first.

definitions.meaning: A register holding the address of the top of the stack.
A register that holds the return address instead of the stack.
A branch whose target is read from a register or memory word and not from the instruction.
A design where only LOAD and STORE access memory; ADD and other computation instructions take registers only.

analogy.text: A call is like putting a bookmark in a book before looking something up, and a return is going back to the bookmark.
analogy.breaksWhen: Nested calls need one bookmark per level, so a single bookmark or one link register is not enough without a stack.

principle.text: CALL pushes the address of the following instruction and jumps; RET pops it into the program counter. With a stack growing to lower addresses, push decreases SP by the entry size before the write, and pop reads then increases SP.
principle.tex: \text{CALL: } SP \leftarrow SP - s,\ M[SP] \leftarrow PC_{\text{next}} \qquad \text{RET: } PC \leftarrow M[SP],\ SP \leftarrow SP + s

lesson.limits: Some machines grow the stack upward or decrement after the write, and many RISC machines put the return address in a link register and push it only for nested calls. Use the order and direction the question states.

example.problem: The stack grows toward lower addresses, return addresses are 4 bytes and SP is 800. A 4-byte CALL at 5000 runs, and the callee executes a 4-byte CALL at 7000. Then two RETs run. Give SP and PC after each step.
steps: The first CALL saves 5004: $SP = 796$, $M[796] = 5004$. The second saves 7004: $SP = 792$, $M[792] = 7004$.
The first RET sets $PC = M[792] = 7004$ and $SP = 796$.
The second RET sets $PC = M[796] = 5004$ and $SP = 800$.
example.result: The stack is empty again at SP = 800 and execution resumes at 5004.

misconceptions: Saving the CALL's own address; the saved value is the address of the instruction after it.
Assuming a single link register handles nested calls, when the second call overwrites the first return address.
Writing ADD Z, X, Y with memory names on a load-store machine; X and Y must be loaded into registers first, and the result stored from a register.

recall.q: What does CALL save, and where?
recall.a: The address of the next instruction, on the stack or in a link register.

recall.q: How does a conditional branch behave when its test fails?
recall.a: It falls through, so the program counter becomes the address of the next instruction.

recall.q: Why do nested calls need a stack?
recall.a: Each call needs its own saved return address, and a stack keeps them in last-in first-out order.

recall.q: On a load-store machine, how is Z = X + Y compiled when X, Y and Z are in memory?
recall.a: LOAD X and Y into two registers, ADD them into a third register, then STORE that register into Z.

practice.stem: A stack grows toward lower addresses and holds 4-byte return addresses. SP is 1000. Three nested CALLs execute, then one RET. What is SP?
practice.explanation: Each CALL lowers SP by 4, so three calls give 1000 - 12 = 988, and the RET raises it by 4 to 992. Answering 988 tempts because it forgets the RET, and 1008 comes from moving the stack in the wrong direction, which gives 1000 + 12 - 4.

lesson.summary: CALL pushes the next instruction's address and jumps, RET pops it back, and the stack lets calls nest to any depth.

topics.title: RISC versus CISC
points: RISC: few simple instructions, fixed length, few addressing modes, large register file, CPI close to 1, and a load-store architecture in which only LOAD and STORE touch memory. ARM, MIPS and RISC-V are RISC.
CISC: many complex instructions, variable length, many addressing modes, and ALU instructions that may take memory operands directly, with cycle counts that vary per instruction. x86 is CISC.
RISC regularity makes pipelining easy and suits hardwired control; CISC traditionally relies on microprogrammed control, and modern x86 cracks instructions into RISC-like micro-operations.
CISC programs need fewer instructions; RISC programs need more instructions but each is cheaper, so neither wins on instruction count alone.

lesson.why: Characteristic-matching questions on RISC versus CISC are quick marks if you know which design traits go together and why.
lesson.intro: A processor's instruction set can be kept small and regular, or made large with powerful instructions. The small, regular style is called RISC. Its instructions all have the same length, only loads and stores reach memory, and each instruction does little, so the hardware to run it can be simple and quick. The large style is called CISC. One instruction may reach memory, do arithmetic and use a complex address, so programs are shorter but each instruction takes a variable number of cycles. The control unit that decodes instructions follows the same split: simple instructions let it be built from fixed logic gates, while complex ones are usually driven from a stored table of steps.

definitions.meaning: A design where only LOAD and STORE access memory and every other instruction uses registers.
Clock cycles per instruction, averaged over a program.
A control unit whose signals come from fixed logic gates, which is fast but hard to change.
A control unit that reads each instruction's steps from a stored table of micro-instructions, the control store, which is easier to change but slower.

principle.text: Run time is the instruction count times the average cycles per instruction times the cycle time. RISC lowers CPI and accepts a higher instruction count; CISC lowers the instruction count and accepts a higher CPI.

lesson.limits: The split is a tendency, not a law: modern x86 chips translate instructions into RISC-like micro-operations internally, so a CISC instruction set can still run on a pipelined core.

example.problem: Compile C = A + B, with A, B and C in memory, for a CISC machine whose ADD may take a memory operand and for a load-store machine. Compare instruction counts.
steps: CISC: MOV R1,A then ADD R1,B then MOV C,R1. That is 3 instructions, and ADD reaches memory itself.
Load-store: LOAD R1,A, LOAD R2,B, ADD R3,R1,R2 and STORE C,R3. That is 4 instructions.
Both move the same three values to or from memory, so the difference is in instruction count and in how simple each instruction is.
example.result: CISC uses 3 instructions and the load-store RISC uses 4, each one simpler.

misconceptions: Believing RISC always runs faster; it executes more instructions, and only the lower CPI and faster clock repay that.
Thinking a hardwired control unit belongs to CISC; simple fixed-length RISC instructions are what make hardwired control practical.

recall.q: Name three typical RISC characteristics.
recall.a: Fixed-length instructions, a load-store architecture and few addressing modes.

recall.q: Which control unit style does RISC usually use?
recall.a: Hardwired, because simple instructions need no control store.

recall.q: Why can a CISC program have fewer instructions?
recall.a: One instruction can combine a memory access, an operation and a complex address.

practice.stem: A CISC program runs 200 instructions at an average of 3 cycles each. The same program on a RISC machine runs 320 instructions at an average of 1.25 cycles each. By how many cycles does the RISC run finish earlier?
practice.explanation: CISC needs 200 x 3 = 600 cycles and RISC needs 320 x 1.25 = 400 cycles, a gap of 200. Choosing the machine with fewer instructions tempts because instruction count alone ignores CPI.

lesson.summary: RISC means simple, fixed-length, load-store instructions with low CPI and hardwired control; CISC trades a lower instruction count for complex, variable-cycle instructions.

topics.title: Byte versus word addressing, alignment and endianness
points: Byte-addressable memory gives every byte its own address, so consecutive 4-byte words sit at addresses differing by 4; word-addressable memory gives each word one address, so they differ by 1.
A K-bit address reaches 2^K cells: 2^K bytes when byte-addressed, 2^K × w bytes when each cell is a w-byte word.
An aligned w-byte access starts at an address divisible by w; RISC ISAs usually trap or split misaligned accesses.
A w-byte item at address a is aligned exactly when a mod w = 0: 1004 is 4-byte aligned but not 8-byte aligned, and 1002 is neither.

Big-endian stores the most significant byte at the lowest address, little-endian the least significant. 0x12345678 at address 100 puts 0x12 at 100 in big-endian and 0x78 at 100 in little-endian; x86 and RISC-V are little-endian.
In little-endian order the byte at address a + i of a word stored at a is byte i counted from the least significant end: 0xA1B2C3D4 at 400 puts 0xB2 at 402, while big-endian puts 0xC3 there.

lesson.why: Address-arithmetic questions depend on knowing what one address names, and endianness or alignment slips give answers that look plausible but are wrong.
lesson.intro: Memory is a long row of cells, and each cell has an address. On a byte-addressable machine every cell is one byte, so a 4-byte word covers four consecutive addresses. On a word-addressable machine every cell is a whole word, and the next word is one address further. When a multi-byte value is stored, the machine must also choose which of its bytes goes at the lowest address: the most significant byte first is big-endian, the least significant first is little-endian. This also fixes how arrays are stepped through: on a byte-addressable machine, consecutive elements of a w-byte array are w addresses apart, and shifting a value left by k bits multiplies it by $2^k$.

definitions.meaning: A w-byte item is aligned when its address is a multiple of w.
The order in which a value's bytes are placed at increasing addresses.

principle.text: A K-bit address names $2^K$ cells, and each cell holds w bytes (1 on a byte-addressable machine). Little-endian places byte $i$ of a value, counted from the least significant end, at address $a + i$; big-endian places it at $a + w - 1 - i$.

lesson.limits: The formula for capacity uses the cell size, so it changes with the machine's addressing unit. Endianness concerns byte order only; the bits inside a byte are not reordered.

example.problem: The 4-byte value 0x5A6B7C8D is stored at address 300. Give the byte at each address for little-endian order, and say whether the word is aligned.
steps: Little-endian puts the least significant byte first: address 300 holds 0x8D, 301 holds 0x7C, 302 holds 0x6B and 303 holds 0x5A.
Big-endian would put 0x5A at 300, so the byte at 300 alone tells the two orders apart.
Alignment: $300 \bmod 4 = 0$, so the word is 4-byte aligned.
example.result: Little-endian bytes are 8D, 7C, 6B, 5A at 300 to 303, and the word is aligned.

misconceptions: Reversing the bits within each byte; only the order of whole bytes differs between the two conventions.
Using $2^K$ bytes for a word-addressable memory, when each of the $2^K$ cells holds a whole word.

recall.q: How far apart are consecutive 4-byte words on a byte-addressable machine?
recall.a: 4 addresses; on a word-addressable machine they are 1 apart.

recall.q: What does little-endian store at the lowest address?
recall.a: The least significant byte of the value.

recall.q: When is a w-byte access aligned?
recall.a: When its starting address is divisible by w.

recall.q: Element i of a 4-byte int array starts at which address on a byte-addressable machine?
recall.a: At the base address plus $4i$, so moving to the next element adds 4.

practice.stem: A machine is word addressable with 4-byte words and a 14-bit address. How many bytes of memory can it address?
practice.explanation: There are $2^{14} = 16384$ words of 4 bytes, so $16384 \times 4 = 65536$ bytes. Answering 16384 tempts because it treats the machine as byte addressable.

lesson.summary: Know the cell size an address names, compute capacity as cells times bytes per cell, check alignment by divisibility, and place bytes by the stated endianness.

formulas.name: Bits for N opcodes or N registers
where: number of distinct opcodes, registers or modes to encode
formulas.note: Always round up: 45 opcodes need 6 bits, 200 need 8. Conversely a b-bit field encodes at most 2^b values.

formulas.name: Instruction width
where: bits of each register, address or immediate field
formulas.note: Count only the fields the format actually has: a register–memory two-address instruction has one register field and one address field.

formulas.name: Range of a k-bit immediate or offset
where: width of the immediate or offset field
formulas.note: The signed range is asymmetric: 8 bits give −128 to +127, not ±128 or ±127.

formulas.name: Addressable memory
where: bytes per addressable cell (1 for byte addressing)
formulas.note: A 24-bit byte address reaches 16 MB; the same 24 bits addressing 4-byte words reach 64 MB.

formulas.name: Byte at offset i of a w-byte word
formulas.text: little-endian: B(a+i) = ⌊x / 2^(8i)⌋ mod 256; big-endian: B(a+i) = ⌊x / 2^(8(w−1−i))⌋ mod 256
where: the w-byte value stored at address a
formulas.note: Little-endian puts the least significant byte at the lowest address. Alignment is a separate test: the word is aligned when a mod w = 0.

formulas.name: Expanding-opcode encoding budget
where: number of instructions in class i
total operand bits of class i
formulas.note: The last class gets ⌊(2^W − encodings used by the other classes) ÷ 2^(b_last)⌋ opcodes.

formulas.name: Direct, indirect and register indirect EA
formulas.text: direct EA = A; indirect EA = M[A]; register indirect EA = R
formulas.note: The operand is M[EA]. Immediate mode has no EA: the operand is A itself.

formulas.name: Displacement-family EA
formulas.note: Drop terms to get the simpler modes: indexed or based is register + d, base + index is R_base + R_index.

formulas.name: PC-relative branch target
where: bytes per offset unit (1 if the offset counts bytes)
formulas.note: If the question already gives the incremented PC, add d × u to it directly; do not add L twice.

formulas.name: Auto-increment and auto-decrement update
formulas.tex: (R)+:\ \mathrm{EA}=R,\ R \leftarrow R + s \qquad -(R):\ R \leftarrow R - s,\ \mathrm{EA}=R
formulas.text: (R)+: EA = R then R ← R + s; −(R): R ← R − s then EA = R
formulas.note: s is the data-item size, 4 for a word on a byte-addressable machine, not always 1.

formulas.name: Address of the k-th instruction
where: load address of the first instruction
size of instruction j in words
addressable units per word (4 for 32-bit words, byte addressing)
formulas.note: The return address saved on an interrupt during instruction k is addr_(k+1).

formulas.name: CALL and RET on a downward-growing stack, SP at the last item pushed
formulas.tex: \text{CALL: } SP \leftarrow SP - r,\ M[SP] \leftarrow PC_{\text{next}},\ PC \leftarrow T \qquad \text{RET: } PC \leftarrow M[SP],\ SP \leftarrow SP + r
formulas.text: CALL: SP ← SP − r, M[SP] ← PC_next, PC ← T; RET: PC ← M[SP], SP ← SP + r
where: stack pointer, holding the address of the last item pushed
size of a return address in addressable units
address of the instruction after the CALL
formulas.note: PC_next = CALL address + CALL length; saving the CALL's own address would re-execute the CALL on return. What SP points to fixes the order: at the last item pushed, move SP and then store; at the next free slot, store and then move SP. Growth direction only decides whether CALL moves SP by −r or +r.

problemTypes.title: Field widths and largest immediate in a fixed-width instruction
recipe: Opcode bits = ⌈log₂ (number of opcodes)⌉, register bits = ⌈log₂ (number of registers)⌉ per register operand, plus any mode bits.
Subtract them from the instruction width to get the immediate or displacement width k.
Answer with 2^k − 1 for unsigned, −2^(k−1) to 2^(k−1) − 1 for signed, or 2^k for the number of values.
problemTypes.trap: Forgetting to round ⌈log₂ N⌉ up for a non-power-of-two count, or counting only one of two register operands.

problemTypes.title: Maximum instructions of one class under an expanding opcode
recipe: Compute the operand bits bᵢ for each class from its register and immediate fields.
Each class consumes nᵢ × 2^(bᵢ) of the 2^W encodings; add these up for every class whose count is given.
Divide the remaining encodings by 2^(b) of the unknown class and round down.
problemTypes.trap: Subtracting opcode counts instead of encoding counts: classes with different operand widths cannot be compared by opcode count alone.

problemTypes.title: Effective address or loaded value under a given mode
recipe: Write the EA rule for the mode: A, M[A], R, R + A, PC + A.
Use the PC after fetch for PC-relative and the register value before any auto-increment for (R)+.
Read the operand as M[EA], except in immediate mode where the operand is the field itself.
problemTypes.trap: Stopping one memory read early in indirect mode (reporting the pointer instead of the operand) or one read late in direct mode.

problemTypes.title: Name the mode, or pick the mode for a purpose
recipe: Look at the syntax: #k is immediate, (R) register indirect, d(R) displacement, @A or (A) memory indirect, (R)+ and −(R) auto modes.
For a purpose, match it: constants to immediate, pointers to indirect, arrays to indexed, relocation to based or PC-relative.
problemTypes.trap: Calling d(R) register indirect because of the parentheses; the added constant makes it displacement addressing.

problemTypes.title: PC-relative target, branch range and return address
recipe: Find the address of the branch and add its length to get the updated PC.
Scale the signed offset by the offset unit (bytes or words) and add it.
For a range, use −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1 units relative to the updated PC; for a return address, take the address of the next instruction.
problemTypes.trap: Adding the offset to the address of the branch itself, or forgetting to multiply a word offset by 4.

problemTypes.title: Memory references and instruction addresses in a loop program
recipe: Mark each instruction's data accesses: a load or store with a memory operand costs 1 (2 if indirect), register-only instructions cost 0.
Find the trip count from the loop counter's initial value and the exit test.
Total = accesses outside the loop + trip count × accesses per iteration; add fetches only if the question asks for all references.
For addresses, accumulate instruction sizes from the load address, scaled to bytes when memory is byte-addressable.
problemTypes.trap: Counting INC, DEC or register-to-register ADD as memory references, or including instruction fetches when only data references are asked.

problemTypes.title: Code length for an expression in 0-, 1-, 2- or 3-address form
recipe: For zero-address code, write the postfix form; every operand is a PUSH, every operator one instruction, plus a final POP.
For one-address code, keep a running value in the accumulator and STORE to a temporary whenever a second subexpression must be computed.
problemTypes.trap: In stack code the non-commutative operators apply (second from top) op (top), so the push order decides the sign.

problemTypes.title: Byte layout, alignment and stack contents after CALL
recipe: For endianness, split the value into bytes; little-endian stores the least significant byte at the lowest address, big-endian the most significant.
For alignment, test address mod item size = 0.

For CALL, compute the return address as CALL address + its length, then apply the stack rule: with SP at the last item pushed, move SP by the address size (down for a downward-growing stack) and then store; with SP at the next free slot, store and then move SP.
problemTypes.trap: Pushing the CALL's own address, or reading byte offsets from the wrong end of the word.

questions.stem: An instruction has a 5-bit opcode, a 4-bit addressing-mode field, a 5-bit register field and a 16-bit memory address field. How many bits wide is the instruction?
questions.explanation: Width is the sum of the fields: 5 + 4 + 5 + 16 = 30 bits. 25 drops the mode field, 26 drops the register field, and 32 is the padded storage size, not the field total.

questions.stem: A machine has 32-bit, one-word instructions and 64 registers. It must support 45 instructions, each with two register operands and an unsigned immediate operand, all in one word. What is the largest value the immediate operand can hold?
questions.explanation: Opcode: ⌈log₂ 45⌉ = 6 bits. Two register fields: 2 × ⌈log₂ 64⌉ = 12 bits. Immediate: 32 − 6 − 12 = 14 bits, so the largest unsigned value is 2¹⁴ − 1 = 16383.

questions.stem: An ISA has 32 opcodes, 16 general-purpose registers and 16-bit memory addresses. A two-address instruction names one register operand and one direct memory operand. What is the minimum width of this instruction?
questions.explanation: Opcode ⌈log₂ 32⌉ = 5 bits, one register field ⌈log₂ 16⌉ = 4 bits, one address field 16 bits: 5 + 4 + 16 = 25. 29 would need two register fields plus the address (three operands); 37 counts two addresses; 21 forgets the register field.

questions.stem: A processor has 16 integer registers and 64 floating-point registers and a 16-bit instruction format. Type-1 has 4 instructions with three integer register operands. Type-2 has 8 instructions with two floating-point register operands. Type-3 has 14 instructions with one integer and one floating-point register operand. Type-4 has N instructions with one floating-point register operand. What is the maximum value of N?
questions.explanation: Operand bits: Type-1 3 × 4 = 12, Type-2 2 × 6 = 12, Type-3 4 + 6 = 10, Type-4 6. Encodings used: 4 × 2¹² = 16384, 8 × 2¹² = 32768, 14 × 2¹⁰ = 14336, total 63488. Left: 65536 − 63488 = 2048. Each Type-4 instruction needs 2⁶ = 64 encodings, so N = 2048 / 64 = 32.

questions.stem: A processor has 64 registers and 16-bit instructions of two types. An I-type instruction holds an opcode, one register name and a 4-bit immediate. An R-type instruction holds an opcode and two register names. If there are 8 distinct I-type opcodes, what is the maximum number of distinct R-type opcodes?
questions.explanation: Register names take 6 bits. I-type operand bits = 6 + 4 = 10, so each I-type opcode consumes 2¹⁰ encodings: 8 × 1024 = 8192. R-type operand bits = 12, so each R-type opcode consumes 2¹² = 4096. Remaining encodings: 65536 − 8192 = 57344, and 57344 / 4096 = 14.

questions.stem: The instruction LD R1, 5(R2) loads into R1 the word at the address formed by adding 5 to the contents of R2. Which addressing mode does the source operand use?
questions.explanation: EA = R2 + 5, a register plus a constant from the instruction: displacement addressing, called indexed or base + offset depending on which part is the base. Register indirect would use EA = R2 with no constant; immediate would load the value 5; memory indirect would read a pointer from memory first.

questions.stem: Memory holds M[100] = 200 and M[200] = 50. The instruction LOAD @100 uses memory indirect addressing. Which value is loaded?
questions.explanation: Indirect: EA = M[100] = 200, operand = M[200] = 50. 200 is the pointer (what direct mode would load), 100 is what immediate mode would load, and 250 adds the two memory words.

questions.stem: A two-word LOAD instruction occupies words 200 and 201 of a word-addressable memory; its address field is 500, and after fetch PC = 202. Register R1 = 400. Memory holds M[400] = 700, M[500] = 800, M[702] = 325, M[800] = 300 and M[900] = 200. Which statements about the value loaded are correct?
options: Indexed mode with R1 as index loads 700
questions.explanation: Direct: EA = 500, value 800. Indirect: EA = M[500] = 800, value M[800] = 300. PC-relative: EA = 202 + 500 = 702, value 325. Indexed: EA = 500 + 400 = 900, value M[900] = 200, not 700; 700 is what register indirect (EA = R1 = 400) loads.

questions.stem: Consider these statements about auto-increment addressing. I. It is useful for creating self-relocating code. II. Including it in an ISA requires an additional ALU for effective-address calculation. III. The amount of increment depends on the size of the data item accessed. Which are true?
questions.explanation: III is true: (R)+ advances R by the operand size, 4 for a 32-bit word on a byte-addressable machine. I is false: relocation comes from based or PC-relative modes, not from a register side effect. II is false: the existing address adder performs the update, so no extra ALU is needed.

questions.stem: Which addressing modes allow a program to be relocated in memory at run time without modifying its instructions?
questions.explanation: Based mode: the OS reloads the base register with the new start address and every EA moves with it. PC-relative: targets are distances from the PC, which do not change when the whole program moves. Absolute and memory indirect fields hold fixed addresses that point to the old location.

questions.stem: A branch instruction holds an 8-bit two's-complement offset, counted in bytes and added to the updated PC. What range of targets can it reach relative to the updated PC?
questions.explanation: An n-bit two's-complement field spans −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1, so 8 bits give −128 to +127. ±127 is sign-magnitude, ±128 needs 9 bits, and 0 to 255 treats the offset as unsigned and allows no backward branch.

questions.stem: On a byte-addressable machine with 4-byte instructions, a PC-relative branch is stored at address 1000. Its offset field is −12 and counts words, added to the PC after the branch is fetched. What is the target address?
questions.explanation: Updated PC = 1000 + 4 = 1004. Offset in bytes = −12 × 4 = −48. Target = 1004 − 48 = 956. 952 adds the offset to 1000; 992 treats −12 as bytes from 1004; 988 treats it as bytes from 1000.

questions.stem: A program runs on a processor with M[3000] = 10: I1: R1 ← M[3000]; I2 (LOOP): R2 ← M[R3]; I3: R2 ← R1 + R2; I4: M[R3] ← R2; I5: INC R3; I6: DEC R1; I7: BNZ LOOP (branch if R1 ≠ 0); I8: HALT. How many data memory references (reads and writes of operands, not instruction fetches) does it make?
questions.explanation: I1 reads M[3000] once, so R1 = 10. Each loop pass makes 2 data references: the read in I2 and the write in I4; I3, I5, I6 and I7 use only registers. R1 counts down 10, 9, …, 1 and the branch falls through after the pass that makes it 0, so the loop runs 10 times. Total = 1 + 10 × 2 = 21.

questions.stem: The program I1 to I8 has instruction sizes 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2 and 1 words. It is loaded at byte address 1000 on a byte-addressable machine with 32-bit words. An interrupt arrives while I6 is executing. What return address is pushed on the stack?
questions.explanation: Each word is 4 bytes, so the instructions start at I1 1000, I2 1008, I3 1012, I4 1016, I5 1020, I6 1024, I7 1028. The interrupt is taken after I6 completes, so the saved address is that of I7: 1028. 1024 is the interrupted instruction itself; 1007 would be the word-addressed answer.

questions.stem: A stack machine with A = 5, B = 3, C = 7 and D = 4 executes PUSH A, PUSH B, ADD, PUSH C, PUSH D, SUB, MUL. Each binary operation pops the top two entries and pushes (second from top) op (top). What is left on top of the stack?
questions.explanation: PUSH A, PUSH B, ADD leaves 8. PUSH C, PUSH D, SUB computes 7 − 4 = 3, leaving 8, 3. MUL gives 24. −24 comes from computing D − C; 32 multiplies 8 by D; 11 adds instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: Which of the following are characteristic of a RISC instruction set?
options: Only load and store instructions access memory
Many addressing modes, including memory-to-memory arithmetic
Instructions whose cycle counts vary widely, typically implemented by microcode
questions.explanation: RISC uses fixed-length instructions and a load-store architecture in which ALU instructions operate only on registers. Rich addressing modes, memory operands in arithmetic and variable microcoded cycle counts are CISC traits.

questions.stem: An x86-style operand uses base + index × scale + displacement addressing. The base register holds 1000, the index register holds 5, the scale is 4 and the displacement is 8. What is the effective address?
questions.explanation: EA = base + index × scale + displacement = 1000 + 5 × 4 + 8 = 1028. Forgetting the scale gives 1013; dropping the displacement gives 1020.

questions.stem: An instruction ADD R1, @X occupies two words: the opcode word and a word holding the address X. Its source operand uses memory indirect addressing, and the result goes to R1. How many memory accesses does the instruction make in total, counting instruction fetch?
questions.explanation: Two fetches bring in both instruction words. Memory indirect then reads the pointer M[X] and finally the operand M[M[X]]: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. 3 treats the mode as direct; 2 counts only the fetches; 5 adds a write, but the result goes to a register.

questions.stem: The 32-bit value 0xA1B2C3D4 is stored at byte address 400 on a little-endian, byte-addressable machine. Which byte is at address 402?
questions.explanation: Little-endian puts the least significant byte first: 400 = 0xD4, 401 = 0xC3, 402 = 0xB2, 403 = 0xA1. 0xC3 is the big-endian answer, 0xD4 is the byte at 400, and 0xA1 is the most significant byte.

questions.stem: On a byte-addressable machine the stack grows toward lower addresses, SP points to the last item pushed, and return addresses are 4 bytes. A 4-byte CALL instruction at address 2000 executes with SP = 1000. Which statements are correct?
options: After the CALL, the word at address 996 holds 2004
The return address saved by the CALL is 2000
After the matching RET, SP = 1000 and PC = 2004
questions.explanation: CALL pre-decrements SP to 1000 − 4 = 996 and stores the address of the next instruction, 2000 + 4 = 2004, at 996. Saving 2000 would make RET re-execute the CALL. RET loads PC ← M[996] = 2004 and restores SP to 996 + 4 = 1000.

pitfalls.text: Immediate mode holds the value, direct mode holds the address of the value: LOAD #200 loads 200, LOAD 200 loads M[200].
Auto-increment advances the register by the operand size, which is 4 for a 32-bit word on a byte-addressable machine, not always by 1.
PC-relative targets are measured from the PC after the branch is fetched, i.e. the address of the next instruction, not from the branch's own address.
Stack code is postfix, and SUB or DIV compute (second from top) op (top); reversing the operands flips the sign of a difference.
⌈log₂ N⌉ rounds up: 45 opcodes need 6 bits and 200 need 8, never log₂ N truncated.
In expanding-opcode questions, compare encodings (n × 2^b), not opcode counts; classes with different operand widths use the opcode space at different rates.
Data-reference counts exclude instruction fetches and register-only instructions such as INC, DEC and register ADD, unless the question asks for all memory accesses.

CALL saves the address after the CALL (its address plus its length); saving the CALL's own address would loop forever on return. When SP points to the last item pushed, CALL moves SP before storing; when SP points to the next free slot, it stores first. Growth direction only sets the sign of the move.

revisionCard.heading: Formats and encoding
lines: 3-addr X ← A op B; 2-addr A ← A op B; 1-addr ACC; 0-addr stack (postfix)
opcode bits ⌈log₂ N⌉, register bits ⌈log₂ R⌉, immediate = W − rest
unsigned k bits: 0..2^k − 1; signed: −2^(k−1)..2^(k−1) − 1
expanding opcode: Σ nᵢ 2^(bᵢ) ≤ 2^W

revisionCard.heading: Modes
lines: Immediate: operand = A; Register: operand = R
Direct: M[A]; Indirect: M[M[A]]; Register indirect: M[R]
Indexed/based: M[R + d]; base + index: M[Rb + Ri × s + d]
PC-relative: M[PC_next + d]; (R)+ use then add size; −(R) subtract then use

revisionCard.heading: Uses and costs
lines: constants immediate, pointers indirect, arrays indexed, relocation based or PC-relative
operand accesses: imm/reg 0, direct/reg-ind/displacement 1, indirect 2
interrupt return address = address of the next instruction
little-endian: least significant byte at lowest address; aligned iff addr mod size = 0
CALL: SP ← SP − r, M[SP] ← next PC; RET: PC ← M[SP], SP ← SP + r

revisionCard.heading: RISC vs CISC
lines: RISC: fixed length, load-store, few modes, CPI near 1, easy pipelining
CISC: variable length, memory operands in ALU ops, many modes, microcode

errata.claim: A two-address instruction with 32 opcodes, 16 registers and 16-bit addresses is 5 + 4 + 4 + 16 = 29 bits wide.
errata.correction: 5 + 4 + 4 + 16 counts three operand fields (two registers and a memory address). A two-address instruction with one register and one memory operand is 5 + 4 + 16 = 25 bits; 29 bits fits a three-operand register–register–memory format.

errata.claim: A branch at PC = 200 with offset −10 targets 190.
errata.correction: This contradicts the rule that the target is the updated PC plus the offset. 190 is right only if 200 is already the incremented PC; if the branch itself sits at address 200, the target is 200 + (instruction length) − 10, e.g. 194 for a 4-byte branch.

errata.claim: An n-bit PC-relative offset bounds the branch range to plus or minus 2^(n−1) bytes.
errata.correction: A two's-complement n-bit offset reaches −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1 units from the updated PC (−128 to +127 for 8 bits), and the units are words rather than bytes when the ISA scales the offset.

references.title: Patterson & Hennessy — Computer Organization & Design (MIPS edition)

chapters.title: ALU, Datapath & Control Unit
chapters.summary: The ALU computes arithmetic, logical and shift results and raises the Z, N, C and V flags that drive conditional branches; its speed is set by how the carry travels, rippling bit by bit or computed ahead with generate and propagate terms. The control unit turns each instruction into a timed sequence of control signals, either with hardwired logic (fast, rigid, RISC) or with microinstructions read from a control memory (flexible, slower, CISC). GATE asks for flag values, adder delays, and the bit widths of microinstruction fields and control memories.
highYield: Size a microinstruction: control field + ⌈log₂(conditions)⌉ select bits + next-address bits, and the control memory has 2^(address bits) words.
Horizontal width = number of control signals; vertical width = Σ ⌈log₂(nᵢ + 1)⌉ over mutually exclusive groups.
Hardwired is faster and suits RISC; microprogrammed is easier to change and suits CISC, but pays a control-memory read per microinstruction.
Signed overflow V = c_n ⊕ c_{n−1}; carry C and overflow V are independent, so check both on every addition.
Ripple-carry delay grows linearly with word length; carry-lookahead makes each block's carry a two-level function of g, p and c₀.
A 4-bit two-level carry-lookahead unit needs 10 AND and 4 OR gates (n(n + 1)/2 and n); a 16-bit two-level CLA gives c₁₆ at 5 and the last sum at 8 gate delays.

topics.title: What the ALU computes
points: The ALU takes two operands A and B plus an operation code and returns a result and a set of status flags.

Its functional units are an adder/subtractor (ADD, SUB, CMP), a logic unit (AND, OR, XOR, NOT) and a shifter (logical and arithmetic shifts, rotates); a multiplexer picks which unit drives the output.
Selecting one of k operations needs ⌈log₂ k⌉ function-select bits: 16 operations need 4 bits, 8 need 3.
CMP is a subtraction whose result is discarded; only the flags are kept for a following conditional branch.

The arithmetic unit is one adder whose B input passes through a 4-way multiplexer (B, B̄, all 0s, all 1s) plus a carry-in: this yields A + B, A + B + 1, A − B − 1, A − B, A, A + 1, A − 1 and A again, eight operations from 3 select bits.

lesson.why: Questions on the ALU ask how many select bits an operation set needs and which unit produces a given result, so the structure has to be second nature.
lesson.intro: The ALU is the part of the processor that does arithmetic and logic. It receives two operands, A and B, and a short code saying which operation to perform. It returns a result and a few one-bit status flags. Inside are three small units: an adder that also subtracts, a logic unit for AND, OR, XOR and NOT, and a shifter. A multiplexer, which is a switch that forwards one of several inputs, picks which unit's answer leaves the ALU.

definitions.meaning: The bits of the operation code that tell the ALU which operation to perform.
A compare: the ALU subtracts, throws the result away and keeps only the flags.

principle.text: Choosing one of k operations needs a function-select field of ceil(log2 k) bits. Subtraction reuses the adder by adding the complement of B with a carry-in of 1.

lesson.limits: The select-bit count counts distinct operations, not instructions: many instructions can share one ALU operation. Compare does not store a result, so it changes no register, only the flags.

example.problem: A 4-bit ALU subtracts B = 3 from A = 6 using its adder. Show the computation.
steps: Write B = 0011 and complement every bit to get 1100.
Add A, the complement of B and a carry-in of 1: 0110 + 1100 + 1 = 10011.
Keep the low 4 bits, 0011, and treat the leftmost 1 as the carry out.
example.result: The result is 0011, which is 3, equal to 6 - 3.

misconceptions: Subtraction does not need a separate subtractor circuit; the adder is reused with B complemented and a carry-in of 1.
Forgetting the carry-in of 1 gives A + complement of B, which is A - B - 1, one less than the right answer.
CMP does not leave a difference in a register; only the flags survive.

recall.q: How many function-select bits does an ALU with 12 operations need?
recall.a: 4 bits, because the ceiling of log2 12 is 4.

recall.q: What does CMP keep from its subtraction?
recall.a: Only the status flags; the numerical result is discarded.

recall.q: What picks which functional unit drives the ALU output?
recall.a: A multiplexer controlled by the function-select bits.

practice.stem: An ALU must support 20 different operations. How many function-select bits does it need?
practice.explanation: Select bits are the ceiling of log2 20, and 2^4 = 16 is below 20 while 2^5 = 32 covers it, so 5. The value 4 tempts because it is the floor of log2 20, but 4 bits only name 16 operations.

lesson.summary: The ALU combines an adder-subtractor, a logic unit and a shifter behind a multiplexer; k operations need ceil(log2 k) select bits, and subtraction is A plus complement of B plus 1.

topics.title: Status flags and condition codes
points: Z is set when every result bit is 0, N (or S) copies the most significant result bit, C is the carry out of the MSB, and V is set on signed (two's-complement) overflow.
C reports unsigned overflow and V reports signed overflow; they are computed independently, so any of the four C/V combinations can occur.
In 8 bits, 0xC0 + 0xC0 = 0x180 leaves result 0x80 with C = 1, N = 1, V = 0 (−64 + −64 = −128 fits), while 0x7F + 0x01 = 0x80 gives C = 0, V = 1.
Branches test flag combinations: BEQ tests Z = 1, an unsigned 'lower' test uses C, and a signed 'less than' after CMP tests N ⊕ V = 1.

lesson.why: Flag questions give two operands and ask for Z, N, C and V, and branch questions ask which flags a condition tests. Both reduce to a few rules applied carefully.
lesson.intro: After an addition or subtraction the ALU sets four one-bit flags that describe the result. Z says the result is all zeros. N copies the leftmost bit of the result, which is the sign in two's complement. C is the carry that falls out of the leftmost bit. V says the answer is wrong when the operands are read as signed numbers. A later branch instruction looks at these flags instead of recomputing anything.

definitions.meaning: The carry out of the most significant bit; it signals overflow for unsigned numbers.
Set when the signed result does not fit: both operands share a sign and the result has the other sign.

principle.text: C and V are independent. C is the carry out of the top bit, and V is set when the carry into the top bit differs from the carry out of it.

lesson.limits: C means unsigned overflow only for addition; for subtraction many machines treat the carry as an inverted borrow. Whether a result is correct depends on whether the program reads the numbers as signed or unsigned, and the flags report both views.

example.problem: An 8-bit ALU adds 0x90 and 0x90. Find Z, N, C and V.
steps: 0x90 + 0x90 = 0x120, which needs 9 bits, so the 8-bit result is 0x20 and the carry out is 1.
The result 0x20 is not zero, so Z = 0, and its top bit is 0, so N = 0.
Both operands have top bit 1 (negative, -112 each) and the result has top bit 0, so the sign changed and V = 1.

misconceptions: A carry out does not imply signed overflow: 0xC0 + 0xC0 sets C = 1 but V = 0, because -64 + -64 = -128 fits in 8 bits.
Overflow does not imply a carry: 0x7F + 0x01 sets V = 1 with C = 0.
Z can be 1 together with C = 1, as in 0xF0 + 0x10, because the result 0x00 is zero after the carry is dropped.

recall.q: When is V set after an addition?
recall.a: When both operands have the same sign and the result has the opposite sign, equivalently when the carry into the top bit differs from the carry out.

recall.q: What does N copy?
recall.a: The most significant bit of the result.

recall.q: Can C and V both be 1 at once?
recall.a: Yes. All four combinations of C and V can occur because they are computed independently.

practice.stem: An 8-bit ALU adds 0xF0 and 0x10. Which values of (Z, N, C, V) result?
practice.explanation: 0xF0 + 0x10 = 0x100, so the 8-bit result is 0x00 with carry out 1: Z = 1, N = 0, C = 1. The operands are -16 and +16, which differ in sign, so no overflow and V = 0. Choosing V = 1 tempts because a carry occurred, but a carry is not an overflow; choosing Z = 0 forgets that the dropped carry leaves an all-zero result.

lesson.summary: Z flags an all-zero result, N copies the sign bit, C is the carry out of the top bit and V is signed overflow; C and V are independent.

topics.title: Ripple-carry adder, adder-subtractor and overflow detection
points: An n-bit ripple-carry adder chains n full adders; stage i cannot settle until carry cᵢ arrives, so the worst-case delay grows linearly in n.
With carry delay t_c per stage and sum delay t_s after the carry-in, the last sum bit settles at (n − 1)·t_c + t_s and the carry-out at n·t_c.
One adder also subtracts: XOR each Bᵢ with a mode bit M and feed M in as c₀, so M = 1 computes A + B̄ + 1 = A − B in two's complement.
Signed overflow happens exactly when the carry into the MSB differs from the carry out of it: V = c_n ⊕ c_{n−1}. Equivalently, two operands of the same sign give a result of the other sign.

lesson.why: Delay of a ripple adder, the adder-subtractor wiring and the overflow test are all standard computations in this chapter.
lesson.intro: A full adder adds two bits and an incoming carry, and produces a sum bit and an outgoing carry. Chaining n of them, with each carry-out feeding the next carry-in, adds two n-bit numbers. This is a ripple-carry adder: the carry has to travel through every stage in turn, so a wider adder is slower. The same adder can subtract if each bit of B is flipped and a 1 is added in at the bottom.

definitions.meaning: A one-bit circuit that adds two bits and a carry-in, giving a sum bit and a carry-out.
A control bit that XORs with every bit of B and is also the carry-in c0; M = 0 adds and M = 1 subtracts.

principle.text: With carry delay t_c per stage and carry-to-sum delay t_s, the last sum bit settles after n-1 carry delays plus one sum delay. Setting M = 1 gives A plus complement of B plus 1, which is A minus B; signed overflow is the carry into the top bit XOR the carry out.

lesson.limits: The delay formula assumes t_c is measured from carry-in to carry-out of a stage and that the operands are present at time zero; read the question for how t_c is defined. The overflow test applies to signed numbers only.

example.problem: A 4-bit adder-subtractor with M = 1 computes 7 - 5. Show the bits and the overflow flag.
steps: B = 0101 XOR 1111 gives 1010, and c0 = M = 1.
Add 0111 + 1010 + 1 = 10010, so the 4-bit result is 0010.
Working stage by stage, every carry c1 to c4 is 1, so the carry into the top bit equals the carry out and V = 1 XOR 1 = 0.
example.result: The result is 0010, which is 2, with no overflow.

misconceptions: The carry out of a subtraction is 1 when no borrow is needed, so a carry of 1 here is normal and not an error.
The last sum bit does not wait for n carry delays; it waits for n-1 carry delays and then one sum delay.
Overflow is not simply the carry out; it compares the carry out with the carry into the top bit.

recall.q: How does one adder subtract?
recall.a: XOR every bit of B with a mode bit M and use M as the carry-in, so M = 1 gives A + complement of B + 1.

recall.q: Why is a ripple-carry adder slow?
recall.a: Each stage waits for the carry from the stage below, so the delay grows linearly with the number of bits.

recall.q: What is the signed overflow test in terms of carries?
recall.a: V is the carry into the most significant bit XOR the carry out of it.

practice.stem: An 8-bit ripple-carry adder has a carry delay of 2 ns per stage (carry-in to carry-out) and a sum delay of 3 ns from carry-in to sum. Operands and the first carry-in are available at time 0. At what time, in ns, does the most significant sum bit settle?
practice.explanation: The carry into the last stage appears after 7 stage delays, 7 x 2 = 14 ns, and the sum then takes 3 ns, giving 17 ns. The value 19 tempts by charging all 8 carry delays before the sum, and 16 is the time of the final carry-out, not the last sum bit.

lesson.summary: A ripple adder's delay grows with n, subtraction reuses it through XOR with a mode bit and a carry-in of 1, and signed overflow is the carry into the top bit XOR the carry out.

topics.title: Carry-lookahead adders
points: Each bit forms generate gᵢ = aᵢbᵢ and propagate pᵢ = aᵢ ⊕ bᵢ; then c_{i+1} = gᵢ + pᵢcᵢ, and the sum is sᵢ = pᵢ ⊕ cᵢ.
Expanding the recurrence writes every carry as a two-level AND-OR of g, p and c₀, for example c₂ = g₁ + p₁g₀ + p₁p₀c₀, so all carries of a block appear after a constant delay.
The cost is fan-in and gate count, which grow quickly with width, so wide adders chain 4-bit lookahead blocks or add a second lookahead level using block generate and propagate signals.
Generating c₁…cₙ in two-level form takes 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 AND gates and n OR gates (gᵢ feeds the OR directly); the widest gate has fan-in n + 1. A 4-bit unit: 10 AND, 4 OR, fan-in 5.
With g/p ready after 1 gate delay and each block's carry-out 2 gate delays after its carry-in, four rippled 4-bit blocks produce c₁₆ at 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 9 gate delays.
A second lookahead level uses block signals P = p₃p₂p₁p₀ and G = g₃ + p₃g₂ + p₃p₂g₁ + p₃p₂p₁g₀, so c₄ = G + P·c₀. In a 16-bit two-level adder c₁₆ is ready at 5 gate delays and the last sum at 8.

lesson.why: Delay and gate-count questions compare ripple and lookahead adders, and they expect the generate and propagate expressions to be written correctly.
lesson.intro: In a ripple adder each carry waits for the one before it. A carry-lookahead adder removes the wait by computing every carry directly from the input bits. For each bit position it forms two signals: generate, which says this position makes a carry by itself, and propagate, which says this position passes an incoming carry along. Every carry is then a short AND-OR expression of these signals and the first carry-in.

definitions.meaning: g_i = a_i AND b_i: position i produces a carry whatever comes in.
p_i = a_i XOR b_i: position i passes an incoming carry to the next position.

principle.text: The carry out of position i is generated there or propagated from below. Expanding the recurrence gives each carry as a two-level circuit, and the sum bit is the propagate XOR the carry in.

lesson.limits: Lookahead trades speed for hardware: gate fan-in and count grow quickly with width, so wide adders chain 4-bit lookahead blocks or add a second lookahead level instead of one huge unit.

example.problem: A 4-bit lookahead adder adds A = 1011 and B = 0110 with c0 = 0. Find the carries and sum.
steps: Per bit from bit 0 to bit 3: g = 0, 1, 0, 0 and p = 1, 0, 1, 1.
Sum bits s_i = p_i XOR c_i give 1, 0, 0, 0 from bit 0 upward, so the sum is 0001 with carry out 1.
example.result: The sum is 0001 with carry out 1, matching 11 + 6 = 17.

misconceptions: Propagate is XOR, not OR in the sum; the sum bit needs p_i XOR c_i.
Lookahead does not make the delay zero; it makes it constant for a block, and wide adders still chain blocks.
A position with g = 1 needs no incoming carry to produce one, so its propagate value does not matter for that carry.

recall.q: What are generate and propagate for bit i?
recall.a: g_i = a_i AND b_i and p_i = a_i XOR b_i.

recall.q: Why does lookahead need extra hardware?
recall.a: Each carry is a wide AND-OR of g, p and c0, so gate count and fan-in grow with the width.

recall.q: How do wide lookahead adders limit that growth?
recall.a: They chain 4-bit blocks or add a second level using block generate and propagate signals.

practice.stem: A two-level AND-OR carry-lookahead unit produces carries c1 to c5, with each g_i term used directly as a literal input of the OR gate. How many AND gates does it need?
practice.explanation: Carry c_i needs i AND gates, since its term g_(i-1) is a single literal and needs none; the total over c1 to c5 is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15, which is n(n+1)/2. The value 20 tempts by counting a separate gate for every product term of each carry, including the lone g term.

lesson.summary: Lookahead forms generate and propagate per bit and writes each carry as a two-level expression, giving constant delay per block at the cost of gates and fan-in.

topics.title: Bit-slice ALUs and shifters
points: A bit-slice ALU replicates one identical 1-bit cell (full adder, logic gates and a result multiplexer) n times, with the carry chained from cell to cell.
A 4-input result multiplexer inside each cell needs 2 select lines; in general an m-input multiplexer needs ⌈log₂ m⌉.

A barrel (logarithmic) shifter shifts by any amount in one pass: stage j shifts by 2^j or passes through, so an n-bit shifter uses log₂ n stages of n 2:1 multiplexers (32 bits: 5 stages, 160 multiplexers).
An arithmetic right shift copies the sign bit into the vacated positions; a logical right shift fills them with 0.

lesson.why: Shifter questions ask how many multiplexers or stages a barrel shifter uses, and the difference between logical and arithmetic shifts decides signed-number answers.
lesson.intro: A bit-slice ALU is built by copying one identical one-bit cell n times. Each cell holds a full adder, some logic gates and a multiplexer that chooses which result the cell outputs, and the carry passes from each cell to the next. Shifting is a separate job. A barrel shifter moves a word by any amount in a single pass through a few stages, where each stage either shifts by a fixed power of two or leaves the word alone.

definitions.meaning: A shifter that moves a word by any amount in one pass using log2 n stages of 2-to-1 multiplexers.
A right shift that copies the sign bit into the vacated positions, keeping the sign of a two's-complement number.

principle.text: Stage j of a barrel shifter shifts by 2^j or passes the word through, so any amount from 0 to n-1 is built from its binary digits. An n-bit barrel shifter has log2 n stages of n multiplexers each.

lesson.limits: The stage count assumes n is a power of two and that shift amounts stay below n. A multiplexer with m inputs needs ceil(log2 m) select lines, so a 4-input result multiplexer in a cell needs 2.

example.problem: An 8-bit register holds 10110100. Shift it right by 2, first logically and then arithmetically.
steps: Moving every bit two places right drops the two lowest bits, leaving 101101 in the low six positions.
A logical shift fills the two vacated top positions with 0, giving 00101101.
An arithmetic shift fills them with the sign bit, which is 1, giving 11101101.
example.result: Logical: 00101101. Arithmetic: 11101101, which is -76 divided by 4 = -19.

misconceptions: Arithmetic right shift is not the same as logical right shift for negative numbers; only the arithmetic form keeps the sign.
A barrel shifter does not shift one position per clock; it reaches any amount in one pass.
The stage count is log2 n, not n: a 32-bit shifter has 5 stages.

recall.q: How many stages does a 32-bit barrel shifter have?
recall.a: 5 stages, each made of 32 two-to-one multiplexers, so 160 multiplexers in total.

recall.q: What fills the vacated bits in a logical right shift?
recall.a: Zeros.

recall.q: How many select lines does a 4-input multiplexer need?
recall.a: 2 select lines.

practice.stem: A 64-bit barrel shifter is built from 2-to-1 multiplexers, with one stage for each power-of-two shift amount. How many multiplexers does it use in total?
practice.explanation: Stages number log2 64 = 6, and each stage has 64 multiplexers, so 6 x 64 = 384. The value 64 tempts by counting a single stage, and 4096 by treating the shifter as one multiplexer per bit per possible shift amount.

lesson.summary: A bit-slice ALU repeats one cell n times; a barrel shifter reaches any shift amount in log2 n stages of n multiplexers, and an arithmetic right shift keeps the sign bit.

topics.title: Datapath registers and buses
points: The datapath holds PC (next instruction address), IR (current instruction), a register file, the ALU, MAR and MDR (the memory interface), multiplexers for ALU inputs and a sign extender for immediates.
Sign extension copies the sign bit to widen a signed immediate (8-bit 0xF5 becomes 0xFFF5); zero extension pads unsigned values with 0s.

Single-bus organisations move one value per clock, so an ALU operation needs a holding register Y and an output register Z; two- and three-bus designs move more operands per cycle at the cost of more wiring.

lesson.why: Datapath figures with registers, multiplexers and an ALU are the stage on which control-step and cycle-time questions are set, and some questions ask only what operand combinations the wiring allows.
lesson.intro: The datapath is the set of storage boxes and wires that data moves through while an instruction runs. PC holds the address of the next instruction, IR holds the instruction being carried out, and a register file holds the program's working values. MAR holds an address sent to memory and MDR holds the word that comes back. A multiplexer is a switch: several inputs, one output, and a select line says which input gets through. The ALU takes two inputs and combines them as its control lines direct.

analogy.text: A multiplexer is a railway points switch: several tracks lead in, one track leads out, and the signal box decides which track is connected.
analogy.breaksWhen: A real switch is set by one lever; two multiplexers in a datapath usually have separate select lines, so their settings combine freely.

definitions.meaning: A constant stored inside the instruction word itself, so it needs no register.
Widening a signed value by copying its sign bit into the new upper bits, which keeps the value unchanged.

principle.text: If each ALU input has its own multiplexer with its own select line, every choice on one side can pair with every choice on the other. With $m$ sources on one side and $n$ on the other the ALU can see $m\times n$ operand pairs. A source wired straight in, with no multiplexer, counts as one choice.

lesson.limits: This counts what the wiring permits, not what the instruction set offers: an instruction set may never use some pairs. If both selects were tied to one line, the settings would move together and the count would drop to the number of select values.

example.problem: The left ALU input comes from a multiplexer choosing PC or R1. The right input comes from a multiplexer choosing R2, the constant 4, or an 8-bit immediate sign-extended to 16 bits. The selects are independent. How many operand pairs can the ALU see, which pair computes PC + 4, and what 16-bit value does the immediate 0x8C become?
steps: Left side has 2 sources and right side has 3, so the pairs number $2\times3=6$.
PC + 4 needs PC on the left and the constant 4 on the right, which is one of the six pairs.
Sign extension copies the top bit of 0x8C. In binary 0x8C is 10001100, whose top bit is 1, so eight 1s are placed above it, giving 0xFF8C.
As an 8-bit signed value 0x8C is $140-256=-116$; as a 16-bit value 0xFF8C is also $-116$, so the value is preserved.
example.result: Six operand pairs; PC and the constant 4 give PC + 4; the immediate 0x8C becomes 0xFF8C, still $-116$.

misconceptions: Believing an immediate can only be paired with a register. If both ALU inputs have a multiplexer offering the immediate, two immediates are possible; the wiring decides, not habit.
Padding a negative immediate with zeros. That turns 0x8C into 0x008C, which is $+140$, not $-116$; zero extension is for unsigned values only.
Treating MAR and MDR as the same register. MAR carries the address going out to memory, MDR carries the data moving in or out.

recall.q: What does PC hold, and what does IR hold?
recall.a: PC holds the address of the next instruction. IR holds the instruction currently being executed.

recall.q: With independent selects, how many operand pairs do a 2-input and a 3-input multiplexer give the ALU?
recall.a: Six, since every choice on one side pairs with every choice on the other.

recall.q: How is a signed 8-bit value widened to 16 bits without changing its value?
recall.a: Copy its sign bit into all the new upper bits.

practice.stem: An 8-bit signed immediate 0xB4 is widened to 16 bits by the sign extender before entering the ALU. Which 16-bit pattern is produced?
practice.explanation: 0xB4 is 10110100, so its sign bit is 1 and eight 1s fill the new upper byte, giving 0xFFB4, which is $-76$ in both widths. 0x00B4 is tempting because it is zero extension, but it would change the value to $+180$. 0xB4B4 repeats the byte, which no extender does.

lesson.summary: A datapath is registers, multiplexers and an ALU joined by wires. Independent multiplexers multiply their choices into operand pairs, and sign extension keeps a signed immediate's value when it is widened.

topics.title: Single-cycle versus multi-cycle implementation
points: A single-cycle CPU finishes every instruction in one clock, so the clock period must fit the slowest instruction, normally a load that uses all five steps.
A multi-cycle CPU spends one clock per step, so the period is the slowest step and each instruction takes only the steps it needs (typically 3 to 5 cycles).
Multi-cycle wins only if the CPI × step time beats the single-cycle period: with steps 200, 100, 150, 200, 100 ps and CPI 4.05 it averages 810 ps against 750 ps, so it is slower.

lesson.why: Questions give per-step delays or per-type cycle counts and ask for a clock period, an average time per instruction or which design is faster, so the two timing rules must be second nature.
lesson.intro: Executing an instruction takes several steps, for example fetching it, decoding it, computing, touching memory and writing a result. A single-cycle processor does all the steps of an instruction inside one clock tick. A multi-cycle processor gives each step its own tick and lets an instruction stop after the steps it needs. The clock period is the time between ticks, and CPI is the average number of ticks an instruction takes.

definitions.meaning: Cycles per instruction: ticks spent on an instruction, averaged over the instruction mix when several types occur.
The time between two ticks; it must be at least as long as the slowest piece of work done in one tick.

principle.text: A single-cycle clock must fit the slowest instruction, which uses every step, so its period is the sum of the step times. A multi-cycle clock must fit only the slowest step, so its period is the maximum step time. Average time per instruction is CPI times the period. Total time is total cycles times the period, with total cycles the sum of count times CPI over the instruction types, so a known total time gives the period by division.
principle.tex: T_{\text{single}}=\sum_i t_i,\qquad T_{\text{multi}}=\mathrm{CPI}\cdot\max_i t_i,\qquad T_{\text{total}}=\Big(\sum_k n_k\,\mathrm{CPI}_k\Big)\cdot T_{\text{clock}}

lesson.limits: The formulas assume no overlap between instructions and equal step lengths per tick; a pipelined design overlaps instructions and follows other rules. The weighted CPI needs the fraction of each instruction type, and an unweighted average of the CPIs is wrong.

example.problem: Five steps take 180, 80, 120, 160 and 60 ps. In the instruction mix, 50% of instructions need 4 cycles, 30% need 5 cycles and 20% need 3 cycles on the multi-cycle design. Which design is faster per instruction?
steps: Single-cycle period is the sum of all steps: $180+80+120+160+60=600$ ps.
Multi-cycle period is the slowest step, 180 ps.
Weighted CPI is $0.5\times4+0.3\times5+0.2\times3=4.1$.
Multi-cycle time per instruction is $4.1\times180=738$ ps, which is more than 600 ps.
Run backwards: if 2000 such instructions took 1476 ns in total, total cycles are $2000\times4.1=8200$, so the period is $1476/8200=0.18$ ns, which is 180 ps.
example.result: Single-cycle takes 600 ps per instruction and multi-cycle 738 ps, so single-cycle is faster here.

misconceptions: Assuming multi-cycle is always faster because its clock is shorter. It spends several ticks per instruction, so it can lose, as the example shows.
Averaging the CPIs of the types without weights. A type that rarely runs would count as much as one that dominates.
Dividing total time by the instruction count to get the clock period. That gives time per instruction; the period needs total cycles.
