steps: The ideal time is $5+3-1=7$ cycles.
I2 reads R1 from the instruction just before it, so it stalls 2 cycles.
I3 reads R4 from I2, which is also adjacent, so it stalls 2 more cycles; it reads nothing from I1, so no extra wait arises there.

misconceptions: Do not count stalls per dependence without checking the distance; a pair two instructions apart waits 1 cycle, not 2.
An independent instruction behind a stalled one is not free; in an in-order pipeline it waits too.
Do not add the stalls of every earlier dependence to a later instruction; only the cycles it actually waits for count.

recall.q: How many stalls does an adjacent RAW pair cost with no forwarding and a split-cycle register file?
recall.a: 2 stalls.

recall.q: What is the formula for total cycles with stalls?
recall.a: $(k+n-1)$ plus the total number of stall cycles.

recall.q: With full forwarding, which pair still stalls?
recall.a: A load followed directly by an instruction that uses the loaded register, for 1 stall.

practice.stem: No forwarding, split-cycle register file, 5 stages. I1 ADD R1,R2,R3; I2 OR R5,R6,R7; I3 SUB R2,R1,R3; I4 AND R4,R2,R8. How many cycles do the four instructions take?
practice.explanation: The ideal time is $5+4-1=8$. I3 uses R1 from I1, two places earlier, so 1 stall. I4 uses R2 from I3, adjacent, so 2 stalls. I2 is independent of both. The total is $8+1+2=11$. Answering 12 comes from charging 2 stalls to the I1 to I3 pair, and 10 from forgetting that I3 uses R1 at all.

lesson.summary: Total cycles are k+n-1 plus stalls; find each producer-consumer pair, apply the stated rule for its distance, and remember every stall delays all later instructions.

topics.title: Multi-cycle EX stages and unequal latencies
points: Some questions give operations different EX latencies, for example MUL taking 3 cycles and ADD 1, on a single non-pipelined EX unit.
A multi-cycle instruction blocks the EX unit, so the next instruction waits in ID even if it is independent; dependent instructions also wait for the forwarded result.
Each cycle an instruction spends in EX beyond the first adds one cycle to the total for everything behind it in an in-order pipeline.
When stage times differ per instruction class, compute the timeline explicitly rather than plugging into (k + n − 1).

lesson.why: GATE sets pipelines where one stage takes a different number of cycles for different instructions. The usual formula for equal stages then gives a wrong total, so you need the method that replaces it.
lesson.intro: In the basic pipeline every stage takes one cycle and one instruction finishes per cycle. Here one stage, say the one that performs the operation, takes 1, 2 or 3 cycles depending on the instruction. A stage can work on only one instruction at a time, so while a slow instruction occupies it, the instructions behind it must wait; an instruction that has finished its stage but cannot move on is on hold. That stage becomes the bottleneck: the rest of the pipeline can only move as fast as it lets instructions through.

analogy.text: A toll booth on a road: cars arrive in a stream, but each one occupies the booth for its own time, so the booth sets how fast cars get through, not the road before or after it.
analogy.breaksWhen: A real road may have several booths in parallel, while this stage is a single unit that serves one instruction at a time.

definitions.meaning: The stage that is busy in every cycle, so its total busy time fixes the speed of the whole pipeline.
A cycle in which an instruction has finished a stage but cannot enter the next because that stage is still occupied.

principle.text: If the long stage is never idle once it has started, the total time is the cycles before the first instruction reaches it, plus the sum of its busy cycles over all instructions, plus the cycles after the last instruction leaves it. The order of fast and slow instructions does not matter.

lesson.limits: This shortcut needs every other stage to take at most as long as the long stage for every instruction, and no data or control hazards. If another stage can also be longer, or an instruction waits for a result, build the timeline cycle by cycle.

example.problem: A pipeline has stages IF, ID, OF, PO and WB. IF, ID, OF and WB take 1 cycle each. For six instructions the PO stage takes 2, 1, 3, 1, 2 and 1 cycles. There are no hazards. How many cycles does the run need?
steps: PO is the only stage that varies and the others take 1 cycle, so PO is the bottleneck and never idles once the first instruction arrives. Instructions behind a slow one are held until PO is free.
The first instruction spends 3 cycles in IF, ID and OF before reaching PO.
PO is busy for 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 10 cycles in total.
The last instruction then needs 1 cycle in WB, so the run takes 3 + 10 + 1 = 14 cycles.
example.result: 14 cycles. Equal stages would have given only 5 + 6 - 1 = 10.

misconceptions: The total is not k + n - 1 when a stage is longer for some instructions; each extra cycle in the long stage delays everything behind it.
Adding all stage times of all instructions counts the overlap as if there were none; only the bottleneck stage's cycles are added in full.
The long stage's cycles already include one pass through that stage, so do not add the full five stages on top of its total; add only the stages before and after it.

recall.q: Why does a stage with unequal times slow the whole pipeline?
recall.a: It serves one instruction at a time, so later instructions wait behind a slow one and cannot enter it.

recall.q: What is the total time when one stage is the never-idle bottleneck?
recall.a: Stages before it, plus the sum of its busy cycles, plus stages after it.

recall.q: Does the order of slow and fast instructions change the total?
recall.a: No, as long as the bottleneck stays busy; only the sum of its cycles matters.

practice.stem: A pipeline has stages IF, ID, OF, PO and WB, each 1 cycle except PO. Among 50 instructions, 10 take 4 cycles in PO, 20 take 2 cycles and 20 take 1 cycle. There are no hazards. How many cycles does the run need?
practice.explanation: PO is busy for 10 x 4 + 20 x 2 + 20 x 1 = 100 cycles. Add 3 cycles before it for the first instruction and 1 for the last WB: 104. Writing 50 + 4 = 54 tempts because it is the equal-stage formula, and adding 100 + 5 = 105 tempts because it counts one extra stage.

lesson.summary: With one varying stage, find the bottleneck, add its total busy cycles, then add the stages before and after it. The order of instructions does not change the total.

topics.title: Control hazards and branch penalty
points: A branch's outcome and target are known only in a later stage, but fetch must continue every cycle, so the instructions fetched behind it may be wrong.
The penalty for a wrongly fetched path equals the number of instructions fetched before resolution: 2 cycles if the branch resolves in EX, 1 cycle if it resolves in ID.
Freezing fetch until every branch resolves charges the penalty on every branch; predict-not-taken charges it only on taken branches.
Deeper pipelines allow a faster clock but resolve branches later, so each misprediction costs more cycles.

lesson.why: Branch penalty and effective CPI with branches are a standard high-frequency calculation, and the single idea to get right is which branches actually pay the penalty.
lesson.intro: A branch decides which instruction runs next, but the pipeline cannot know the decision until the branch reaches a later stage. Fetch keeps running every cycle, so the instructions fetched in the meantime may be from the wrong place. If the guess was wrong, they are thrown away, which is called a flush, and the cycles they used are lost. The number of lost cycles is called the branch penalty. The simplest policy, predict not-taken, keeps fetching the next instruction in sequence and pays the penalty only when the branch is taken.

definitions.meaning: The number of cycles lost when instructions fetched after a branch have to be discarded.
Discarding wrongly fetched instructions from the pipeline.

principle.text: If a branch resolves in stage $r$ (IF is stage 1), the penalty per wrongly fetched path is $r-1$ cycles. Freezing fetch charges it on every branch; predict not-taken charges it only on taken branches. The effective CPI adds the branch fraction times the fraction that pays times the penalty.

lesson.limits: The formula assumes every other instruction completes at one per cycle and that a correct path costs nothing. A taken branch with a branch target buffer, or a delayed branch, changes who pays.

example.problem: 20% of instructions are branches and a branch resolves in EX. Find the CPI when fetch freezes on every branch, and when the pipeline predicts not-taken and 60% of branches are taken.
steps: Resolving in EX means stage 3, so the penalty is $3-1=2$ cycles.
Freezing pays on every branch: $1+0.2\times1\times2=1.4$.
Predict not-taken pays only on the 60% taken: $1+0.2\times0.6\times2=1.24$.
example.result: CPI is 1.4 with freezing and 1.24 with predict not-taken.

misconceptions: Predict not-taken does not remove the penalty; every taken branch still costs it in full.
The penalty is not the pipeline depth; it counts only the stages before the branch resolves.
Do not apply the penalty to all instructions; only the branch fraction, and under prediction only the wrong ones, pay it.

recall.q: What is the branch penalty if a branch resolves in EX of a 5-stage pipeline?
recall.a: 2 cycles, the instructions fetched in IF and ID after it.

recall.q: Which branches pay under predict not-taken?
recall.a: Only taken branches.

recall.q: Why do deeper pipelines make mispredictions cost more?
recall.a: The branch resolves in a later stage, so more instructions have been fetched down the wrong path.

practice.stem: A 5-stage pipeline resolves branches in EX and predicts not-taken. Of 100 instructions, 25 are branches and 40% of branches are taken. Counting no other stalls, how many cycles do the 100 instructions take?
practice.explanation: The ideal time is $5+100-1=104$. Taken branches number $25\times0.4=10$, and each costs 2 cycles, so $20$ more. The total is 124. Charging all 25 branches gives 154, which is the answer for freezing on every branch.

lesson.summary: A branch loses the cycles fetched before it resolves, r-1 per wrong path; freezing charges every branch while predict not-taken charges only taken ones, and CPI adds branch fraction times wrong fraction times penalty.

topics.title: Delayed branch
points: With a delayed branch, the instruction(s) in the delay slot right after the branch always execute, whatever the outcome.
The compiler fills the slot with a useful instruction, typically one from before the branch that the branch condition does not depend on; if none qualifies it inserts a NOP.
A 5-stage pipeline that resolves branches in ID needs one delay slot to hide the whole branch penalty.

lesson.why: Delayed branch questions test whether you count the delay-slot instruction as executed work, which decides the cycle count and whether a stall is hidden.
lesson.intro: After a branch, the pipeline already holds the next instruction by the time the branch outcome is known. Instead of throwing it away, a delayed branch makes a rule: the instruction right after the branch, in the delay slot, always runs, whether the branch is taken or not. The compiler then moves a useful instruction into that slot, one that the branch does not depend on. The cycle that would have been lost does real work. If the compiler can find nothing safe to move, it fills the slot with a NOP, an instruction that does nothing.

definitions.meaning: The instruction position right after a branch whose instruction always executes.
An instruction that does no work, used to fill a delay slot when nothing useful can be moved there.

principle.text: With a delayed branch the delay-slot instruction executes on both paths. A 5-stage pipeline that resolves branches in ID loses one cycle, so one delay slot hides the whole penalty when the slot holds useful work. A slot filled with a NOP still takes a cycle, so nothing is saved.

lesson.limits: The slot hides only as many cycles as it has instructions. If the branch resolves in EX, the penalty is 2 cycles and one slot hides only half of it. A moved instruction must not feed the branch condition.

example.problem: A 5-stage pipeline resolves branches in ID. A program executes 10 instructions including one branch. Compare the cycles with a stall, a delay slot filled with a useful instruction, and a delay slot filled with a NOP.
steps: With a stall after the branch: $5+10-1=14$ plus 1 stall gives 15.
With a useful instruction in the slot, that instruction is one of the 10 and the slot hides the stall, so the time is $5+10-1=14$.
With a NOP, the program has 11 executed instructions and no stall, so $5+11-1=15$.
example.result: 15 cycles with a stall, 14 with a useful slot, 15 with a NOP.

misconceptions: A NOP in the slot is not free; it takes a pipeline cycle like any instruction.
The delay-slot instruction is not skipped when the branch is taken; it always runs.
The instruction moved into the slot cannot be one the branch condition depends on.

recall.q: When does the delay-slot instruction execute?
recall.a: Always, on both the taken and not-taken paths.

recall.q: How many delay slots hide the penalty of a branch that resolves in ID?
recall.a: One delay slot.

recall.q: What fills the slot when no useful instruction can be moved?
recall.a: A NOP.

practice.stem: A 5-stage pipeline that resolves branches in ID, with one delay slot, runs a loop whose body is 3 instructions plus a branch, 10 iterations. The compiler fills each delay slot with a NOP and there are no other stalls. How many cycles does the loop take?
practice.explanation: Each iteration executes 4 instructions plus the NOP, which is 5, so 50 in total. The time is $5+50-1=54$. Answering 44 assumes the slot holds useful work and is not an extra instruction, and 50 forgets the 4 extra cycles the pipeline needs to fill.

lesson.summary: The delay slot always executes, so a useful instruction there hides the branch penalty while a NOP only changes where the lost cycle appears.

topics.title: Static and dynamic branch prediction
points: Static schemes fix the guess at design or compile time: always taken, always not-taken, or BTFN (backward branches taken, forward not taken), which suits loops.
A 1-bit predictor stores the last outcome; on a loop branch it mispredicts twice per loop execution, at the exit and again on the next entry.
A 2-bit saturating counter (00 strongly NT, 01 weakly NT, 10 weakly T, 11 strongly T) predicts taken in states 10 and 11 and moves one step towards each actual outcome.
From a strong state it takes two consecutive mispredictions to flip the prediction; from a weak state one misprediction flips it.
A branch target buffer, indexed by PC, caches predicted targets so a taken prediction can redirect fetch in IF; correlating predictors add global history.

lesson.why: Branch prediction decides how many stall cycles a branch costs. GATE asks both for a predictor's behaviour on a sequence of outcomes and for the CPI or speed-up that a given accuracy produces.
lesson.intro: A branch is an instruction that may send the program to a different place. The branch is taken when the program jumps to the new place and not taken when it simply continues with the next instruction. The pipeline fetches the next instruction before it knows which case applies, so a wrong guess wastes the fetched instructions. A branch predictor guesses the outcome early. A correct guess costs nothing; a wrong guess pays the full branch penalty, which is the number of cycles of fetched work thrown away. Simple predictors keep a little memory of past outcomes of a branch and guess it will repeat.

definitions.meaning: A guess that differs from the actual outcome; it costs the branch penalty.
A counter from 0 to 3 that moves up on taken and down on not taken, stopping at the ends; values 2 and 3 predict taken.

principle.text: A 1-bit predictor repeats the last outcome. A 2-bit saturating counter predicts taken in states 2 and 3 and moves one step towards each actual outcome, so a single surprise does not flip a strong state. The CPI adds the average stall per instruction to the base CPI, and only mispredicted branches stall. With equal clocks, speed-up is the ratio of the two CPIs.

lesson.limits: The CPI formula assumes a correct prediction costs nothing and a wrong one costs the full penalty. If a question gives a different cost for correct taken predictions or a target buffer miss, add that term separately.

example.problem: A 2-bit saturating counter starts in state 2 (weakly taken). Ten executions of one branch are T, T, N, T, T, T, N, N, T, T. Twenty percent of all instructions are branches and a misprediction costs 3 cycles. What is the CPI, against a machine that stalls on every branch?
steps: Walk the counter: T (predicted T, ok, state 3), T (ok, 3), N (predicted T, wrong, state 2), T (ok, 3), T (ok), T (ok), N (wrong, 2), N (predicted T, wrong, 1), T (predicted N, wrong, 2), T (ok, 3).
That is 4 mispredictions in 10, so the accuracy is 60 percent.
With the predictor, CPI = 1 + 0.2 x 0.4 x 3 = 1.24.
Without it every branch stalls: CPI = 1 + 0.2 x 3 = 1.6.
Both machines have the same clock, so the speed-up is the ratio of the CPIs: 1.6 / 1.24 = 1.29.
example.result: CPI 1.24 with the predictor against 1.6 without, a speed-up of 1.29.

misconceptions: The stall probability is 1 minus the accuracy, not the accuracy itself; using the accuracy makes a good predictor look costly.
The stall applies only to the branch share of instructions, not to every instruction.
A 1-bit predictor on a loop branch mispredicts twice per loop run (at the exit and again on re-entry), while a 2-bit counter mispredicts only once, at the exit.

recall.q: What does a 2-bit saturating counter predict in each state?
recall.a: States 0 and 1 predict not taken; states 2 and 3 predict taken.

recall.q: Which fraction of branches stalls when a predictor is correct 90 percent of the time?
recall.a: The 10 percent that are mispredicted, each paying the full penalty.

recall.q: How many mispredictions does a 1-bit predictor make per run of a loop branch after the first run?
recall.a: Two: one at the exit and one on the first iteration of the next run.

recall.q: With the same clock, how is the speed-up from a predictor found?
recall.a: Divide the CPI without the predictor by the CPI with it.

practice.stem: In a program of 1000 instructions, 25 percent are branches. A predictor is correct for 90 percent of them, a correct prediction costs nothing, and each misprediction stalls 4 cycles. How many stall cycles does the program lose to branches?
practice.explanation: There are 250 branches and 10 percent, which is 25, are mispredicted. Each costs 4 cycles, so 25 x 4 = 100 stall cycles. Using the accuracy instead of the error gives 225 x 4 = 900, and charging all 250 branches gives 1000; both tempt because they ignore which branches actually stall.

lesson.summary: A predictor stalls only on wrong guesses, so CPI is 1 plus branch share times error rate times penalty. A 2-bit counter needs two surprises to flip a strong state, which suits loops.

topics.title: Out-of-order execution and register renaming
points: Out-of-order execution lets an independent later instruction run ahead of a stalled one, which exposes WAR and WAW hazards.
Register renaming maps each new destination to a fresh physical register, removing WAR and WAW (name) dependences; RAW dependences are true data flow and remain.
Speculative execution follows the predicted path and discards its results if the prediction was wrong.

lesson.why: Out-of-order execution questions are rare, but they use the same dependence vocabulary as hazard classification, and renaming is a short, precise idea worth getting right.
lesson.intro: A simple pipeline runs instructions strictly in order. If one instruction has to wait for its data, everything behind it waits too, even instructions that do not need that data. Out-of-order execution lets a later independent instruction run ahead while the earlier one waits. This is safe only if the instructions do not interfere through register names. Two kinds of name clashes appear: a later instruction writing a register an earlier one still has to read (WAR), and two instructions writing the same register (WAW). Register renaming removes these clashes by giving each new write its own hidden physical register.

definitions.meaning: Mapping each new destination register to a fresh physical register so that WAR and WAW clashes disappear.
Running instructions from a predicted path and discarding their results if the prediction was wrong.

principle.text: Renaming removes WAR and WAW dependences, which are only reuse of a name. RAW dependences carry real data from producer to consumer and remain, so a consumer still waits for its producer. Speculative results are kept only if the prediction is confirmed.

lesson.limits: Renaming needs spare physical registers and extra hardware to track the mapping. It does nothing for true data flow, and in an in-order five-stage pipeline WAR and WAW do not cause stalls at all.

example.problem: I1 DIV R1,R2,R3; I2 ADD R4,R1,R5; I3 SUB R5,R6,R7. Name each dependence, and say which renaming removes.
steps: I2 reads R1, which I1 writes, so there is a RAW dependence from I1 to I2.
I3 writes R5, which I2 reads, so there is a WAR dependence from I2 to I3.
Renaming gives I3 a new physical register for its result, so I3 can run before I2 reads the old R5.
example.result: RAW (I1, I2) remains; WAR (I2, I3) is removed by renaming.

misconceptions: Renaming does not remove RAW dependences; they are real data flow and still force the consumer to wait.
WAR and WAW do not stall an in-order five-stage pipeline; they become a problem only when instructions can complete out of order.
Speculative execution is not the same as renaming; speculation guesses a branch path, renaming resolves name clashes.

recall.q: Which dependences does register renaming remove?
recall.a: WAR and WAW, the name dependences.

recall.q: Why does out-of-order execution expose WAR and WAW hazards?
recall.a: A later instruction may finish before an earlier one that still needs the old value or must write first.

recall.q: What happens to speculative results if the prediction was wrong?
recall.a: They are discarded.

practice.stem: Count the WAR and WAW dependences, each ordered pair of instructions and register counted once per kind, in: I1 LW R1,0(R2); I2 ADD R3,R1,R4; I3 SUB R4,R5,R6; I4 MUL R1,R7,R8; I5 ADD R5,R3,R1.
practice.explanation: WAW: I1 and I4 both write R1. WAR: I2 reads R4 and I3 writes it; I2 reads R1 and I4 writes it; I3 reads R5 and I5 writes it. That is 4 in all. The RAW pairs, such as I1 to I2 on R1, are not counted, and counting them is the tempting mistake.

lesson.summary: Out-of-order execution exposes WAR and WAW name dependences, which renaming removes, while RAW data flow remains and speculation is undone if the guess was wrong.

formulas.name: Pipeline clock cycle
formulas.note: Use the maximum, not the sum or the average, of the stage delays.

formulas.name: Time for n instructions on a k-stage pipeline
formulas.note: Assumes no stalls; add the total stall cycles to (k + n − 1) when hazards occur.

formulas.name: Time for n instructions without pipelining
formulas.note: Equals n · k · τ only when all stages take the same time τ and there are no latches; with unequal stages use the sum.

formulas.name: Pipeline speedup
formulas.text: S = n·Στᵢ / ((k + n − 1)·τ), tending to Στᵢ/τ ≤ k as n grows
formulas.note: The limit is exactly k only with equal stages and zero latch delay.

formulas.name: Pipeline throughput
formulas.note: The 1/τ approximation holds after the pipeline fills, i.e. for large n.

formulas.name: Effective CPI with stalls
where: fraction of instructions of class j (branches, loads)
fraction of those that actually stall (taken, mispredicted, load-use)

formulas.name: Speedup with stalls
formulas.text: S = non-pipelined time per instruction / (CPI_pipe × τ)
formulas.note: With balanced stages and no latch overhead this reduces to k / (1 + stalls per instruction).

formulas.name: Branch stall cycles per instruction
formulas.text: branch stalls per instruction = f_branch × p_wrong × (r − 1)
where: stage number in which the branch resolves (IF = 1)
fraction of branches whose fetched path is wrong
formulas.note: r − 1 is 2 for resolution in EX (stage 3) and 1 for ID (stage 2). With freeze-on-every-branch, p_wrong = 1.

problemTypes.title: Cycle time, total time and speedup from stage delays
recipe: Cycle τ = largest stage delay + latch delay.
Pipelined time = (k + n − 1) · τ.
Non-pipelined time = n · (sum of stage delays), with no latch delay unless the question says otherwise.
Speedup = non-pipelined / pipelined; efficiency = speedup / k if asked.
problemTypes.trap: Using n · k · τ for the non-pipelined time when stages are unequal, or forgetting the latch delay in τ.

problemTypes.title: Effective CPI from branch and load statistics
recipe: List each stall source with its frequency, the fraction that actually stalls, and the cycles lost.
Multiply the three numbers per source and add them to the base CPI of 1.
If asked for speedup or time, combine the CPI with the cycle time: T = IC × CPI × τ.
problemTypes.trap: Charging the branch penalty on all branches when only taken (or mispredicted) branches pay it.

problemTypes.title: Stall or cycle count for a code sequence
recipe: Mark every RAW dependence: which register, which producer, how far apart.
Fix the rules given: forwarding or not, split-cycle register file, EX latency per operation.
Fill the space-time table one instruction at a time, delaying a stage until its operands and the stage itself are free.
Read the WB cycle of the last instruction as the total; subtract k + n − 1 to get the stall count.
problemTypes.trap: Forgetting that a stalled instruction delays everything fetched after it, including independent instructions.

problemTypes.title: Classify the dependences in an instruction sequence
recipe: For every ordered pair (earlier, later), compare the earlier one's destination with the later one's sources (RAW).
Compare the earlier one's sources with the later one's destination (WAR), and the two destinations (WAW).
Decide which of these can actually stall the given pipeline: in-order 5-stage pipelines stall only on RAW.
problemTypes.trap: Reading the register list backwards: in ADD R1,R2,R3 the destination is R1.

problemTypes.title: Misprediction count for a branch predictor
recipe: Write the branch outcome sequence (a loop of m iterations gives m − 1 taken and one not-taken).
Track the predictor state: one bit for a 1-bit predictor, a 0–3 counter for a 2-bit one, starting from the given initial state.
At each outcome compare prediction with outcome, count mismatches, then update the state.
problemTypes.trap: Moving a 2-bit counter directly from strongly taken to not-taken on a single miss.

problemTypes.title: Effect of splitting or rebalancing stages
recipe: Compute the old cycle as old maximum stage + latch.
Replace the split stage by its parts and recompute the maximum; add the latch again.
Throughput ratio = old cycle / new cycle for large n.
problemTypes.trap: The latch delay is added to both cycles, so the gain is smaller than the ratio of raw stage delays.

questions.stem: A 4-stage pipeline has stage delays 200, 250, 300 and 200 ps, and each pipeline register adds 50 ps. What is the clock cycle of the pipeline?
questions.explanation: Every stage must fit in one clock, so τ = slowest stage + latch = 300 + 50 = 350 ps. 300 ps forgets the latch, 950 ps is the non-pipelined instruction time, and 1150 ps adds a latch to every stage.

questions.stem: A 4-stage pipeline runs with a 4 ns clock. The non-pipelined version of the processor takes 16 ns per instruction. What is the speedup for a program of 1000 instructions, assuming no stalls?
questions.explanation: Pipelined time = (k + n − 1)τ = (4 + 999) × 4 = 4012 ns. Non-pipelined time = 1000 × 16 = 16000 ns. Speedup = 16000 / 4012 ≈ 3.988 ≈ 3.99, just under the ideal 4 because of the 3 fill cycles.

questions.stem: A 5-stage pipeline has stage delays 200, 150, 250, 200 and 150 ps and a 50 ps pipeline-register delay. The non-pipelined datapath takes the sum of the stage delays per instruction and has no pipeline registers. What is the speedup of the pipeline for 100 instructions with no stalls? (2 decimals)
questions.explanation: τ = 250 + 50 = 300 ps. Pipelined time = (5 + 99) × 300 = 31200 ps. Non-pipelined time = 100 × (200 + 150 + 250 + 200 + 150) = 100 × 950 = 95000 ps. Speedup = 95000 / 31200 ≈ 3.04 to 3.05, far below 5 because the stages are unbalanced and the latch adds 50 ps. Efficiency is 3.045 / 5 ≈ 61%.

questions.stem: A 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding predicts every branch not taken and resolves branches in EX, losing 2 cycles on a taken branch. In a program, 20% of instructions are branches and 60% of branches are taken; 25% of instructions are loads, and 40% of loads are immediately followed by an instruction that uses the loaded value. What is the effective CPI? (2 decimals)
questions.explanation: Branch stalls per instruction = 0.20 × 0.60 × 2 = 0.24. Load-use stalls per instruction = 0.25 × 0.40 × 1 = 0.10 (one cycle each, since forwarding cannot help a load followed directly by its use). CPI = 1 + 0.24 + 0.10 = 1.34.

questions.stem:
A 5-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) has no operand forwarding. The register file is written in the first half of a cycle and read in the second half, so an instruction can read a register in ID during the cycle in which the producer is in WB. How many clock cycles does this sequence take, from the first IF to the last WB?
I1: ADD R1, R2, R3
I2: SUB R4, R1, R5
I3: AND R6, R1, R7
I4: OR R8, R4, R6
questions.explanation: I1: IF 1, ID 2, EX 3, MEM 4, WB 5. I2 needs R1, so its ID read waits until cycle 5 (stalled in ID during 3 and 4): EX 6, MEM 7, WB 8. I3 is held in IF until I2 leaves ID, so ID 6 (R1 already written), EX 7, MEM 8, WB 9. I4 needs R4 (WB 8) and R6 (WB 9), so ID is in cycle 9: EX 10, MEM 11, WB 12. The stall-free time is 5 + 4 − 1 = 8 cycles, so there are 4 stall cycles in total.

questions.stem:
An in-order 5-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) has a single non-pipelined EX unit. MUL spends 3 cycles in EX; every other instruction spends 1. Full forwarding is available: a result produced at the end of EX can be used by an instruction starting EX in the next cycle. An instruction waits in ID until the EX unit is free and its operands are available, and instructions behind it wait in their stages. How many cycles does this sequence take, from the first IF to the last WB?
I1: MUL R1, R2, R3
I2: ADD R4, R1, R5
I3: SUB R6, R7, R8
I4: MUL R9, R4, R6
questions.explanation: I1: IF 1, ID 2, EX 3–5, MEM 6, WB 7. I2 needs R1 (ready after cycle 5) and the EX unit, so EX 6, MEM 7, WB 8. I3 is independent but stays in IF until I2 leaves ID: ID 6, EX 7, MEM 8, WB 9. I4: IF 6, ID 7, EX 8–10 (R4 and R6 are forwarded from the ends of cycles 6 and 7), MEM 11, WB 12. Total 12 cycles: the base 8 plus 2 cycles waiting for I1's EX and 2 extra EX cycles of I4.

questions.stem: The branch at the bottom of a 4-iteration loop is taken 3 times and then not taken, giving the outcome sequence T, T, T, N. The loop is executed 3 times in a row (12 branch executions). A 2-bit saturating counter starts in the strongly not-taken state and predicts taken in its two upper states. How many mispredictions occur?
questions.explanation: Counter states 0–3, predict taken when ≥ 2. First pass: T at state 0 (miss, → 1), T at 1 (miss, → 2), T at 2 (hit, → 3), N at 3 (miss, → 2). Second pass: T, T, T all hit (→ 3), N miss (→ 2). Third pass: the same, 1 miss. Total 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5. A 1-bit predictor starting at not-taken would miss 6 times: the first T and then both the exit and the re-entry of every loop.

questions.stem: On the standard 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding, LW R1, 0(R2) is immediately followed by ADD R3, R1, R4. How many stall cycles does the ADD suffer?
questions.explanation: The loaded value exists only at the end of the load's MEM stage, while the ADD would want it at the start of its EX stage in that same cycle. Forwarding from MEM/WB into EX works one cycle later, so exactly one bubble is needed. Without forwarding it would be two.

questions.stem: The sequence LW R1, 0(R2); ADD R3, R1, R4; SW R3, 0(R5) runs on a 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding (EX/MEM and MEM/WB to EX). How many clock cycles does it take from the first IF to the last WB?
questions.explanation: Without stalls 3 instructions take 5 + 3 − 1 = 7 cycles. LW → ADD is a load-use pair: 1 stall. ADD → SW is an ALU result needed by the following store, which forwarding delivers in time: 0 stalls. Total 7 + 1 = 8 cycles. 9 would charge the store a stall it does not need, and 11 is the no-forwarding count.

questions.stem: A 5-stage pipeline predicts branches not taken. Moving branch resolution from the EX stage to the ID stage changes the penalty of a taken branch from:
questions.explanation: The penalty equals the number of instructions fetched after the branch before it resolves. Resolved in EX (stage 3), two wrong instructions are in IF and ID: 2 cycles. Resolved in ID (stage 2), only the one in IF is wrong: 1 cycle.

questions.stem: A pipelined processor has a single memory port shared by instruction fetch and data access. Which pair of stages can conflict, and what removes the conflict?
options: IF and MEM; separate instruction and data caches
IF and ID; a branch delay slot
questions.explanation: A load or store accesses memory in MEM in the same cycle that a later instruction is being fetched in IF, so both need the single port. Split instruction and data caches give each its own port. ID and WB share the register file but are separated by the split-cycle read and write.

questions.stem: A 5-stage pipeline has stage delays 5, 7, 10, 8 and 6 ns and a 1 ns pipeline-register delay. The 10 ns stage is split into two 5 ns stages, giving 6 stages. For a long instruction stream with no stalls, by what factor does throughput increase?
questions.explanation: Old cycle = 10 + 1 = 11 ns. New stage delays are 5, 7, 5, 5, 8, 6, so the new cycle = 8 + 1 = 9 ns. Throughput for large n is 1/τ, so the gain is 11/9 ≈ 1.22. Ignoring the latch gives 10/8 = 1.25, and 2.00 assumes the clock halves.

questions.stem: A pipeline has one branch delay slot. The code is: ADD R5, R6, R7; SUB R1, R1, R3; BEQ R1, R2, L. Which is the best way for the compiler to fill the delay slot after BEQ?
options: Move ADD R5, R6, R7 into the slot
Move SUB R1, R1, R3 into the slot
Leave the slot empty, since the hardware discards it
Put a copy of BEQ R1, R2, L into the slot
questions.explanation: The slot always executes, so it needs an instruction that must run anyway and that the branch does not depend on. ADD writes R5, which the branch neither reads nor needs, so moving it after BEQ preserves the program. SUB produces R1, which BEQ compares, so it must stay before the branch. Hardware does not discard a delay-slot instruction; an unfillable slot gets a NOP.

questions.stem: Consider I1: ADD R1, R2, R3; I2: SUB R2, R4, R5; I3: MUL R1, R6, R2, where the first register is the destination. Which statements are correct?
options: There is a RAW dependence from I2 to I3 on R2
There is a WAR dependence from I1 to I2 on R2
There is a WAW dependence from I1 to I3 on R1
There is a RAW dependence from I1 to I3 on R1
questions.explanation: I2 writes R2 and I3 reads it: RAW. I1 reads R2 and I2 later writes it: WAR. I1 and I3 both write R1: WAW. I3 does not read R1 (its sources are R6 and R2), so there is no RAW on R1.

questions.stem: Which statements about data hazards are correct?
options: In an in-order 5-stage pipeline that reads registers in ID and writes them in WB, WAR and WAW dependences cause no stalls
Register renaming removes WAR and WAW hazards
Full operand forwarding removes every RAW stall in the 5-stage pipeline
questions.explanation: In order, every read in ID precedes a later instruction's write in WB, and writes happen in program order, so WAR and WAW are harmless. Renaming gives each write a fresh physical register, eliminating name dependences. Forwarding still leaves the 1-cycle load-use stall, and renaming cannot remove RAW, which is real data flow.

questions.stem: Which statements about branch predictors are correct?
options: A 1-bit predictor mispredicts a loop branch twice per loop execution once the loop has run before: at the exit and at the next entry
A 2-bit saturating counter in the strongly-taken state needs two consecutive not-taken outcomes before it predicts not-taken
A 2-bit saturating counter never changes its prediction after a single misprediction
Static BTFN prediction predicts backward branches as not taken
questions.explanation: The 1-bit predictor learns N at the loop exit and then mispredicts the first T on re-entry. From strongly taken (11), one N gives weakly taken (10), still predicting taken; a second N gives 01. But from a weak state a single miss does flip the prediction, so the third statement is false. BTFN predicts backward branches (loops) taken.

pitfalls.text: The fill term: n instructions on k stages take k + n − 1 cycles, not n·k and not n + k.
Forwarding does not remove the load-use stall: a use immediately after a load still waits 1 cycle.
The branch penalty depends on where the branch resolves: 2 cycles in EX, 1 in ID. Charge it only on branches whose fetched path is wrong under the given policy.
Effective CPI is 1 plus the stall cycles per instruction; quoting CPI = 1 for a pipeline with hazards overstates performance.
The non-pipelined instruction time is the sum of the stage delays without latches, while the pipelined cycle is the maximum stage plus the latch.
A stalled instruction delays every instruction behind it, including independent ones; recount the later rows of the space-time table after each stall.

revisionCard.heading: Timing
lines: τ = max stage + latch
T_pipe = (k + n − 1)·τ; T_non-pipe = n·Σ stages
Speedup → k (ideal), efficiency = S/k, throughput → 1/τ
CPI = 1 + stalls per instruction; T = IC × CPI × τ

revisionCard.heading: Hazards
lines: Structural: same unit, fix with split I/D caches or duplicates
Data: RAW (true), WAR (anti), WAW (output); in-order 5-stage stalls only on RAW
Control: branch penalty = stages before resolution (EX: 2, ID: 1)

revisionCard.heading: Remedies
lines: Forwarding: ALU-to-ALU RAW costs 0, load-use costs 1
No forwarding, split register file: adjacent RAW costs 2
Delay slot: fill with an independent instruction, else NOP
Renaming removes WAR and WAW, never RAW

revisionCard.heading: Predictors
lines: 1-bit: two misses per loop execution
2-bit: 00 SNT, 01 WNT, 10 WT, 11 ST; predict taken at 10 and 11
BTFN: backward taken, forward not taken

errata.claim: Non-pipelined time is T = n · k · τ_nonpipelined, with τ_nonpipelined taken as the sum of the stage delays.
errata.correction: If τ_nonpipelined is the sum of the stage delays (the whole instruction time), the non-pipelined time is n · τ_nonpipelined, not n · k · τ_nonpipelined. The form n · k · τ holds only when τ is a single stage's delay and all stages are equal.

errata.claim: With a 2-bit saturating counter a single anomaly does not flip the prediction; it takes two consecutive wrong outcomes to flip.
errata.correction: This holds only from a strong state (00 or 11). From a weak state (01 or 10) one misprediction moves the counter across the threshold and flips the prediction.

errata.claim: The RAW dependence cannot be eliminated without forwarding.
errata.correction: Forwarding does not eliminate a RAW dependence; it only shortens or removes the stall it causes (and cannot remove the load-use stall). The dependence is real data flow and remains under any technique.

references.title: Hennessy & Patterson — Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach

chapters.title: Memory Hierarchy
chapters.summary: The memory hierarchy stacks small fast storage over large slow storage so that, thanks to locality, most references are served near the CPU. GATE tests it almost entirely through computation: split an address into tag, index and offset, size the tag directory, trace hits and misses under a mapping and replacement policy, and compute the average access time for one or more cache levels under hierarchical or simultaneous access. Memory interfacing (building a memory from smaller chips) and interleaving complete the 2027 syllabus.
highYield: Tag, index and offset widths for a direct-mapped, k-way or fully associative cache: a short NAT calculation: take the logarithm of each size and subtract.
Average memory access time for two cache levels, with the hierarchical vs simultaneous distinction and local hit ratios.
Tag-directory size: lines × (tag + valid + dirty + replacement bits).
Hit/miss trace of a short block-address sequence under direct mapping vs set-associative LRU.
Miss counts for row-wise vs column-wise array traversal, and the stall-cycle CPI that follows from a miss rate.

topics.title: The hierarchy and locality of reference
points: From registers through L1, L2, L3, main memory and SSD/HDD, each level is larger, slower and cheaper per byte than the one above it.

Temporal locality: an address used now is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality: addresses near it are likely to be used soon. Caches keep recent blocks to exploit the first and fetch whole blocks to exploit the second.
In an inclusive hierarchy every block held in L1 is also held in L2; in an exclusive one a block lives in at most one of the two levels, so the total capacity is the sum.
The hierarchy works only because a small fast level serves most references: with a 95% hit ratio, 1 ns cache and 100 ns memory, the average stays near 6 ns, not 100.

lesson.why: Every cache question rests on one fact: a small fast memory can stand in for a huge slow one because programs reuse data. Knowing why lets you judge when the average access time stays low and when it does not.
lesson.intro: A computer keeps data in several memories. Registers are tiny and instant, the cache is small and fast, main memory is larger and slower, and disk is huge and slowest. Faster memory costs more per byte, so a machine cannot be built from fast memory alone. Instead it keeps the data in use near the top. This works because programs are predictable: they tend to use the same addresses again, and addresses close to one they just used. The first habit is called temporal locality and the second spatial locality.

analogy.text: A desk, a bookshelf and a library: you keep the books you are using on the desk, the likely ones on the shelf, and the rest in the library.
analogy.breaksWhen: A person chooses what goes on the desk with understanding, while a cache guesses from past accesses only, so a program with no reuse gets no benefit.

definitions.meaning: An address used now is likely to be used again soon.
Addresses near the one just used are likely to be used soon.
Every block in the smaller level is also present in the next larger level.

principle.text: Because most references are served by the small fast level, the average access time is close to that level's time. With hit ratio $h$, fast time $t_c$ and slow-level time $t_m$, a miss pays the extra $t_m$ on top of $t_c$.

lesson.limits: The gain disappears when references do not repeat or stay near each other, such as a scan over data larger than the cache that touches each address once. In an exclusive hierarchy the capacities add up, while in an inclusive one the larger level's size is the total.

example.problem: A cache takes 2 ns and has hit ratio 0.9. Main memory adds 80 ns on a miss. What is the average access time?
steps: The miss ratio is $1 - 0.9 = 0.1$.
The average extra cost of misses is $0.1 \times 80 = 8$ ns.
Add the cache time paid on every access: $2 + 8 = 10$ ns.
example.result: 10 ns, against 82 ns if every access went to memory after checking the cache.

misconceptions: Spatial locality is not the same as temporal locality: reusing the same address is temporal, touching its neighbours is spatial, and fetching a whole block is what exploits the second.
A high hit ratio does not mean the average equals the cache time; the miss ratio times the large penalty still adds to it.
Inclusion does not add capacity: in an inclusive pair the L1 contents are duplicated in L2, so only an exclusive pair offers the sum.

recall.q: Which kind of locality does fetching a whole block exploit?
recall.a: Spatial locality, because the neighbours of the requested address are likely to be needed next.

recall.q: Why is the hierarchy not built from fast memory alone?
recall.a: Fast memory costs much more per byte, so a small fast level backed by larger slower ones gives low average time at low cost.

recall.q: What is the difference between an inclusive and an exclusive cache pair?
recall.a: Inclusive keeps every L1 block also in L2; exclusive keeps a block in at most one of them, so the capacities add.

practice.stem: A cache with access time 1 ns has hit ratio 0.8. A miss costs an extra 50 ns from main memory. What is the average access time in ns?
practice.explanation: Miss ratio is 0.2, so the miss cost averages $0.2 \times 50 = 10$ ns, and adding the 1 ns paid on every access gives 11 ns. A tempting 10 ns forgets the cache time that a miss also pays, and 41 ns multiplies by the hit ratio instead of the miss ratio.

lesson.summary: Programs reuse addresses and their neighbours, so a small fast level serves most references and the average time is the fast time plus the miss ratio times the penalty.

topics.title: Blocks, hits and the tag | index | offset split
points: Memory and cache are divided into blocks (lines) of B bytes, a power of 2; a hit means the referenced block is already in the cache.
Offset = log₂ B bits picks the byte inside a block; index = log₂ S bits picks the set, where S = number of lines ÷ associativity; the tag is everything left over.
Example: 32-bit address, 4 KB cache, 16-byte blocks, 4-way gives 256 lines, 64 sets, offset 4, index 6 and tag 32 − 4 − 6 = 22 bits.
The index is computed from sets, not lines: doubling associativity at fixed capacity removes one index bit and adds one tag bit.

lesson.why: Questions on tag width, index width and total cache size all begin with the same step: cutting the address into three fields. Once that cut is automatic, each of those questions is one line of arithmetic.
lesson.intro: A cache keeps copies of memory in blocks (also called lines) of a fixed size. To find an address, the cache reads it as three fields, from the right. The offset says which byte inside the block. The index says which set to look in, where a set is the group of lines in which a block is allowed to live. The tag is all the bits left over; it is stored beside each line so the cache can tell which of the many blocks sharing that set is currently there.

definitions.meaning: The fixed-size chunk of memory that moves between memory and the cache as one unit.
A group of lines; a block can sit in any line of exactly one set. A direct-mapped cache has one line per set.
The high address bits stored with a line to identify which block it holds.

principle.text: Let $A$ be the address bits, $C$ the cache capacity in bytes, $B$ the block size in bytes and $k$ the lines per set. The three fields add up to the address width. The offset needs enough bits to name every byte of a block, the index enough bits to name every set, and the tag takes the rest.

lesson.limits: The index counts sets, not lines: with more ways per set there are fewer sets, so the index shrinks and the tag grows by the same amount. A fully associative cache has one set, so its index has 0 bits. The rule assumes a byte-addressable memory; if the block size is given in words, convert to bytes first.

example.problem: A byte-addressable machine has 32-bit addresses and a direct-mapped cache of 8 KB with 32-byte blocks. How many bits are in the offset, the index and the tag?
steps: A block holds 32 bytes, so the offset needs $\log_2 32 = 5$ bits.
The cache holds $8192 / 32 = 256$ lines. Direct mapping gives one line per set, so there are 256 sets and the index needs $\log_2 256 = 8$ bits.
The tag is what remains of the address: $32 - 8 - 5 = 19$ bits.
example.result: Offset 5 bits, index 8 bits, tag 19 bits.

misconceptions: The index is not the number of lines in the cache. It is the number of sets, so a 4-way cache has a quarter as many index values as it has lines.
The tag is not a separate piece of the cache size calculation: it never reduces the data capacity. Capacity is lines times block size, and the tags are extra storage beside it.
A bigger block does not add tag bits. It adds offset bits and, for a fixed capacity, removes index bits, so the tag stays the same in a direct-mapped cache.

recall.q: In which order are the three address fields read, and what does each pick?
recall.a: From the right: offset picks the byte in the block, index picks the set, and the tag is the remaining high bits identifying the block.

recall.q: How many index bits does a fully associative cache have?
recall.a: None, since all lines form a single set and $\log_2 1 = 0$.

recall.q: What happens to the tag width when associativity doubles at fixed capacity and block size?
recall.a: The number of sets halves, so the index loses one bit and the tag gains one bit.

practice.stem: A processor uses 30-bit byte addresses and a 2-way set-associative cache of 8 KB with 32-byte blocks. How many bits are in the tag?
practice.explanation: The offset is $\log_2 32 = 5$ bits. The cache has $8192/32 = 256$ lines, grouped in pairs, so 128 sets and 7 index bits. The tag is $30 - 7 - 5 = 18$. The tempting answer is 17: it takes the index from the 256 lines (8 bits) and forgets that two lines share each set.

lesson.summary: Cut the address into offset (log of block size), index (log of the number of sets) and tag (the rest). Associativity changes the set count, so it moves bits between index and tag.

topics.title: Direct mapping
points: Block number b = ⌊address ÷ B⌋ can live only in line b mod L, where L is the number of lines.
Lookup reads one line and compares one tag, so hit time is the lowest and the hardware the simplest.
Two frequently used blocks with the same index evict each other on every access (ping-pong), producing conflict misses even when the rest of the cache is empty.
With 4 lines and 1-byte blocks, addresses 0, 4, 8, 12 all land in line 0, so the sequence 0, 4, 8, 12, 0, 4, 8 misses every time.

lesson.why: Direct mapping is the simplest placement rule and the base case for every other mapping. Questions ask which addresses collide and how many misses a sequence causes.
lesson.intro: A cache holds memory in fixed-size blocks and stores each block in a slot called a line. In a direct-mapped cache each block is allowed in exactly one line, found by dividing the block number by the number of lines and keeping the remainder. To look up an address, the cache goes to that one line and compares a stored label, the tag, with the block's own. A match is a hit; otherwise the block is fetched and replaces whatever was there.

definitions.meaning: One slot of the cache that holds a single block plus its tag and status bits.
A miss caused by two blocks needing the same line while other lines may be empty.

principle.text: Block $b$ is the address divided by the block size, rounded down. With $L$ lines it can live only in line $b \bmod L$.

lesson.limits: The rule is rigid: blocks whose numbers differ by a multiple of $L$ share a line and evict each other even if the cache is mostly empty. Associative caches relax this at the cost of more comparators. There is no replacement choice to make, since each block has one possible line.

example.problem: A direct-mapped cache has 8 lines of 16 bytes. Byte addresses 0, 16, 128, 0, 16, 32 are read in order. Which are hits?
steps: Block numbers are $\lfloor a/16 \rfloor$: 0, 1, 8, 0, 1, 2. Lines are block mod 8: 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 2.
Address 0 and 16 miss and fill lines 0 and 1. Address 128 is block 8, also line 0, so it misses and evicts block 0.
Address 0 now misses again and evicts block 8. Address 16 finds block 1 still in line 1, a hit. Address 32 is a first use of line 2, a miss.
example.result: Only the fifth access (address 16) hits: 5 misses out of 6.

misconceptions: Using the byte address mod the number of lines is wrong; divide by the block size first, because every byte of a block shares one line.
A conflict miss does not mean the cache is full; in a direct-mapped cache two blocks can fight over one line while the others stay empty.
Hit time is lowest because one tag is compared, but that does not make the hit ratio the best, since conflicts lower it.

recall.q: How is the line of an address found in a direct-mapped cache?
recall.a: Divide the address by the block size to get the block number, then take it mod the number of lines.

recall.q: Why do blocks 0 and 8 collide in a cache of 8 lines?
recall.a: Both have remainder 0 when divided by 8, so both can only use line 0.

recall.q: Why does a direct-mapped cache need no replacement policy?
recall.a: Each block has exactly one possible line, so there is never a choice of victim.

practice.stem: A direct-mapped cache has 4 lines of 16 bytes. Byte addresses 0, 16, 64, 16, 0, 64 are read in this order, starting from an empty cache. How many accesses miss?
practice.explanation: Blocks are 0, 1, 4, 1, 0, 4 and lines are 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0. Addresses 0, 16 and 64 miss, and 64 evicts block 0 from line 0. The second 16 hits. Then 0 misses and evicts block 4, and 64 misses again, giving 5 misses. Counting 3 treats only first uses as misses and ignores the conflict between blocks 0 and 4.

lesson.summary: A direct-mapped cache places block $b$ in line $b \bmod L$, so lookup is one tag compare but blocks with the same remainder keep evicting each other.

topics.title: Set-associative and fully associative mapping
points: A k-way set-associative cache has S = L/k sets; block b goes to set b mod S and may occupy any of the k lines there.
Direct mapping is the 1-way case and fully associative is the L-way case with a single set, zero index bits and a tag of all non-offset bits.
Fully associative placement has no conflict misses but needs a comparator on every line; typical caches are 4- to 16-way as a compromise.
On the block sequence 0, 4, 0, 4, 8, 0, 4 with 4 lines, direct mapping misses 7 times, 2-way LRU 5 times and fully associative LRU 3 times.

lesson.why: GATE asks where a block may be placed and how many sets a cache has, and these decide the miss counts of every access sequence. The three mappings are one idea with a single dial, the number of lines per set.
lesson.intro: Suppose the cache has $L$ lines. A direct-mapped cache gives each memory block exactly one line it may use, so two blocks that want the same line keep evicting each other (removing the other to make room). A fully associative cache lets a block use any line, which removes that fight but means the hardware must check every line. A $k$-way set-associative cache sits between: the lines are grouped into sets of $k$, the block number picks the set, and the block may use any of the $k$ lines in it.

definitions.meaning: Each set holds $k$ lines, so a block has $k$ places it may occupy.
A miss caused by blocks competing for the same set while other sets stay unused.

principle.text: With $L$ lines and $k$ lines per set there are $S = L/k$ sets, and block number $b$ goes to set $b \bmod S$. Setting $k=1$ gives direct mapping and $k=L$ gives fully associative.

lesson.limits: More ways do not always mean fewer misses on a given sequence: with a short sequence or an unlucky replacement order, 2-way can tie direct mapping. Associativity also costs a comparator per way, so every extra way adds a comparator and a slower, costlier lookup. Fully associative placement removes conflict misses but not the misses on first use.

example.problem: A cache has 4 lines. Blocks are requested in the order 0, 2, 4, 0, starting empty. Count the misses for direct mapping, 2-way with least recently used (LRU) replacement, and fully associative with LRU.
steps: Direct mapped: 4 sets, so blocks 0 and 4 share line 0. Block 0 misses, 2 misses, 4 misses and evicts 0, and the final 0 misses again: 4 misses.
Two-way: 2 sets, and the even blocks 0, 2 and 4 all map to set 0. Blocks 0 and 2 fill it. Block 4 evicts the least recently used one, block 0, so the last request for 0 misses: 4 misses.
Fully associative: one set of 4 lines holds 0, 2 and 4 together, so only the first three requests miss and the final 0 hits: 3 misses.
example.result: Direct mapped 4 misses, 2-way 4 misses, fully associative 3 misses.

misconceptions: Set-associative does not mean the block can go anywhere in the cache. It can go in any line of one specific set, chosen by the block number, so a conflict can still happen.
Direct mapped is not a different design from set-associative. It is the case with one line per set, and fully associative is the case with a single set.

recall.q: How many sets does a $k$-way cache with $L$ lines have, and which set does block $b$ use?
recall.a: It has $L/k$ sets, and block $b$ uses set $b \bmod (L/k)$.

recall.q: What are the number of sets and the index width of a fully associative cache?
recall.a: One set and 0 index bits, so the tag is every address bit except the offset.

recall.q: Why not make every cache fully associative?
recall.a: Every line would need its own comparator, and the search slows and costs more as the cache grows.

practice.stem: A 4-way set-associative cache of 16 KB has 32-byte blocks and a 32-bit address. Byte address 0x1A7C is accessed. Which set does it map to?
practice.explanation: The offset is 5 bits, so the block number is $6780 / 32 = 211$ (6780 is 0x1A7C in decimal). The cache has 512 lines, hence 128 sets, and the set is $211 \bmod 128 = 83$. The value 211 is the line a direct-mapped cache would use, so it ignores the ways. The value 19 divides the lines by the wrong factor. The value 124 uses the byte address and forgets to remove the offset first.

lesson.summary: A $k$-way cache has $L/k$ sets and sends block $b$ to set $b \bmod (L/k)$; direct mapping and full associativity are the two ends of the same scale.

topics.title: Tag directory size and lookup hardware
points: Each line stores its tag plus a valid bit; a write-back cache adds a dirty bit, and LRU replacement adds log₂ k bits per line in a k-way set.
Tag-directory size = number of lines × (tag + valid + dirty + replacement bits); the data array is not part of it.
A k-way lookup reads the k tags of one set in parallel, so it needs k comparators of tag width and a k-to-1 multiplexer to pick the data.
A fully associative cache needs one comparator per line; a direct-mapped cache needs exactly one comparator and no way-select multiplexer.

lesson.why: A cache is more than its data: each line carries tag and status bits, and the question may ask for the total storage or the number of comparators. Both follow from the address split and a short list of what each line stores.
lesson.intro: The tag directory is the table of bookkeeping kept next to the data array, with one entry per cache line. An entry holds the tag, so the cache can tell which block the line contains, and a valid bit, which says whether the line holds anything yet. A write-back cache, where a store updates only the cache and memory is updated later, adds a dirty bit, which says the line was changed after loading. A cache with LRU replacement, which evicts the line unused for the longest time, also stores a few bits per line to track recency. On a lookup the cache compares the tags of the chosen set with the tag of the address.

definitions.meaning: One bit per line that is 1 once the line holds a real block, so stale contents after power-up never count as a hit.
One bit per line in a write-back cache that is 1 when the line differs from main memory and must be written back on eviction.

principle.text: The directory has one entry per line, and each entry stores the tag plus the status bits the design needs. The data array is counted separately. A $k$-way lookup compares $k$ tags at once, so it needs $k$ comparators.

lesson.limits: Include a bit only if the design has it: a write-through cache has no dirty bit, and a direct-mapped cache has no replacement bits because there is no choice of victim. If a question asks only for the total tag bits, count the tag field alone and leave out the status bits.

example.problem: A 4-way set-associative write-back cache has 16 KB of data, 32-byte blocks, 32-bit addresses and LRU replacement using $\log_2 4$ bits per line. Find the size of the tag directory in bits and the number of comparators.
steps: The cache has $16384/32 = 512$ lines in 128 sets, so the index is 7 bits, the offset 5 bits and the tag $32-7-5 = 20$ bits.
Each entry stores the tag, one valid bit, one dirty bit and $\log_2 4 = 2$ LRU bits: $20+1+1+2 = 24$ bits.
The directory has 512 entries, so it holds $512 \times 24 = 12288$ bits. A lookup reads one set, so it uses 4 comparators of 20 bits and a 4-to-1 multiplexer.
example.result: 12288 bits (1.5 KB) of directory and 4 comparators.

misconceptions: The tag directory is not part of the cache capacity quoted for the data. A 16 KB cache holds 16 KB of data, and the directory is extra storage on top.
A cache does not compare the tags of every line on each access unless it is fully associative. A set-associative cache compares only the $k$ tags of the one selected set.

recall.q: What does one tag directory entry hold?
recall.a: The tag, a valid bit, a dirty bit if the cache is write-back, and any replacement bits the policy needs.

recall.q: How many comparators does a direct-mapped cache need?
recall.a: One, since each address can live in only one line, and no way-select multiplexer is needed.

recall.q: Why does a write-through cache need no dirty bit?
recall.a: Every store also goes to memory, so no line is ever newer than memory.

practice.stem: A direct-mapped write-back cache holds 8 KB of data with 16-byte blocks and 32-bit addresses. Each line stores a tag, a valid bit and a dirty bit. How many bits does the tag directory contain in total?
practice.explanation: The cache has $8192/16 = 512$ lines, so 9 index bits and 4 offset bits, which leaves a tag of $32-9-4 = 19$ bits. With the two status bits each entry has 21 bits, and $512 \times 21 = 10752$. Counting only the tags gives 9728, which is tempting but misses the valid and dirty bits that the question includes.

lesson.summary: Directory size is the number of lines times the bits per entry (tag and status), and a $k$-way lookup needs $k$ comparators.

topics.title: Replacement policies
points: When the target set is full, LRU evicts the line used longest ago, FIFO the line loaded longest ago, LFU the least often used line, and Random any line.
Belady's optimal (MIN) evicts the line whose next use is farthest in the future; it needs future knowledge, so it serves only as a benchmark.
FIFO can suffer Belady's anomaly: on 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 it faults 9 times with 3 frames and 10 with 4. LRU is a stack algorithm and never does.
Direct mapping needs no policy at all: each block has exactly one possible line.

lesson.why: When a set is full, the cache must choose a victim, and traces under LRU or FIFO are routine exam work. The policies differ only in what they remember.
lesson.intro: A cache set holds a few blocks. When a new block arrives and the set is full, one resident block must leave. The replacement policy decides which. Least Recently Used removes the block unused for the longest time, betting that the past predicts the future. First In First Out removes the block that arrived earliest, whether or not it was used since. An ideal policy would remove the block needed farthest in the future, but that needs knowledge of the future, so it serves only as a yardstick.

definitions.meaning: Evict the block whose last use is the oldest.
Evict the block that has been resident the longest, ignoring later uses.
Evict the block whose next use is farthest away; it needs the future and is only a benchmark.

principle.text: A policy ranks the resident blocks and evicts the lowest-ranked one. LRU ranks by last use, which a hit refreshes; FIFO ranks by arrival, which a hit leaves unchanged.

lesson.limits: Policies apply only within a set, and direct mapping has no choice to make. FIFO can fault more with more frames (Belady's anomaly), while LRU never does. Optimal cannot be built in hardware.

example.problem: A set has 3 frames, initially empty. The block references are 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 1, 2, 5. How many misses occur under LRU and under FIFO?
steps: Both policies miss on 1, 2, 3 and hit on the second 1. The set then holds 1, 2, 3.
At 4: LRU evicts 2, the oldest use, while FIFO evicts 1, the earliest arrival. LRU then hits on 1; FIFO misses on 1 and evicts 2.
At 2: LRU misses and evicts 3; FIFO misses and evicts 3. At 5 both miss, LRU evicting 4 and FIFO evicting 4. Count: LRU has 6 misses, FIFO has 7.
example.result: LRU 6 misses, FIFO 7 misses.

misconceptions: A hit does not change a block's place under FIFO; only LRU treats a hit as a fresh use.
More frames do not always mean fewer faults for FIFO: on 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 it faults 9 times with 3 frames and 10 with 4.
Optimal is not a usable policy; it needs the future and is used only to measure how good the others are.

recall.q: Which block does LRU evict?
recall.a: The one whose most recent use is the oldest.

recall.q: How does FIFO differ from LRU on a hit?
recall.a: FIFO leaves the block's arrival order unchanged, while LRU moves it to most recent.

recall.q: What is Belady's anomaly?
recall.a: Giving a FIFO cache more frames can increase the number of faults; LRU does not behave this way.

practice.stem: A fully associative cache of 3 blocks starts empty and sees block references 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Which statement is true?
options: FIFO has 9 misses and LRU has 10 misses.
FIFO has 10 misses and LRU has 9 misses.
FIFO has 9 misses and LRU has 8 misses.
practice.explanation: FIFO faults on 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 3, 4 for 9 misses, since 1 and 2 hit after 5 arrives. LRU, in this cyclic pattern, always evicts the block that is needed soonest, so it misses 10 times. The second option reverses the two and tempts because LRU is usually better; here the pattern cycles through more blocks than fit.

lesson.summary: On a full set, LRU evicts the oldest use and FIFO the oldest arrival; optimal evicts the farthest next use but needs the future, and only FIFO can show Belady's anomaly.

topics.title: Write policies
points: Write-through updates the cache and main memory on every store: memory is always current, but every store costs memory bandwidth.
Write-back updates only the cache and sets the dirty bit; the block is written to memory when it is evicted, so repeated stores to one block cost one memory write.
On a write miss, write-allocate fetches the block and then writes it; no-write-allocate sends the write straight to memory and leaves the cache unchanged.
The usual pairings are write-back with write-allocate and write-through with no-write-allocate.

lesson.why: Statements about write-through, write-back and the two write-miss policies are a standard true-or-false item. Each one follows from a single question: when does main memory learn about a store?
lesson.intro: When the processor stores a value and the block is in the cache, the cache copy changes, and memory still holds the old value. A write-through cache fixes this at once by sending every store to memory as well. A write-back cache does not: it marks the line with a dirty bit and writes the block to memory only when the line is evicted (removed from the cache to make room for another block). A separate choice applies when the store misses. Write-allocate loads the block into the cache first and then writes it. No-write-allocate sends the store to memory and leaves the cache alone.

definitions.meaning: Every store updates the cache and main memory together, so memory is never out of date.
A store updates only the cache and sets the dirty bit; memory is updated when a dirty line is evicted.

principle.text: Write-through spends memory bandwidth on every store and needs no dirty bit. Write-back saves bandwidth by merging repeated stores to one block into a single block write on eviction, at the price of a dirty bit and lines that are newer than memory.

lesson.limits: The pairings write-back with write-allocate and write-through with no-write-allocate are habits, not rules; any pairing works. A read miss in a write-back cache can force a write-back, because the victim line may be dirty, while a read miss in a write-through cache never does.

example.problem: A program stores to the same block 10 times while it stays in the cache, and then the block is evicted. How many writes reach main memory under write-through and under write-back?
steps: Write-through sends each store to memory immediately, so 10 stores cause 10 memory writes.
Write-back updates the cache line and sets the dirty bit on the first store, and later stores find the bit already set, so memory is untouched.
At eviction the line is dirty, so the block is written back once.
example.result: 10 memory writes for write-through and 1 block write for write-back.

misconceptions: Write-back does not lose data. The dirty line is the only copy of the newest value until eviction, and the dirty bit guarantees it is written then.
Write-allocate is not tied to write-back by necessity. Either write policy can be combined with either miss policy.
Evicting a block does not always cost a memory write in a write-back cache. Only a dirty block is written; a clean block is simply dropped.

recall.q: What does the dirty bit record?
recall.a: That the line was modified after it was loaded, so memory is stale and the block must be written back on eviction.

recall.q: What do write-allocate and no-write-allocate each do on a write miss?
recall.a: Write-allocate loads the block and then writes it in the cache; no-write-allocate sends the store to memory and does not load the block.

recall.q: Why can a read miss cause a memory write in a write-back cache?
recall.a: The line chosen for replacement may be dirty, and it must be written back before the new block replaces it.

practice.stem: A cache is empty and uses write-through with no-write-allocate. Block X and block Y are different blocks. The processor performs: write X, read X, write X, write Y, read Y, write Y. How many of these operations send a write to main memory?
practice.explanation: Write-through sends every store to memory, whether it hits or misses. The stores are write X (a miss, no-write-allocate so the block is not loaded), write X (a hit after the read loaded X), write Y (a miss) and write Y (a hit after the read loaded Y): 4 memory writes. Counting only the 2 write misses is tempting because a hit looks cheap, but write-through forwards the hits too. A write-back cache with write-allocate would send none until a dirty line is evicted.

lesson.summary: Write-through forwards every store to memory; write-back sets a dirty bit and writes the block once on eviction. Write-allocate loads on a write miss, while no-write-allocate goes straight to memory.

topics.title: Effective memory access time: hierarchical vs simultaneous
points: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty: a 1 ns hit, 5% misses and a 100 ns penalty give 1 + 0.05 × 100 = 6 ns.
Hierarchical (look-through) access tries the cache first and goes to memory only on a miss, so a miss pays both: T = h·t_c + (1 − h)(t_c + t_m) = t_c + (1 − h)·t_m.
Simultaneous (look-aside) access starts the cache and memory lookups together and takes whichever answers, so a miss pays only memory: T = h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m.
When a question says nothing, a miss penalty quoted on top of the hit time is hierarchical; read the wording before choosing the form.

lesson.why: Average access time is the most direct way GATE asks how well a cache pays off. The two forms differ only in whether a miss also pays for the failed cache lookup, and the wording of the question decides which applies.
lesson.intro: Not every access takes the same time. A hit is served by the cache in the cache access time. A miss must also reach the next level, which takes longer. The average access time weights each outcome by how often it happens. With hit ratio $h$, a fraction $h$ of accesses hit and a fraction $1-h$ miss. If the processor looks in the cache first and goes to memory only after the cache fails, the miss pays both times. If the cache and memory are started together, the miss pays only the memory time.

definitions.meaning: The fraction of accesses found in the cache; the miss ratio is one minus this.
The extra time a miss costs beyond the cache access time, which is the time to get the block from the next level.

principle.text: In the hierarchical (look-through) form, every access pays the cache time and only the misses add the memory time. In the simultaneous (look-aside) form, a hit costs the cache time and a miss costs the memory time alone.

lesson.limits: Use the hierarchical form unless the question says the levels are accessed simultaneously. If the question gives complete access times for each outcome, such as "20 ns when found in L2", those already include the earlier lookups, and adding them again is double counting. A miss penalty quoted separately is added to the hit time.

example.problem: A cache has access time 2 ns and hit ratio 0.9. Main memory has access time 50 ns. Find the average access time with hierarchical access and with simultaneous access.
steps: Hierarchical: every access pays 2 ns and the 0.1 fraction of misses adds 50 ns, so $T = 2 + 0.1 \times 50 = 7$ ns.
Simultaneous: hits take 2 ns and misses take 50 ns, so $T = 0.9 \times 2 + 0.1 \times 50 = 6.8$ ns.
example.result: 7 ns hierarchical and 6.8 ns simultaneous, since the simultaneous form skips the wasted cache lookup on a miss.

misconceptions: The average time is not the arithmetic mean of the cache time and the memory time. It is a weighted mean, and with a high hit ratio it stays close to the cache time.
If a time is quoted as the total for an outcome (for example 20 ns when found in L2), it already includes the earlier lookups. Adding the cache time to it again counts the lookup twice.

recall.q: What is the hierarchical access time in terms of $t_c$, $t_m$ and $h$?
recall.a: $t_c + (1-h)\,t_m$: every access pays the cache time, and misses add the memory time.

recall.q: Why is the simultaneous time never larger than the hierarchical time?
recall.a: On a miss it skips the cache lookup that the hierarchical form pays first, and a hit costs the same in both.

practice.stem: A system looks in the cache first and goes to memory only on a miss. The cache access time is 3 ns and the memory access time is 60 ns. What is the minimum cache hit ratio for the average access time to be at most 6 ns?
practice.explanation: The hierarchical form gives $3 + (1-h) \times 60 \le 6$, so $(1-h) \le 3/60 = 0.05$ and $h \ge 0.95$. The simultaneous form would give $3h + 60(1-h) \le 6$, so $h \ge 54/57 \approx 0.947$. That is a lower hit ratio than 0.95, which is why the form must be read from the wording.

lesson.summary: The hierarchical time is $t_c + (1-h)t_m$ and the simultaneous time is $h t_c + (1-h)t_m$; use the first unless the question says the levels start together.

topics.title: Multilevel caches and local vs global hit ratios
points: With two levels, AMAT = t₁ + m₁ × (t₂ + m₂ × t_mem), where m₂ is the local miss rate of L2: misses at L2 divided by accesses that reach L2.

The global miss rate of L2 is misses at L2 divided by all CPU references, which equals m₁ × m₂. If L1 misses 40 and L2 misses 20 of 1000 references, L2's local miss rate is 0.5 and its global miss rate 0.02.
Quoting L2's miss rate as global and plugging it into the local formula is the classic error; convert first.
With local hit ratios h₁, h₂, hierarchical T = h₁t₁ + (1 − h₁)h₂(t₁ + t₂) + (1 − h₁)(1 − h₂)(t₁ + t₂ + t_m); the simultaneous form charges each level only its own time.

lesson.why: Two-level cache questions test one habit: a miss rate must be measured against the accesses that reach that level. Mixing the local and global rates is the usual cause of a wrong answer.
lesson.intro: A second cache, L2, sits behind the first, L1. The processor always asks L1 first. Only the accesses that miss in L1 reach L2, and only those that miss in L2 reach main memory. So the L2 miss rate can be stated two ways. The local rate divides L2 misses by the accesses L2 actually received. The global rate divides L2 misses by all processor references. The global rate is the smaller number, and the average time formula needs the local one.

definitions.meaning: Misses at a level divided by the accesses that reach that level.
Misses at a level divided by all references made by the processor.

principle.text: Each level adds its own time weighted by the fraction of accesses that reach it. The global miss rate of L2 is the product of the two local rates.
principle.tex: T = t_1 + m_1\,(t_2 + m_2\,t_{\text{mem}}), \qquad m_{2,\text{global}} = m_1 m_2

lesson.limits: This nested form is the hierarchical one: a miss pays the time of every level it visits. If a question gives total times for each outcome, weight them by the probabilities of those outcomes instead. A global rate is only convertible to a local rate when the L1 miss rate is known. If accesses are a mix, such as instruction and data caches with a 60/40 split, first weight the miss ratios into one rate per reference; if misses are counted per instruction, divide by the accesses per instruction first. A quoted miss penalty for a level is the added time $t_2$ of the nested formula.

example.problem: Out of 1000 processor references, L1 misses 50 and L2 misses 10 of those. The times are $t_1=1$ ns, $t_2=10$ ns and memory 100 ns. Find the local and global miss rates of L2 and the average access time.
steps: L1 misses 50 of 1000, so $m_1 = 0.05$, and these 50 are the accesses that reach L2.
L2 misses 10 of the 50 it receives, so its local miss rate is $m_2 = 0.2$. Over all 1000 references its global miss rate is 0.01, which equals $0.05 \times 0.2$.
The average time is $1 + 0.05\,(10 + 0.2 \times 100) = 2.5$ ns.
example.result: Local miss rate 0.2, global miss rate 0.01, average access time 2.5 ns.

misconceptions: A global L2 miss rate cannot be put straight into the nested formula in place of $m_2$. Divide it by $m_1$ first, because the formula multiplies by $m_1$ separately.
A low global L2 miss rate does not mean L2 is effective. It is small mainly because L1 already filtered most accesses, and the local rate is the honest measure of L2 itself.

recall.q: What is the difference between the local and global miss rate of L2?
recall.a: Local divides L2 misses by the accesses reaching L2; global divides them by all processor references.

recall.q: How is the global L2 miss rate related to the local rates?
recall.a: It is the product $m_1 m_2$ of the L1 and L2 local miss rates.
