recall.q: Which accesses pay the main-memory time in a two-level cache?
recall.a: Only those that miss in both L1 and L2, a fraction $m_1 m_2$ of all references.

practice.stem: In a two-level cache the L1 miss rate is 0.1 and the global miss rate of L2 is 0.02. The access times are 2 ns for L1, 12 ns for L2 and 120 ns for main memory. What is the average memory access time in ns?
practice.explanation: The local L2 miss rate is $0.02/0.1 = 0.2$. Then $T = 2 + 0.1\,(12 + 0.2 \times 120) = 5.6$ ns. Using 0.02 as if it were the local rate gives 3.44 ns, which is tempting because it is the only L2 figure in the question, but it is measured against all references and must be converted first.

lesson.summary: Weight each level by the accesses that reach it: $T = t_1 + m_1(t_2 + m_2 t_{\text{mem}})$ with local miss rates, and convert a global L2 rate by dividing by $m_1$.

topics.title: The three Cs of misses
points: Compulsory (cold) misses are first references to a block; they occur even in an infinite cache.
Capacity misses happen because the working set is larger than the cache; they would occur even with full associativity.
Conflict misses come from too many blocks mapping to one set; they vanish in a fully associative cache of the same size.
Bigger caches cut capacity misses, higher associativity cuts conflict misses, and larger blocks cut compulsory misses until the fewer, larger blocks start raising conflicts and the miss penalty.

lesson.why: Questions that ask which kind of miss a change removes (more ways, a bigger cache, bigger blocks) or that count conflict misses in a trace all need the three-way split.
lesson.intro: A cache miss means the wanted block is not in the cache. Not all misses have the same cause. The very first use of a block always misses, because nothing could have loaded it earlier. A later miss happens because the block was thrown out. It was thrown out either because the whole working set is bigger than the cache, or because several blocks were forced into the same place while other places sat unused. Telling these causes apart tells you which design change would help.

definitions.meaning: The first reference to a block. It happens even in an infinitely large cache.
A miss on a block that was evicted because the cache is too small for the blocks in use, so a fully associative cache of the same size would miss too.
A miss on a block that was evicted only because other blocks map to the same set; a fully associative cache of the same size would have hit.

principle.text: Run the trace through a fully associative LRU cache of the same size. A first reference is compulsory. A miss that the fully associative cache also suffers is a capacity miss. Every other miss of the real cache is a conflict miss.

lesson.limits: The split depends on the cache size, block size and replacement rule, so changing one can move misses from one class to another. In a fully associative cache the conflict count is zero by definition. In a trace that touches fewer blocks than the cache has lines, the capacity count is zero.

example.problem: A direct-mapped cache has 4 lines. Block numbers are referenced in the order 0, 4, 0, 4, 1, 2, 3. Classify each miss.
steps: Block $b$ goes to line $b \bmod 4$. Blocks 0 and 4 both go to line 0; blocks 1, 2, 3 go to lines 1, 2, 3.
References 0 and 4 are first uses, so both are compulsory misses. The next 0 finds block 4 in line 0 and misses, and so does the next 4.
A fully associative cache of 4 lines would hold both 0 and 4 together, so those two repeat misses are conflict misses, not capacity misses.
References 1, 2 and 3 are first uses: three more compulsory misses.
example.result: 7 misses in all: 5 compulsory, 0 capacity, 2 conflict.

misconceptions: A miss on a block that was loaded before is not automatically a capacity miss. If a fully associative cache of the same size would have hit, the cause is a conflict.
Making blocks larger does not always lower the miss count: fewer, bigger blocks can raise conflicts and make each miss cost more.

recall.q: Which design change removes conflict misses but not capacity misses?
recall.a: Raising associativity at the same total size, since it lets blocks that share a set spread over more lines.

recall.q: How do you separate capacity misses from conflict misses in a trace?
recall.a: Replay the trace on a fully associative cache of the same size; its repeat misses are capacity, and the extra repeat misses of the real cache are conflict.

recall.q: Which miss class survives an infinitely large cache?
recall.a: Compulsory misses, because the first use of a block always misses.

practice.stem: A direct-mapped cache has 4 lines. Block numbers are referenced in the order 0, 4, 8, 0, 4, 8, 0, 4, 8. How many of the misses are conflict misses?
practice.explanation: Blocks 0, 4 and 8 all map to line 0, so every reference misses: 9 misses. The first use of each of the 3 blocks is compulsory, leaving 6. A fully associative cache of 4 lines holds all three blocks, so none of the 6 is a capacity miss; they are conflicts. The tempting answer 9 counts first uses as conflicts, and 0 comes from thinking the cache is big enough.

lesson.summary: Compulsory misses are first uses, capacity misses are what a fully associative cache of the same size would also suffer, and conflict misses are the rest; associativity attacks only the last class.

topics.title: Miss penalty, stall cycles and CPI
points: Memory stall cycles per instruction = memory accesses per instruction × miss rate × miss penalty, and effective CPI = base CPI + stall cycles.
Every instruction makes one instruction fetch plus its data accesses: with 0.3 data references per instruction, 1.3 accesses per instruction feed the stall count.
In a write-back cache a miss that evicts a dirty block also writes it back, so the average miss cost is (1 + d) block transfers when a fraction d of victims is dirty.
Speed-up from a cache is the access time without it divided by the access time with it, e.g. 100 ns ÷ 6 ns ≈ 16.7.

lesson.why: Speed-up and effective CPI questions reappear in many papers, and the usual error is forgetting that every instruction also makes an instruction fetch.
lesson.intro: A processor without memory delays finishes an instruction in some base number of cycles, the base CPI (cycles per instruction). A cache miss makes the processor wait for the slower memory, and that waiting is added on top. So the real CPI is the base CPI plus the average stall cycles per instruction. The stall depends on how often an instruction touches memory, how often that access misses, and how many cycles one miss costs.

definitions.meaning: The extra cycles the processor waits when an access misses in the cache.
Memory accesses per instruction times miss rate times miss penalty, summed over instruction and data accesses.

principle.text: Add the stalls of the instruction stream and the data stream. Every instruction is fetched once; only loads and stores make a data access. Speed-up compares the CPI before and after.

lesson.limits: The formula assumes every miss stalls the processor for the full penalty. It does not hold when the processor overlaps misses with other work, and a write-back cache adds the cost of writing dirty victims to the penalty.

example.problem: Base CPI is 1.5. 30% of instructions are loads or stores. The instruction cache misses 4% of the time, the data cache 10%, and every miss costs 50 cycles. Find the CPI and the speed-up of a perfect cache.
steps: Instruction stream: every instruction is fetched, so the stall is $1 \times 0.04 \times 50 = 2$ cycles.
Data stream: only 30% of instructions access data, so the stall is $0.3 \times 0.10 \times 50 = 1.5$ cycles.
A perfect cache removes the stalls and leaves CPI $1.5$, so the speed-up is $5 / 1.5$.
example.result: CPI is 5 and the speed-up of a perfect cache is 3.33.

misconceptions: The data miss rate applies only to the fraction of instructions that are loads or stores, not to every instruction.
Forgetting the instruction fetch is the common slip: even an instruction with no data access makes one cache access.

recall.q: How many cache accesses does an instruction make if 25% of instructions are loads or stores?
recall.a: On average 1.25: one instruction fetch plus 0.25 data accesses.

recall.q: How is the speed-up of a perfect cache found?
recall.a: Divide the real CPI by the base CPI, since the instruction count and clock stay the same.

practice.stem: Base CPI is 1.2 and 40% of instructions are loads or stores. The instruction cache misses 2% of the time, the data cache 5%, and each miss costs 80 cycles. What is the effective CPI?
practice.explanation: Instruction stalls are $0.02 \times 80 = 1.6$ cycles. Data stalls are $0.4 \times 0.05 \times 80 = 1.6$ cycles. CPI $= 1.2 + 1.6 + 1.6 = 4.4$. Applying the 5% data miss rate to every instruction gives 6.8 and leaving out the instruction fetch gives 2.8, which are the tempting wrong values.

lesson.summary: Effective CPI is the base CPI plus instruction-fetch stalls on every instruction plus data stalls on the load and store fraction; speed-up is the ratio of CPIs.

topics.title: Read/write mixes, line fill time, target hit ratio and cost per bit
points: With write-through and no-write-allocate, every write goes to memory whether it hits or not, so T = f_r·T_read + f_w·t_m. Example: t_c = 10 ns, t_m = 100 ns, read hit ratio 0.9, 80% reads: 0.8 × (10 + 0.1 × 100) + 0.2 × 100 = 36 ns.
The miss penalty of a line fill is latency + line size ÷ bandwidth: a 64-byte line over a 1 GB/s bus (1 byte per ns) after 32 ns of latency takes 32 + 64 = 96 ns.
A target access time T fixes the hit ratio by inverting the EMAT formula: hierarchical h = 1 − (T − t_c)/t_m, simultaneous h = (t_m − T)/(t_m − t_c).

The average cost per bit of a hierarchy is Σ cᵢSᵢ ÷ Σ Sᵢ, weighted by size, while its average time is weighted by the share of references each level serves; a small fast level buys speed close to its own at a cost close to the large level's.
Example: an 8 MB level at 4 units per byte over a 56 MB level at 1 unit per byte averages (32 + 56) ÷ 64 = 1.375 units per byte, not the plain mean 2.5.

lesson.why: These questions extend the average access time formula to block fills, memory bandwidth and write-through, and each one rewards writing down the time of a single miss first.
lesson.intro: On a miss the cache loads a whole block, not a single word. Memory needs some time to deliver the first word and then a shorter time for each following word, so the cost of a miss grows with the block size. Once the time of one miss is known, the average access time is the hit time plus the miss rate times that cost. Bandwidth is the same idea turned around: bytes delivered divided by the time to deliver them.

definitions.meaning: Loading one whole block from memory into the cache after a miss.
Bytes delivered per unit time; for a block fill it is the block size divided by the fill time.

principle.text: The miss penalty is the time to fill the whole block: the first-word latency plus the remaining words at their own rate. The average access time adds the miss rate times that penalty to the hit time.

lesson.limits: Whether the lookup time is added to the penalty or overlapped with it changes the answer, so read how the question describes a miss. With write-through and no write allocate, writes go to memory whether they hit or not, so the plain formula does not apply to them.

example.problem: A cache has hit time 2 ns and hit rate 95%. Blocks are 64 bytes and words are 4 bytes. On a miss, the first word takes 30 ns and every later word takes 5 ns. Find the average access time.
steps: A block holds $64 / 4 = 16$ words.
The fill time is $30 + 15 \times 5 = 105$ ns.
The miss rate is $1 - 0.95 = 0.05$, so the expected extra time is $0.05 \times 105 = 5.25$ ns.
Add the hit time that every access pays: $2 + 5.25$.
example.result: The average access time is 7.25 ns.

misconceptions: Charging the first-word time for every word of the block overstates the penalty; only the first word pays the full latency.
A larger block does not lower the average time by itself, because the fill time grows with the number of words.

recall.q: What is the miss penalty when a block has W words, the first word takes a and each later word takes b?
recall.a: $a + (W-1)b$, the time to fill the whole block.

recall.q: How is the bandwidth of a block fill computed?
recall.a: Divide the block size in bytes by the fill time in seconds, where the fill time is the number of cycles times the clock period.

practice.stem: A memory system runs on a 50 MHz clock. Serving a miss takes 2 cycles to accept the address, 2 cycles to fetch the block, and then 1 cycle per word to send 4 words of 4 bytes each. What is the maximum bandwidth in units of $10^6$ bytes per second?
practice.explanation: One miss moves $4 \times 4 = 16$ bytes and takes $2 + 2 + 4 = 8$ cycles. That is 2 bytes per cycle, and 50 million cycles per second give 100 million bytes per second. Using only the 4 transfer cycles gives 200, which is the tempting wrong choice.

lesson.summary: The cost of a miss is the time to fill a whole block, first word plus the rest; average access time and bandwidth both follow from that one number.

topics.title: Counting misses for array traversals
points: C stores arrays row-major: element A[i][j] of an R × C array of w-byte elements sits at base + (i·C + j)·w.
Row-wise traversal touches each block once in order, so misses = array size ÷ block size when the cache starts empty.
Column-wise traversal jumps one row per access; if the rows of one column map to fewer lines than there are rows, each block is evicted before the next column reuses it and every access misses.
For int A[64][64] with a 4 KB direct-mapped cache and 16-byte blocks: row-wise 1024 misses, column-wise 4096; a 16 KB cache brings column-wise back to 1024.

lesson.why: Counting the misses of a loop over an array tests whether you can turn an address into a block and a cache line, and the row-wise versus column-wise contrast is a recurring theme.
lesson.intro: A C array is stored row by row. Walking along a row visits neighbouring bytes, so every block that is loaded is used completely before the walk moves on. Walking down a column jumps over a whole row between accesses, so each access lands in a different block. Whether a loaded block survives until the next column needs it depends on the cache size. Counting misses means finding the block of each access, the line that block uses, and whether the line still holds it.

definitions.meaning: Storing a two-dimensional array row after row, so element $A[i][j]$ of an $n \times n$ array of $w$-byte elements sits at base $+ (in + j)w$.

principle.text: The block of an access is its byte address divided by the block size, and in a direct-mapped cache it uses line block mod number of lines. An access hits only if that line holds the same block; otherwise it misses and replaces the line.

lesson.limits: Row-wise counting as array size divided by block size assumes the cache starts empty and the array base is aligned to a block. Column-wise counting needs the line numbers of one column; when they spread over all lines and the rows fit, the blocks survive and the count drops back to the row-wise value.

example.problem: int A[32][32] with 4-byte ints is read row by row and then separately column by column, each time from an empty 1 KB direct-mapped cache with 32-byte blocks. How many misses does each traversal cause?
steps: The array is $32 \times 32 \times 4 = 4096$ bytes. The cache has $1024 / 32 = 32$ lines.
Row-wise, each block is read in full before the next one, so misses $= 4096 / 32 = 128$.
One row is $128$ bytes, so it spans 4 blocks and $A[i][j]$ lies in block $4i + \lfloor j/8 \rfloor$, which uses line $(4i + \lfloor j/8 \rfloor) \bmod 32$.
Down one column the lines repeat every 8 rows, so the 32 rows land on only 8 lines. Each block is replaced before the next column returns to it, so every access misses: $32 \times 32 = 1024$.
example.result: Row-wise 128 misses; column-wise 1024 misses.

misconceptions: Column-wise traversal does not always miss on every access. If the rows of a column map to distinct lines and fit in the cache, the blocks stay and the next column hits.
The number of misses is not the number of elements divided by the block size in a column-wise walk; that formula holds only when blocks are used in order.

recall.q: Why is row-wise traversal of a C array cache-friendly?
recall.a: Rows are stored contiguously, so each loaded block is used completely before the walk leaves it.

recall.q: When does column-wise traversal miss on every access?
recall.a: When the blocks of one column map to fewer lines than there are rows, so each block is evicted before the next column reuses it.

practice.stem: int A[16][16] with 4-byte ints is read column by column, starting with an empty 256-byte direct-mapped cache with 16-byte blocks. How many misses occur?
practice.explanation: The cache has $256 / 16 = 16$ lines. A row is 64 bytes, 4 blocks, so element $A[i][j]$ is in block $4i + \lfloor j/4 \rfloor$ on line $(4i + \lfloor j/4 \rfloor) \bmod 16$. Down a column the line repeats every 4 rows, so 16 rows use only 4 lines and each block is evicted before the next column returns. All $16 \times 16 = 256$ accesses miss. The tempting answer is 64, the row-wise count, which wrongly assumes each block is reused.

lesson.summary: Find each access's block and line; row-wise walks miss once per block, while a column-wise walk misses every time when its rows crowd into too few lines.

topics.title: Memory interfacing: building memory from chips
points: A chip of m words × n bits has log₂ m address lines and n data lines; a memory of M × N built from it needs (M/m) × (N/n) chips.

Chips placed side by side share address and chip-select lines and widen the word; rows of chips stacked vertically deepen the memory, and a log₂(M/m)-to-M/m decoder on the high-order address bits selects one row.
Example: 16K × 8 from 1K × 4 chips needs 16 rows of 2 chips, 32 in all; the 14 address bits split into 10 for every chip and 4 for a 4-to-16 decoder.
The address range of a row is fixed by the decoder input: row r covers addresses r·m to (r + 1)·m − 1, which is how a memory map with RAM and ROM regions is read off a circuit.

Full decoding gates every unused high address bit into the chip select, so each word has exactly one address. Partial decoding leaves u address bits unconnected, so every word answers at 2ᵘ aliased addresses.

Example: a 16-bit CPU with four 2K × 8 chips, A10–A0 to every chip, a 2-to-4 decoder on A12 A11 and A15 = A14 = A13 = 0 required to enable it: output 3 selects 1800H–1FFFH. If A15–A13 are ignored instead, each byte appears at 2³ = 8 addresses.

lesson.why: Chip-count questions and address-range questions from a decoder circuit appear regularly, and both are short once the address bits are split correctly.
lesson.intro: A memory chip stores a fixed number of words of a fixed width, such as 2K words of 8 bits. A larger memory is built from several chips. Chips placed side by side make the word wider, because each supplies some of the bits. Chips stacked as separate rows make the memory deeper, because each row holds different addresses. A decoder looks at the high address bits and switches on only the row that holds the wanted address, using each chip's chip-select input.

definitions.meaning: An input that lets a chip respond only when it is 1.
A circuit that turns the high address bits into one active chip-select line.

principle.text: To build an $M \times N$ memory from $m \times n$ chips, use $M/m$ rows of $N/n$ chips. The low $\log_2 m$ address bits go to every chip and the high bits go to the decoder.

lesson.limits: With partial decoding some high address bits are ignored, so one word answers at several addresses and the address range is larger than the memory. The counts above assume the sizes divide evenly.

example.problem: Build an 8K x 16 memory from 2K x 8 chips. How many chips are needed, how are the 13 address bits used, and where does each row start?
steps: Rows: $8K / 2K = 4$. Chips per row: $16 / 8 = 2$. Total $4 \times 2 = 8$ chips.
Each chip has 2K words, so the low $\log_2 2048 = 11$ address bits go to every chip.
The remaining $13 - 11 = 2$ bits feed a 2-to-4 decoder that selects one row.
Row $r$ starts at $r \times 2048$: 0000, 0800, 1000 and 1800 in hexadecimal.
example.result: 8 chips, 11 shared address bits, 2 decoder bits, rows starting at 0000, 0800, 1000, 1800 (hex).

misconceptions: Chips in the same row are not selected one by one. They share one chip-select and each supplies part of the word.
A decoder that ignores some high address bits does not make the memory bigger; it makes copies of the same words appear at several addresses.

recall.q: How do you find the number of chips for an M x N memory built from m x n chips?
recall.a: Multiply the number of rows $M/m$ by the number of chips per row $N/n$.

recall.q: Which address bits go to the decoder?
recall.a: The high-order bits left over after the low bits that address a word inside one chip.

recall.q: What does partial decoding cause?
recall.a: Each word answers at $2^u$ addresses, where $u$ is the number of unconnected high address bits.

practice.stem: How many 32K x 4 chips are needed to build a 256K x 8 memory?
practice.explanation: Rows: $256K / 32K = 8$. Chips per row: $8 / 4 = 2$. Total $8 \times 2 = 16$ chips. Dividing capacities in bits gives the same count. Counting only the rows gives 8, which forgets that each row must be two chips wide.

lesson.summary: Rows of chips deepen the memory and chips within a row widen it; the low address bits go to every chip and the high bits go to a decoder that picks the row.

topics.title: Memory interleaving
points: Memory is split into m banks that can be accessed in parallel, so consecutive accesses can overlap.
Low-order interleaving picks the bank with the low address bits (bank = address mod m), sending consecutive words to different banks: ideal for block fetches into a cache.
High-order interleaving picks the bank with the high bits (bank = ⌊address ÷ words per bank⌋), so a contiguous region stays in one bank; it suits independent regions, not sequential bursts.
With 4 banks, a 15-cycle access, 1 cycle to send the address and 1 cycle per word transferred, a 4-word block costs 1 + 4 × (15 + 1) = 65 cycles from one bank but 1 + 15 + 4 = 20 interleaved.

lesson.why: Fetching a cache block is slow if one memory chip must answer every word in turn. Interleaving explains how banks overlap that wait, and the time formulas are short, exact calculations.
lesson.intro: Main memory can be split into several banks, each able to work on its own request at the same time. A bank needs a long time to start up after an address arrives, but moving one word out is quick. If the words of a block sit in different banks, all banks can start together, and the words then leave one after another. Which bank holds a word depends on which address bits select the bank: the low bits or the high bits.

definitions.meaning: One independent memory module that can start an access while others are busy.
The low address bits pick the bank, so consecutive addresses fall in different banks.
The high address bits pick the bank, so a contiguous region stays inside one bank.

principle.text: With $m$ banks, low-order interleaving puts address $a$ in bank $a \bmod m$. Fetching a block of $k$ words with address time $t_a$, bank access time $t_{acc}$ and word transfer time $t_x$ costs $k$ separate accesses from one bank but a single overlapped access from $k$ banks.
principle.tex: T_{\text{single}} = t_a + k(t_{acc} + t_x), \qquad T_{\text{interleaved}} = t_a + t_{acc} + k\,t_x

lesson.limits: The saving needs consecutive words in different banks, so it works for low-order interleaving but not for high-order. It also needs the block to span all the banks; an access pattern that keeps hitting one bank, such as a stride equal to $m$, gets no overlap.

example.problem: Four banks, 1 cycle to send the address, 10 cycles per bank access, 1 cycle to transfer a word. Compare a 4-word block fetch from a single bank with low-order interleaving.
steps: Single bank: the access repeats for every word, so $1 + 4 \times (10 + 1) = 45$ cycles.
Interleaved: with low-order bits, words 0 to 3 are in banks 0 to 3, and all four accesses run in parallel for 10 cycles.
The four words then transfer one per cycle: $1 + 10 + 4 = 15$ cycles.
example.result: 45 cycles single, 15 cycles interleaved.

misconceptions: High-order interleaving does not speed up a sequential block fetch; consecutive addresses stay in one bank, so the accesses cannot overlap.
Interleaving does not make one access faster; it hides the access time of several words behind each other.
Under low-order interleaving the bank is the remainder of the word address divided by the bank count, not the quotient by the block size.

recall.q: Which address bits select the bank in low-order interleaving?
recall.a: The lowest bits, so the bank is the address mod the number of banks and consecutive words use different banks.

recall.q: Why does high-order interleaving not help a block fetch?
recall.a: A contiguous block lies in one bank, so its accesses cannot overlap.

recall.q: What is the interleaved fetch time for a k-word block?
recall.a: One address time plus one access time plus k transfer times.

practice.stem: A memory has 8 low-order interleaved banks. Sending the address takes 1 cycle, a bank access 12 cycles and a word transfer 1 cycle. How many cycles does it take to fetch an 8-word block?
practice.explanation: All eight banks start together, so the time is $1 + 12 + 8 = 21$ cycles. The value 105 is the single-bank time $1 + 8 \times (12 + 1)$, which tempts if the banks are thought to work one after another. The value 13 forgets that the eight words still leave one per cycle.

lesson.summary: Low-order interleaving spreads consecutive words across banks so one access time is shared by a whole block, giving $t_a + t_{acc} + k\,t_x$ instead of $t_a + k(t_{acc}+t_x)$.

topics.title: SRAM and DRAM
points: SRAM stores a bit in a 6-transistor latch: fast, needs no refresh, and is used for caches.
DRAM stores a bit as charge on one capacitor behind one transistor: dense and cheap but slower, and it must be refreshed periodically because the charge leaks.

lesson.why: The refresh overhead of a DRAM is a numeric calculation of rows times refresh time over the refresh period, and the SRAM versus DRAM contrast supports the choice of memory for caches and main memory.
lesson.intro: Memory chips store each bit in one of two ways. SRAM keeps a bit in a small circuit of six transistors that holds its state as long as power is on. It is fast but takes more area per bit, so it is used for caches. DRAM keeps a bit as charge on a tiny capacitor with one transistor. It is small and cheap, so main memory is built from it, but the charge leaks away. Every row must therefore be read and rewritten before the charge is lost. This refresh occupies the chip for part of the time.

definitions.meaning: Reading a DRAM row and writing it back to restore the leaking charge.
The time within which every row must have been refreshed once.

principle.text: In every refresh period the chip refreshes each row once, one row per refresh operation. The busy fraction is rows times refresh time over the period, and the rest is available for reads and writes.

lesson.limits: Chips of a memory that share a row address refresh the same row together, so the refresh time is that of one chip, not the sum over chips. The formula also assumes refresh and access cannot overlap.

example.problem: A DRAM chip has $2^{13}$ rows, a refresh operation takes 40 ns and the refresh period is 4 ms. What fraction of time is free for reads and writes?
steps: The number of rows is $2^{13} = 8192$.
One full sweep takes $8192 \times 40\ \text{ns} = 327\,680\ \text{ns} = 0.32768$ ms.
The busy fraction is $0.32768 / 4 = 0.08192$, which is 8.192%.
The free fraction is $100\% - 8.192\%$.
example.result: About 91.8% of the time is available for reads and writes.

misconceptions: SRAM does not need refresh; only DRAM does, because only DRAM stores a bit as leaking charge.
The refresh time is not multiplied by the number of chips in the memory when the chips refresh the same row together.

recall.q: Why must DRAM be refreshed?
recall.a: A bit is stored as charge on a capacitor that leaks, so each row must be read and rewritten within the refresh period.

recall.q: Why is SRAM used for caches and DRAM for main memory?
recall.a: SRAM is faster but takes more area per bit; DRAM is slower but denser and cheaper.

practice.stem: A DRAM chip has $2^{12}$ rows. One refresh operation takes 60 ns and the refresh period is 2 ms. What percentage of time is available for reads and writes, to one decimal place?
practice.explanation: The sweep takes $4096 \times 60 = 245\,760$ ns, which is 0.24576 ms. Out of 2 ms that is 12.288%, so the available time is $100 - 12.288 = 87.712$, or 87.7%. The value 12.3 is the refresh share, which is the tempting wrong answer.

lesson.summary: SRAM is a fast latch that needs no refresh; DRAM is a dense capacitor cell that loses time to refresh, and the lost fraction is rows times refresh time over the period.

topics.title: Virtual memory and the TLB
points: Paging splits virtual memory into pages and physical memory into equal frames; the page table maps a virtual page number to a frame, and the offset passes through unchanged.
A 32-bit virtual address with 4 KB pages has a 20-bit VPN, so a flat table has 2²⁰ entries: 4 MB at 4 bytes each.
The TLB caches recent VPN-to-frame translations. With hit ratio h, TLB time t and memory time m and a one-level table: EAT = h(t + m) + (1 − h)(t + 2m).
A TLB miss is not a page fault: the page may be resident and only the walk is needed. A page fault (valid bit 0) traps to the OS, which loads the page from disk.

lesson.why: GATE asks both for the effective access time with a TLB and for which chains of TLB, page table and cache events are possible, and both rest on knowing whether a page is in memory.
lesson.intro: A program uses virtual addresses, which are translated into physical addresses before memory is touched. Memory is cut into equal pages (virtual side) and frames (physical side). A page table stores, for each virtual page number, the frame that holds the page, or marks the page as absent. The low bits of the address, the offset, are copied through unchanged, so a virtual address with $v$ bits and pages of $2^{o}$ bytes has $v-o$ page number bits and the table has $2^{v-o}$ entries, one per virtual page (a flat table is that many entries times the entry size). Reading the page table costs a memory access, so a small fast table of recent translations, the TLB, is kept next to the processor and checked first.

definitions.meaning: A reference to a page whose valid bit is 0; the operating system must bring the page in from disk.
The translation for the page is found in the TLB, so the page table is not read.
The page table lookup finds the page absent from memory (valid bit 0), the same event as a page fault. A page table hit means the page is resident.

principle.text: The TLB is checked first. On a hit the frame is known at once; on a miss the page table is read, costing one more memory access. A TLB entry exists only for a page that is in memory. A cache indexed by physical address holds only blocks of resident pages, and when a page is evicted its cached blocks are invalidated, so a page table miss forces a cache miss too. With a one-level table, hit ratio $h$, TLB time $t$ and memory time $m$:

lesson.limits: The formula assumes a one-level page table and no page faults; a multi-level table adds one memory access per level on a miss, and a fault adds the disk time. Whether the cache is indexed by physical or virtual address changes which events can follow which.

example.problem: A one-level page table is used with TLB time 10 ns, memory time 100 ns and TLB hit ratio 0.9. Find the effective access time.
steps: A hit costs the TLB probe plus one memory access: 10 + 100 = 110 ns.
A miss costs the TLB probe, one memory access for the page table and one for the data: 10 + 200 = 210 ns.
Weight by the ratios: 0.9 × 110 + 0.1 × 210 = 99 + 21.
example.result: The effective access time is 120 ns.

misconceptions: A TLB miss is not a page fault: the page is usually in memory and only the translation is missing from the TLB.
A TLB miss does not force a cache miss, because the two are separate structures; a block can stay cached after its translation leaves the TLB.
The offset is not translated: only the page number goes through the TLB or page table.

recall.q: What does the TLB store?
recall.a: Recent translations from virtual page number to frame number.

recall.q: What does a TLB hit tell you about the page?
recall.a: The page is in main memory, so the page table cannot report it absent.

recall.q: If a page table lookup finds the page absent, can the cache hit? Why?
recall.a: No. The cache holds blocks only of resident pages and an evicted page's blocks are invalidated, so the access must miss in the cache.

practice.stem: A machine has 36-bit virtual addresses and 8 KB pages. Each page table entry takes 4 bytes and the page table is a single flat table. What is its size in MB?
practice.explanation: The offset takes 13 bits, leaving a 23-bit page number, so the table has $2^{23}$ entries of 4 bytes, which is $2^{25}$ bytes = 32 MB. Using all 36 bits as the page number gives a far larger figure, and forgetting the 4-byte entry size gives 8 MB.

lesson.summary: The TLB caches translations; a hit skips the page table, a miss costs one extra memory access, and a TLB entry or a cached block implies the page is in memory.

formulas.name: Block offset bits
where: block (line) size in addressable units, usually bytes
formulas.note: If the memory is word-addressable, measure B in words, not bytes.

formulas.name: Number of sets and index bits
formulas.note: Fully associative: S = 1, so there are no index bits.

formulas.name: Tag bits
formulas.text: tag = A − log₂ S − log₂ B
formulas.note: Equivalently tag = log₂(memory size ÷ cache size) + log₂ k.

formulas.name: Placement of a block
formulas.text: b = ⌊address / B⌋, set = b mod S
formulas.note: Direct mapped: S equals the number of lines, so set is the line number.

formulas.name: Tag directory size
where: replacement bits per line, e.g. log₂ k for LRU

formulas.name: Average memory access time
where: extra time to serve a miss from the level below
formulas.note: This is the hierarchical form: the hit time is paid on every access, including misses.

formulas.name: Single-level EMAT, simultaneous access
formulas.note: Cache and memory are probed together, so a miss costs only t_m. Always at most the hierarchical value.

formulas.name: Two-level AMAT
formulas.note: m₂ must be local. If the question gives a global L2 miss rate g, use m₂ = g / m₁.

formulas.name: Two-level EMAT, simultaneous access
where: local hit ratios of L1 and L2
formulas.note: The hierarchical version replaces t₂ by t₁ + t₂ and t_m by t₁ + t₂ + t_m.

formulas.name: Global miss rate of L2
formulas.text: g₂ = m₁ × m₂ = L2 misses / CPU references

formulas.name: CPI with memory stalls
where: memory accesses per instruction (1 fetch + data accesses)
formulas.note: With separate instruction and data miss rates, add the two products.

formulas.name: Write-back miss cost
where: fraction of evicted blocks that are dirty

formulas.name: Average time with reads and writes, write-through
where: fractions of references that are reads and writes, f_r + f_w = 1
formulas.note: Write-through with no-write-allocate and no write buffer: each write costs a memory write. If the question says reads are simultaneous, replace the read term by h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m.

formulas.name: Miss penalty of a line fill
formulas.note: Units first: 1 GB/s moves one byte per ns. Without interleaving or a burst, each word pays the full latency again.

formulas.name: Hit ratio needed for a target access time
formulas.text: hierarchical h = 1 − (T − t_c)/t_m; simultaneous h = (t_m − T)/(t_m − t_c)
formulas.note: The two forms give different answers on the same data: T = 12.5, t_c = 5, t_m = 80 needs 0.90625 hierarchical but 0.9 simultaneous.

formulas.name: Average cost per bit of a hierarchy
formulas.text: average cost = Σ cᵢSᵢ / Σ Sᵢ
where: cost per bit (or byte) of level i
formulas.note: Weighted by capacity, not by hit ratio; the plain mean of the costs is the usual wrong option.

formulas.name: Chips needed to build a memory
where: target memory: words × bits per word
one chip: words × bits per word

formulas.name: Address range of a chip row and partial-decoding aliases
formulas.text: row r spans r·m to (r + 1)·m − 1 above the base the fixed high bits select; aliases = 2^u
where: address bits left out of the decoding
formulas.note: With full decoding u = 0 and the map is one-to-one; with partial decoding the same row answers 2^u separate ranges.

formulas.name: Bank of an address
formulas.text: low-order bank = a mod m; high-order bank = ⌊a / (W/m)⌋

formulas.name: Block fetch time with and without interleaving
formulas.tex: T_{\text{single}} = t_a + k(t_{\text{acc}} + t_x), \qquad T_{\text{interleaved}} = t_a + t_{\text{acc}} + k\,t_x
formulas.text: T_single = t_a + k(t_acc + t_x); T_interleaved = t_a + t_acc + k·t_x

formulas.name: Effective access time with a TLB
formulas.note: For a k-level page table the miss term becomes t + (k + 1)m.

problemTypes.title: Tag, index and offset widths
recipe: Convert every size to a power of 2 in the addressable unit (byte or word).
Offset = log₂(block size); lines = cache size ÷ block size; sets = lines ÷ k.
Index = log₂(sets) (0 for fully associative); tag = address bits − index − offset.
problemTypes.trap: Using the number of lines instead of the number of sets for the index of a set-associative cache.

problemTypes.title: Average access time for one or two cache levels
recipe: Decide whether access is hierarchical (miss pays the upper level too) or simultaneous (miss pays only the level that answers).
Make every miss rate local: divide a global L2 miss rate by the L1 miss rate.
Apply AMAT = t₁ + m₁(t₂ + m₂·t_mem) for hierarchical, or weight each level's own time by the share of references it serves for simultaneous.
problemTypes.trap: Mixing a global L2 miss rate into the local formula, or adding t₁ to the miss path in a simultaneous system.

problemTypes.title: Tag-directory (tag memory) size
recipe: Compute the tag width from the address split.
Add the per-line status bits the question names: valid, dirty for write-back, and replacement bits.
Multiply by the number of lines (not sets).
problemTypes.trap: Forgetting the dirty bit of a write-back cache, or counting the data array as part of the directory.

problemTypes.title: Hit/miss trace of a block-address sequence
recipe: Turn each byte address into a block number ⌊a ÷ B⌋, then into a set number b mod S.
Keep one small list per set ordered by recency (LRU) or by load time (FIFO).
Mark H or M for each reference and count; the first reference to each block is always a compulsory miss.
problemTypes.trap: Mapping byte addresses straight to lines without dividing by the block size first.

problemTypes.title: Misses for a loop over an array
recipe: Write the address of A[i][j] in row-major order and the block it falls in.
Find which line each block maps to and how many rows of one column share a line.
If a block survives until its next use, count one miss per block; otherwise count one miss per access.
problemTypes.trap: Assuming column-wise traversal always misses: if the whole column fits without conflicts, it costs the same as row-wise.

problemTypes.title: Effective CPI from cache miss rates
recipe: Count memory accesses per instruction: one fetch plus the data references.
Stall cycles per instruction = accesses × miss rate × miss penalty (sum separately for instruction and data caches).
Effective CPI = base CPI + stall cycles; speed-up between two designs is the ratio of their CPIs at the same clock.
problemTypes.trap: Counting only data accesses and forgetting the instruction fetch every instruction makes.

problemTypes.title: Chips, decoders and address ranges in memory interfacing
recipe: Chips per row = target word width ÷ chip width; rows = target words ÷ chip words.
Every chip gets log₂(chip words) address lines; the remaining high-order bits drive a decoder that selects a row.
Row r spans addresses r·m to (r + 1)·m − 1.
Read the decoder enable: bits that must be 0 or 1 fix the base of the map; bits left unconnected (partial decoding) make each word answer at 2ᵘ addresses.
problemTypes.trap: Sizing the decoder by the chip count instead of the row count, or picking a chip from the decoder inputs while the enable bits disable it.

problemTypes.title: Read/write mix, line fill time and target hit ratio
recipe: Split references into reads and writes; under write-through every write pays a memory write, under write-back only dirty evictions do.
Compute the miss penalty from latency + line size ÷ bandwidth (or address + access + words × transfer for an interleaved memory).
Weight each class by its fraction; for a target time, solve the EMAT equation for h in the access model the question names.
problemTypes.trap: Charging writes only the cache time in a write-through cache, or mixing up hierarchical and simultaneous when solving for h.

questions.stem: A 32-bit byte-addressable machine has a 32 KB, 8-way set-associative cache with 32-byte blocks. How many bits wide is the tag?
questions.explanation: Offset = log₂ 32 = 5 bits. Lines = 32 KB ÷ 32 B = 1024, so sets = 1024 ÷ 8 = 128 and index = 7 bits. Tag = 32 − 7 − 5 = 20 bits.

questions.stem: L1 has a 1 ns hit time and a 10% miss rate. L2 has a 10 ns hit time and a 1% local miss rate. Main memory takes 100 ns. What is the average memory access time?
questions.explanation: AMAT = 1 + 0.10 × (10 + 0.01 × 100) = 1 + 0.10 × 11 = 2.1 ns. 2.0 ns drops the memory term; 3.0 ns treats the 1% as a global rate and adds it as a separate term; 11.0 ns charges L2 on every access.

questions.stem: A system has L1 (access time 2 ns, hit ratio 0.8), L2 (access time 10 ns, local hit ratio 0.9) and main memory (100 ns, always hits). Access is hierarchical: a request that misses at a level has already spent that level's access time before going down. What is the average access time in ns?
questions.explanation: Served by L1: 0.8 × 2 = 1.6. Served by L2: 0.2 × 0.9 = 0.18 of references, each costing 2 + 10 = 12 ns, giving 2.16. Served by memory: 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02, each costing 2 + 10 + 100 = 112 ns, giving 2.24. Total = 1.6 + 2.16 + 2.24 = 6.0 ns. The same answer comes from t₁ + m₁(t₂ + m₂·t_m) = 2 + 0.2 × (10 + 0.1 × 100) = 6. Under simultaneous access it would be 1.6 + 0.18 × 10 + 0.02 × 100 = 5.4 ns.

questions.stem: Out of 1000 CPU memory references, 40 miss in L1 and 20 miss in L2. What are the local and the global miss rates of L2?
questions.explanation: Only the 40 L1 misses reach L2, so its local miss rate is 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5. The global miss rate divides by all references: 20 ÷ 1000 = 0.02, which equals 0.04 × 0.5. 0.04 is L1's miss rate.

questions.stem: A direct-mapped cache has 4 lines with 1-byte blocks and starts empty. The CPU reads byte addresses 0, 4, 8, 12, 0, 4, 8. How many hits and misses occur?
questions.explanation: Every address is a multiple of 4, so each maps to line a mod 4 = 0. Each reference replaces the block the previous one loaded, and no address repeats back to back, so all 7 references miss. 3 hits and 4 misses would be the result in a 4-line fully associative cache.

questions.stem: A cache holds 4 blocks, is 2-way set-associative with LRU replacement and starts empty. The CPU references main-memory block numbers 0, 4, 0, 4, 8, 0, 4 in that order. How many misses occur?
questions.explanation: There are 2 sets, and every block here is even, so all go to set 0, which holds 2 blocks. 0 M, 4 M, 0 H, 4 H. Block 8 misses and evicts the LRU block 0; then 0 misses and evicts 4; then 4 misses and evicts 8. Misses = 5. A direct-mapped cache with 4 lines would miss all 7 (all map to line 0); a fully associative LRU cache would miss only 3 (the compulsory misses).

questions.stem: A 32-bit byte-addressable machine has a 16 KB, 4-way set-associative write-back cache with 64-byte blocks. Each line stores its tag, one valid bit and one dirty bit, and no replacement bits. What is the total size of the tag directory in bits?
questions.explanation: Lines = 16 KB ÷ 64 B = 256; sets = 256 ÷ 4 = 64. Offset = 6, index = 6, tag = 32 − 6 − 6 = 20 bits. Each line stores 20 + 1 + 1 = 22 bits, so the directory holds 256 × 22 = 5632 bits.

questions.stem: A 1024-line, 4-way set-associative cache uses 20-bit tags. What comparison hardware does one lookup need?
options: 4 comparators of 20 bits and a 4-to-1 multiplexer
4 comparators of 28 bits and a 4-to-1 multiplexer
questions.explanation: The index selects one set, and the 4 tags of that set are compared with the address tag in parallel, so 4 comparators each as wide as the tag (20 bits). A 4-to-1 multiplexer then passes the data of the matching way. One comparator is the direct-mapped case; one per line is the fully associative case; the index bits are never compared.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about cache write policies are correct?
options: A write-back cache writes a block to memory only when it is evicted and its dirty bit is set.
With write-through, main memory holds the current value after every store.
No-write-allocate brings the block into the cache on a write miss.
Write-back produces one memory write for every store instruction.
questions.explanation: Write-back defers memory updates to eviction and skips clean blocks, which is why it cuts memory writes. Write-through updates memory on every store. No-write-allocate is the opposite of fetching on a write miss: it writes to memory and leaves the cache alone. One memory write per store describes write-through, not write-back.

questions.stem: An L2 cache is said to be inclusive of L1. What does that mean?
options: Every block present in L1 is also present in L2
Every block present in L2 is also present in L1
L1 and L2 never hold the same block
L1 and L2 are probed simultaneously
questions.explanation: Inclusion means L1's contents are a subset of L2's, so evicting a block from L2 forces it out of L1 too. The reverse cannot hold since L2 is larger; never holding the same block is the exclusive policy; probing both together is simultaneous access, an unrelated property.

questions.stem: Which statements about the three classes of cache misses are correct?
options: Raising associativity while keeping capacity fixed reduces conflict misses.
A fully associative cache has no conflict misses.
Doubling the cache size removes compulsory misses.
Increasing the block size always lowers the miss rate.
questions.explanation: Conflict misses arise from too many blocks competing for one set, so more ways per set reduce them, and with a single set they cannot occur. Compulsory misses are first references and happen at any cache size. Larger blocks cut compulsory misses at first, but with fixed capacity there are fewer lines, so conflict misses eventually rise.

questions.stem: With 4 frames, initially empty, the reference string is 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. How many faults do FIFO and LRU replacement incur?
questions.explanation: FIFO: 1, 2, 3, 4 fault (4); 1, 2 hit; 5 replaces 1, 1 replaces 2, 2 replaces 3, 3 replaces 4, 4 replaces 5, 5 replaces 1: 6 more, total 10. LRU: 4 cold faults; 1, 2 hit; 5 replaces 3; 1, 2 hit; 3 replaces 4; 4 replaces 5; 5 replaces 1: total 8. With 3 frames FIFO faults only 9 times, which is Belady's anomaly.

questions.stem: A processor has CPI 1.0 with a perfect cache. Every instruction is fetched from memory, and 30% of instructions also make one data access. The miss rate is 2% for all accesses and the miss penalty is 100 cycles. What is the effective CPI?
questions.explanation: Memory accesses per instruction = 1 fetch + 0.3 data = 1.3. Stall cycles per instruction = 1.3 × 0.02 × 100 = 2.6. Effective CPI = 1.0 + 2.6 = 3.6. Forgetting the instruction fetches gives 1.6.

questions.stem: int is 4 bytes and int A[64][64] is stored row-major starting at address 0. A 4 KB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte blocks starts empty. The program reads A[i][j] in the order for (j = 0; j < 64; j++) for (i = 0; i < 64; i++). How many cache misses occur?
questions.explanation: A[i][j] is at 256i + 4j, in block 16i + ⌊j/4⌋, which maps to line (16i + ⌊j/4⌋) mod 256. Rows i and i + 16 share a line, so the 64 elements of one column fall into only 16 lines, 4 rows per line. By the time the inner loop finishes, each line holds the block of the last of its 4 rows, so the next column (which needs the blocks of the earlier rows) misses again. Every one of the 4096 reads misses. Row-wise order would give 4096 ÷ 4 = 1024 misses, and so would this column order with a 16 KB cache.

questions.stem: A 16K × 8 memory is built from 1K × 4 RAM chips. How many chips are needed, and what decoder selects among the rows of chips?
questions.explanation: Two 4-bit chips side by side make an 8-bit word, and 16K ÷ 1K = 16 rows give the depth: 16 × 2 = 32 chips. Of the 14 address bits, 10 go to every chip and the top 4 drive a 4-to-16 decoder whose outputs are the row chip-selects. A 5-to-32 decoder would wrongly treat each chip as its own row.

questions.stem: An 8K-word memory is made of 8 modules of 1K words each. Which module holds word address 1234 (decimal) under low-order interleaving and under high-order interleaving?
questions.explanation: Low-order interleaving uses the 3 low address bits: 1234 mod 8 = 2. High-order interleaving uses the 3 high bits, i.e. which 1K block the address falls in: ⌊1234 ÷ 1024⌋ = 1.

questions.stem: A cache line holds 8 words. Main memory takes 1 cycle to receive an address, 20 cycles for a bank access and 1 cycle to transfer one word over a one-word bus. The memory has 8 banks with low-order interleaving, all accessed in parallel after the address is broadcast. How many cycles does one line fill take?
questions.explanation: The address is sent once (1 cycle), all 8 banks access their word in parallel (20 cycles), then the 8 words cross the bus one at a time (8 cycles): 1 + 20 + 8 = 29. From a single bank each word pays its own access: 1 + 8 × (20 + 1) = 169 cycles, so interleaving speeds the fill up by about 5.8. High-order interleaving would put all 8 consecutive words in one bank and also give 169.

questions.stem: A CPU has a 16-bit byte address bus. Four 2K × 8 RAM chips share A10–A0. A 2-to-4 decoder takes A12 (high input) and A11, and it is enabled only when A15 = A14 = A13 = 0; output r drives the chip select of chip r. Which statements are correct?
options: The four chips together occupy 0000H to 1FFFH.
If A15–A13 were left out of the enable logic, every byte of chip 0 would answer at 8 different addresses.
questions.explanation: Each chip covers 2K = 800H bytes, and A12 A11 = r selects chip r, so chip r spans r × 800H to r × 800H + 7FFH: chip 3 is 1800H–1FFFH and the four chips fill 0000H–1FFFH. 2800H is 0010 1000 0000 0000 in binary: A13 = 1 disables the decoder, so no chip answers; reading only A12 A11 = 01 gives the wrong choice of chip 1. Ignoring the 3 bits A15–A13 is partial decoding: each byte answers for all 2³ = 8 values of those bits.

questions.stem: A write-through, no-write-allocate cache has a 10 ns access time and main memory a 100 ns access time; there is no write buffer. 80% of references are reads and 20% writes. Reads hit with ratio 0.9, and a read miss is served hierarchically (cache probed first, then memory). Every write updates main memory. What is the average access time in ns?
questions.explanation: Read time = 10 + 0.1 × 100 = 20 ns. Each write costs a memory write, 100 ns, hit or miss. Average = 0.8 × 20 + 0.2 × 100 = 16 + 20 = 36 ns. Charging writes only the cache time gives 18; treating reads as simultaneous gives 0.8 × (9 + 10) + 20 = 35.2.

questions.stem: A cache with a 5 ns access time and a main memory with an 80 ns access time are probed simultaneously, and a reference takes whichever answers. What hit ratio gives an average access time of 12.5 ns?
questions.explanation: Simultaneous access: 5h + 80(1 − h) = 12.5, so 80 − 75h = 12.5 and h = 67.5 ÷ 75 = 0.9. Under hierarchical access the equation would be 5 + 80(1 − h) = 12.5, giving h = 0.90625.

questions.stem: A cache has 64-byte lines. Main memory has a 32 ns latency and a peak bandwidth of 1 GB/s (take 1 GB = 10⁹ bytes). How long, in ns, does it take to fetch one line from memory?
questions.explanation: 1 GB/s moves 10⁹ bytes in 10⁹ ns, one byte per ns, so the 64 bytes stream in 64 ns after the 32 ns latency: 32 + 64 = 96 ns. Paying the latency per byte, or forgetting it, are the usual slips.

questions.stem: A two-level memory has an 8 MB fast level costing 4 units per byte and a 56 MB slow level costing 1 unit per byte. What is the average cost per byte of the whole memory?
questions.explanation: Average cost = total cost ÷ total capacity = (8 × 4 + 56 × 1) ÷ 64 = 88 ÷ 64 = 1.375. 2.5 is the plain mean of the two prices; 3.625 swaps the capacities; 1.0 ignores the fast level.

pitfalls.text: The index counts sets, not lines: a 1024-line 4-way cache has 256 sets and an 8-bit index.
AMAT weights the miss penalty by the miss rate; hit time + miss penalty is the cost of one miss, not the average.
Hierarchical and simultaneous access give different answers on the same data (6.0 ns vs 5.4 ns in the two-level example); check which one the question describes.
A global L2 miss rate must be divided by the L1 miss rate before it goes into t₁ + m₁(t₂ + m₂·t_mem).
Pair write policies correctly: write-back goes with write-allocate, write-through with no-write-allocate, and only write-back needs a dirty bit.
A TLB miss is not a page fault: the page may be in memory and only the page-table walk is needed.
Divide a byte address by the block size before taking it mod the number of sets; mapping raw addresses to lines is only right for 1-byte blocks.
In a write-through cache without a write buffer every write costs a memory access, even on a hit: with 20% writes and t_m = 100 ns, writes alone add 20 ns to the average.

revisionCard.heading: Address split
lines: offset = log₂ B
sets = lines ÷ k; index = log₂ sets (0 if fully associative)
tag = address bits − index − offset
tag directory = lines × (tag + valid + dirty + LRU bits)

revisionCard.heading: Access time
lines: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty
Hierarchical: t_c + (1 − h)t_m; simultaneous: h·t_c + (1 − h)t_m
Two levels: t₁ + m₁(t₂ + m₂·t_mem), m₂ local
Global L2 miss rate = m₁ × m₂
CPI = base + accesses/instr × miss rate × penalty
Write-through mix: f_r(t_c + (1 − h)t_m) + f_w·t_m
Line fill = latency + line size ÷ bandwidth; cost/bit = Σ cᵢSᵢ ÷ Σ Sᵢ

revisionCard.heading: Policies and misses
lines: Write-back + write-allocate; write-through + no-write-allocate
LRU, FIFO (Belady's anomaly), optimal = farthest next use
3 Cs: compulsory, capacity, conflict (none in fully associative)

revisionCard.heading: Interfacing and VM
lines: M × N from m × n chips: (M/m)(N/n) chips, log₂(M/m)-to-(M/m) decoder
Partial decoding with u free address bits: 2ᵘ aliases per word
Low-order bank = a mod m; high-order bank = ⌊a ÷ (W/m)⌋
TLB: EAT = h(t + m) + (1 − h)(t + 2m)

errata.claim: Q3: a 32-bit address with a 4-byte offset and an 8-bit index has a 20-bit tag.
errata.correction: The 20-bit tag needs a 4-bit offset (16-byte blocks). A 4-byte block would give a 2-bit offset and a 22-bit tag.

errata.claim: PYQ-3: with 4 frames on 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, LRU incurs 10 faults (FIFO also 10).
errata.correction: FIFO incurs 10 faults but LRU incurs 8: after the 4 cold faults, LRU faults only on 5, 3, 4 and 5.

errata.claim: PYQ-4: LRU with 4 frames on 1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 1, 2, 3, 7, 6, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 6 gives the classic count of 14 faults.
errata.correction: LRU with 4 frames gives 10 faults; 14 is the FIFO count for 4 frames.

errata.claim: PYQ-5: addresses 0, 4, 8, 12, 0, 4, 8 on a 4-line direct-mapped cache with 1-byte blocks give 6 misses and 1 hit.
errata.correction: All seven addresses map to line 0 and each evicts the previous block, so there are 7 misses and no hits.

references.title: Hennessy & Patterson — Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach

chapters.title: I/O Interface
chapters.summary: The I/O interface decides how data moves between peripherals and memory. Programmed I/O makes the CPU poll a status register; interrupt-driven I/O lets the device signal readiness so the CPU can do other work; DMA hands whole blocks to a controller that becomes bus master and interrupts the CPU only at the end. GATE asks the definitions (vectored vs polled, maskable vs NMI, burst vs cycle stealing, memory-mapped vs isolated I/O) and short numericals on CPU overhead and DMA bus acquisitions.
highYield: Fraction of CPU time lost to polling, interrupts or DMA: events per second × cost per event ÷ clock rate, usually a 2-mark NAT.
Minimum number of DMA bus acquisitions for a file, given the width of the data count register: ⌈file size ÷ 2^c units⌉.
DMA modes: burst stalls the CPU for the whole block, cycle stealing takes one bus cycle per word, transparent uses only cycles the CPU leaves free.
Vectored vs polled interrupts and maskable vs non-maskable interrupts: one-line definition questions.
Daisy-chain priority is fixed by physical position: the device nearest the arbiter or CPU wins.

topics.title: Three ways to move I/O data
points: Programmed I/O: the CPU issues the command, then loops reading the device status register until it reports ready, then moves each word itself.
Interrupt-driven I/O: the CPU issues the command and continues other work; the device raises an interrupt when it is ready and an ISR moves the word.
DMA: a DMA controller moves a whole block between device and memory without the CPU; the CPU only programs the transfer and services one completion interrupt.
CPU involvement falls from every poll, to every word, to once per block, which is why DMA suits high-bandwidth devices such as disks and network adapters.

lesson.why: Almost every I/O question in the chapter assumes you know which of the three techniques is in use and who does the work per word. Naming the technique correctly settles half the question.
lesson.intro: A device holds data that must end up in memory. The first technique has the CPU ask the device again and again whether it has a word ready, then copy the word itself; this is programmed I/O. The second lets the CPU do other work and has the device send a signal, an interrupt, when a word is ready; a small routine then copies the word. The third gives the job to a separate helper circuit, the DMA controller (direct memory access), which copies a whole block between device and memory and tells the CPU only when the block is done.

definitions.meaning: The CPU commands the device, waits in a loop on its status, and moves every word itself.
A circuit that moves a block between a device and memory on its own after the CPU programs it.

principle.text: The techniques differ in how often the CPU is involved for a block of $n$ words: programmed I/O involves it at least $n$ times (every word, plus every poll), interrupt-driven I/O $n$ times (one interrupt per word), and DMA a small constant number of times, one setup and one completion interrupt, independent of $n$.
principle.tex: \text{CPU events per block:}\quad \text{polling} \ge n,\qquad \text{interrupts} = n,\qquad \text{DMA} = O(1)

lesson.limits: For a slow device that sends a few words per second, the setup cost of DMA is not worth paying and the simpler techniques are fine. DMA also needs the bus: while the controller transfers, the CPU may be delayed.

example.problem: A disk block of 4096 bytes is read into memory over a bus with 4-byte words. Count how many times the CPU must handle a word or an interrupt under interrupt-driven I/O and under DMA.
steps: Words in the block: $4096 / 4 = 1024$.
Interrupt-driven I/O raises one interrupt per word, so the CPU runs the ISR 1024 times.
DMA needs one setup by the CPU and one completion interrupt, so 2 CPU events in total.
example.result: 1024 ISR runs with interrupts against 2 CPU events with DMA.

misconceptions: Interrupt-driven I/O is not the same as DMA: with interrupts the CPU still copies every word inside the ISR, only the waiting has gone.
DMA does not mean the CPU is never involved; it programs the transfer and takes the completion interrupt.

recall.q: Who copies each word in programmed I/O and in interrupt-driven I/O?
recall.a: The CPU, in both. They differ only in whether it busy-waits or is told by an interrupt.

recall.q: How many times is the CPU involved in a DMA block transfer?
recall.a: Twice in the simple case: once to program the controller and once for the completion interrupt.

recall.q: Which devices is DMA aimed at?
recall.a: High-bandwidth devices such as disks and network adapters.

practice.stem: A 16 KB block ($16 \times 1024$ bytes) is read with 4-byte words using interrupt-driven I/O, one interrupt per word. How many interrupts occur for the block?
practice.explanation: Words = $16 \times 1024 / 4 = 4096$, one interrupt each. Answering 1 tempts because DMA raises a single interrupt per block, but that is DMA, not per-word interrupts; answering 16384 comes from counting bytes instead of words.

lesson.summary: Polling and interrupts make the CPU handle every word; DMA hands over the block and costs the CPU a fixed setup plus one completion interrupt, which is why it suits fast devices.

topics.title: The device interface: data, status and control registers
points: Each device controller exposes a data register (the word being moved), a status register (ready, busy, error bits) and a control register (command, interrupt-enable bit).
The CPU never drives the device directly: it reads and writes these registers, either through memory addresses or through I/O ports.
The controller buffers data and converts between the bus protocol and the device's own signalling and speed, so slow devices do not hold the bus.

lesson.why: Polling and interrupt questions talk about status flags, control bits and the data buffer. Knowing what each register is for tells you which one the CPU reads and which one it writes.
lesson.intro: A device is not wired to the CPU directly. A small circuit called the device controller sits between them and shows the CPU a few registers, which are tiny storage cells with addresses. One holds the data being moved, one holds the device's condition, and one accepts commands. The CPU does all its I/O by reading and writing these registers. The controller also buffers the data, so a slow device does not tie up the bus.

definitions.meaning: Read by the CPU; its bits tell whether the device is ready, busy or in error.
Written by the CPU; its bits carry the command and the interrupt-enable setting.
Holds the word currently being moved between the device and the CPU.

principle.text: Data register: the word. Status register: the CPU reads it to learn the device state. Control register: the CPU writes it to give a command or enable interrupts. A status flag is tested by masking: AND the status value with a mask that has a 1 only in the flag position.

lesson.limits: The exact bit positions differ from device to device, so a question must state them. Some controllers combine status and control in one register or add more registers.

example.problem: A status register uses bit 0 as ready, bit 1 as error and bit 2 as busy. The CPU reads the value 0110 in binary. Is the device ready, and is there an error?
steps: Test ready with the mask 001: $0110 \mathrm{AND} 001 = 000$, so bit 0 is clear and the device is not ready.
Test error with the mask 010: $0110 \mathrm{AND} 010 = 010$, which is nonzero, so the error flag is set.
Bit 2 is also set, so the device is busy.
example.result: Not ready, error flag set, device busy.

misconceptions: The CPU does not write the status register to give a command; commands go to the control register, and the status register only reports.
A controller is not just a wire: it buffers data and converts between the bus protocol and the device's own speed.

recall.q: Which register does a polling loop read?
recall.a: The status register, testing the ready flag.

recall.q: Where does the interrupt-enable bit live?
recall.a: In the control register, written by the CPU.

recall.q: Why does a controller buffer data?
recall.a: So slow devices do not hold the bus and the bus and device speeds can differ.

practice.stem: A driver wants to start a transfer and turn on interrupts for the device. Which register does it write?
practice.explanation: Commands and the interrupt-enable bit are control bits, so the driver writes the control register. The status register tempts because it also holds flags, but it is read by the CPU to learn the device state, not written to command it.

lesson.summary: Data register carries the word, status register reports the device state to the CPU, control register takes commands and the interrupt enable; the controller sits between bus and device and buffers.

topics.title: Programmed I/O and polling cost
points: The CPU busy-waits: while it tests the status flag it does no useful work, so a slow device wastes almost all CPU time between words.
Polling cost per second = polls per second × cycles per poll; divide by the clock rate for the fraction of CPU time lost.
Example: a disk delivering 4×10⁶ bytes/s in 16-byte units needs 250,000 polls/s; at 400 cycles per poll on a 500 MHz CPU that is 10⁸ cycles, 20% of the CPU.
Polling is acceptable only for slow-rate devices polled rarely (a mouse at 30 polls/s) or in simple embedded loops where the CPU has nothing else to do.

lesson.why: Polling cost is a standard calculation: how much of the CPU is burned waiting for a device. It also explains why interrupts and DMA exist.
lesson.intro: In programmed I/O the CPU repeatedly reads the device status register and checks the ready flag. This repeated check is called polling, and the CPU doing nothing else meanwhile is called busy waiting. The device sets the pace: if it produces a chunk of data every so often, the CPU must check at least that often or data is lost. Each check takes some CPU cycles, so the checks add up to a share of the CPU's time.

definitions.meaning: Reading the device status repeatedly to find out whether it is ready.
Looping on a test while doing no useful work.

principle.text: The poll rate is the data rate divided by the bytes taken per poll. The CPU fraction lost is polls per second times cycles per poll, divided by the clock rate.

lesson.limits: This counts only the polling cycles. If the CPU has nothing else to do, as in a small embedded loop, the lost time costs nothing, and a very slow device polled rarely loses almost nothing.

example.problem: A device delivers 2,000,000 bytes per second in 8-byte units. One poll takes 200 cycles on a 1 GHz CPU. What fraction of the CPU does polling use?
steps: Cycles per second spent polling = $250{,}000 \times 200 = 5 \times 10^{7}$.
Divide by the clock rate: $5 \times 10^{7} / 10^{9} = 0.05$.
example.result: 5 percent of the CPU.

misconceptions: The poll rate is not the CPU clock rate; it is set by how fast the device produces data. Polling slower than that loses data.
Dividing by the bytes per second without the unit size overstates the polls; each poll collects one whole unit.

recall.q: What is busy waiting?
recall.a: The CPU loops on a status test and does no useful work until the device is ready.

recall.q: How is the number of polls per second found?
recall.a: Divide the device data rate by the bytes moved per poll.

recall.q: When is polling acceptable?
recall.a: For slow devices polled rarely, or in simple embedded loops where the CPU has nothing else to do.

practice.stem: A device delivers 1,000,000 bytes per second in 4-byte units. Each poll costs 80 cycles on a 500 MHz CPU. What percentage of the CPU is spent polling?
practice.explanation: Polls per second = $10^6 / 4 = 250{,}000$; cycles = $250{,}000 \times 80 = 2 \times 10^{7}$; divided by $5 \times 10^{8}$ gives 0.04, which is 4 percent. Using 10^6 polls per second (one per byte) tempts and gives 16 percent.

lesson.summary: Polling wastes CPU time in proportion to polls per second times cycles per poll; compute polls as rate over unit size, then divide by the clock rate.

topics.title: Interrupt-driven I/O: the service sequence
points: The CPU samples the interrupt request line at the end of each instruction cycle, so it always finishes the current instruction before responding.
On an accepted interrupt the hardware saves at least the PC and status word, disables further maskable interrupts and acknowledges the device.
The ISR address comes from the interrupt vector table, indexed by the vector number; the ISR saves any registers it uses, moves the data and clears the request.
A return-from-interrupt instruction restores the PC and status word, and the interrupted program resumes as if nothing happened.
Each word still costs one interrupt, so for a device delivering R words/s with ISR overhead O seconds per word the CPU loses a fraction R × O.

The CPU can keep up only while R × O ≤ 1, so the fastest device interrupt I/O can serve is R_max = 1/O: a 3 µs overhead caps it at about 333,333 interrupts per second, and any faster device needs DMA.

lesson.why: Questions ask for the order of events when a device interrupts, and for how much CPU time interrupts consume. Both follow from one fixed service sequence.
lesson.intro: In interrupt-driven I/O the CPU does other work and the device raises a signal when it is ready. The CPU does not stop mid-instruction. It finishes the instruction it is on, remembers where it was by saving the program counter (the address of the next instruction), and jumps to a small routine written for that device, called the interrupt service routine (ISR). When the routine ends, the saved state is restored and the program carries on.

definitions.meaning: The interrupt service routine: the short program that serves one device's request.
A number sent by the device or hardware that selects the ISR address from a table.

principle.text: Service order: finish the current instruction, save the return state, load the program counter with the ISR address, run the ISR, restore the state. If a device sends one interrupt per word at rate $R$ words per second and each costs $O$ seconds, the CPU loses a fraction $R \times O$ of its time.

lesson.limits: The fraction formula counts only the ISR overhead per event and assumes one interrupt per word. A device that interrupts once per block, as under DMA, pays the cost per block instead.

example.problem: A device delivers 20,000 words per second and each interrupt costs 15 microseconds of ISR overhead. What fraction of the CPU is lost, and what is the fastest rate this overhead allows?
steps: Convert the overhead to seconds: 15 microseconds is $15 \times 10^{-6}$ s.
Fraction lost = $20{,}000 \times 15 \times 10^{-6} = 0.3$, so 30 percent of the CPU.
The limit is reached when the fraction is 1: $R_{\max} = 1 / (15 \times 10^{-6}) \approx 66{,}667$ words per second.
example.result: 30 percent of the CPU is used; the ceiling is about 66,667 interrupts per second.

misconceptions: The CPU does not respond the instant the signal rises; it samples the request only at the end of the instruction cycle and finishes the current instruction first.
Saving the program counter must come before loading the ISR address; loading first overwrites the return address and the program can never resume.

recall.q: When does the CPU act on an interrupt request?
recall.a: At the end of the current instruction, never in the middle of it.

recall.q: Why is the program counter saved before the ISR address is loaded?
recall.a: Loading the ISR address overwrites the counter, so the return address would be lost.

recall.q: What does a device interrupting once per word cost the CPU per second?
recall.a: The rate in words per second times the ISR overhead per word.

practice.stem: A device delivers 40,000 words per second and each word causes one interrupt costing 5 microseconds. What percentage of the CPU time goes to interrupt handling?
practice.explanation: Fraction lost = $40{,}000 \times 5 \times 10^{-6} = 0.2$, which is 20 percent. A common slip is to forget the microsecond conversion and report 200,000; another is to give 0.2 without turning it into a percentage.

lesson.summary: Finish the instruction, save the state, jump to the ISR, run it, restore. Per-word interrupts cost rate times overhead, so rate can never exceed one over the overhead.

topics.title: Maskable vs non-maskable, vectored vs polled
points: A maskable interrupt can be disabled by software through the interrupt-enable flag or a mask register; ordinary device interrupts are maskable.
A non-maskable interrupt (NMI) cannot be disabled by software and is reserved for critical events such as power failure or memory parity errors.
Vectored: the interrupting device supplies a vector (an ISR address or an index into the vector table) during acknowledge, so the CPU branches straight to its ISR.
Polled (non-vectored): all devices share one generic handler that reads each device's status in turn; response time grows with the number of devices checked before the source.

By source: external hardware interrupts arrive asynchronously from devices; exceptions (divide by zero, page fault, illegal opcode) are raised by the instruction itself; software interrupts (INT, system-call traps) are executed on purpose, so the last two are synchronous.

An external interrupt waits for the instruction to finish, but a fault such as a page fault is taken in the middle of the instruction, which is then restarted from the beginning once the handler returns.

lesson.why: Interrupt classification questions are frequent and are answered by matching a definition to a property. The vocabulary below is the whole syllabus for them.
lesson.intro: An interrupt makes the CPU leave its program and run a handler. Interrupts differ along three lines. Can software switch them off? A maskable interrupt can be disabled, a non-maskable one cannot. How is the handler found? A vectored interrupt brings an address or table index with it, while a polled one sends the CPU to one common routine that asks each device in turn. Where does it come from? From an outside device at any moment, or from the running instruction itself, such as a divide by zero or a system call.

definitions.meaning: An interrupt that software can block with the interrupt-enable flag or a mask register.
A non-maskable interrupt, reserved for critical events such as power failure or memory parity error.
The ISR address, or an index into the vector table, supplied by the device during acknowledge.

principle.text: Maskable versus NMI: whether software can disable it. Vectored versus polled: whether the device supplies the ISR address or the CPU must query devices one by one. By source: external interrupts are asynchronous, while exceptions and software interrupts are synchronous because the instruction causes them.

lesson.limits: The three classifications are independent of each other, so an interrupt is described by one choice from each. A fault taken mid-instruction, such as a page fault, restarts the instruction; an external interrupt waits for the instruction to finish.

example.problem: Classify a keyboard key press, a page fault and a power failure. Then, with a polled scheme that checks 4 devices in order at 10 cycles per check, how long does it take to find that device 3 is the source?
steps: A key press is a maskable external interrupt, asynchronous; a power failure is a non-maskable external interrupt, because it is critical.
A page fault is an exception raised by the instruction itself, so it is synchronous, and the instruction restarts after the handler.
Polled scheme: devices 1, 2 and 3 are checked before device 3 is found, so $3 \times 10 = 30$ cycles.
example.result: Key press: maskable and external. Page fault: exception, synchronous. Power failure: non-maskable. Identification takes 30 cycles.

misconceptions: A software interrupt (INT, system call) is not asynchronous; the program executes it on purpose, so it is synchronous.
In the polled scheme the response time depends on the device position in the checking order; a vectored scheme jumps straight to the ISR.

recall.q: What can software do to a maskable interrupt that it cannot do to an NMI?
recall.a: Disable it through the interrupt-enable flag or a mask register.

recall.q: What does a vectored interrupt supply?
recall.a: The ISR address, or an index into the vector table, so the CPU branches directly.

recall.q: Which interrupt sources are synchronous?
recall.a: Exceptions and software interrupts, because the running instruction raises them.

recall.q: What happens to an instruction that raised a page fault?
recall.a: It is restarted from the beginning after the handler returns.

practice.stem: Which of these events is the best example of an interrupt that software cannot disable?
practice.explanation: Power failure is a critical event handled as a non-maskable interrupt. The other three are ordinary device interrupts, which are maskable; the timer tick tempts because it is hardware-generated, but being hardware-generated does not make an interrupt non-maskable.

lesson.summary: Classify an interrupt by maskability, by how the ISR is found (vectored or polled) and by source (external asynchronous, or exception and software synchronous).

topics.title: Priority among interrupting devices
points: Daisy chain (serial): the acknowledge signal passes from device to device; the first requesting device in the chain keeps it and places its vector, so priority equals physical position.
Daisy chaining needs few wires and scales easily, but priority is fixed and a far-end device can starve under heavy load.
Parallel scheme: each device has its own request line into a priority encoder, whose output is the vector of the highest-priority active request; a mask register can block chosen levels.
With nesting enabled, an ISR can be interrupted only by a request of higher priority; equal or lower requests wait until it returns.

lesson.why: Statements about daisy chains, vectored interrupts and nesting recur in the exam, and each is decided by who answers the CPU first.
lesson.intro: Several devices can ask for service together, so the CPU needs a rule for who goes first. In a daisy chain the devices sit on one wire in a line. The CPU sends an acknowledge signal into the line, and the first device that is requesting keeps it and sends its identity; devices behind it never see the signal. In a parallel scheme each device has its own request line, and a circuit called a priority encoder picks the highest active one.

analogy.text: A daisy chain is a queue at a counter where the person nearest the front is always served first.
analogy.breaksWhen: Nobody in a real queue is blocked forever by newcomers, but a far device in a busy chain can starve because nearer devices keep winning.
